en: Preface to the Abridged Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sūtra:
The Buddha, in preaching his various sūtras, employed manifold metaphors; yet all were intended solely to elucidate the fundamental source, the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*).
Now, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* consists of one hundred and twelve fascicles, divided into sixty-two chapters. This particular chapter corresponds to the Ground of the Bodhisattva’s Mind.
It is further divided into upper and lower sections. The upper section exclusively elucidates the stages of cultivation and realization for the Three Sages and Ten Saints.
The lower section specifically clarifies the Threefold Pure Precepts, which serve to complete the Bodhisattva’s six perfections and myriad practices;

these are indeed the foundation of meditative concentration and wisdom, and the path traversed by the Three Sages and Ten Saints. Formerly, the Tiantai Master Zhiyi composed a commentary on its meaning. By...
Clarifying its essential tenets and marking its general outline, Master Yunqi further annotated the *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden) to reveal what had not yet been revealed by Tiantai.
Now, the Venerable Dingshu has compiled and organized this *Lueshu* (Brief Commentary), further supplementing those points left incomplete in the *Fayi*.
Like pearls reflecting one another, the sequence is brilliantly radiant, enabling those who behold it to clarify the underlying principles through each specific matter. Following...

By investigating the principle, one attains the essential meaning; by penetrating the meaning, one naturally ceases to be deluded regarding the fundamental source. By examining phenomena, one naturally becomes diligent in upholding the precepts.
Once the significance of the Brahmajāla Sūtra is clarified, it will be evident that the ground of our own minds has never been different from that of the All-Illuminating Vairocana.
However, the fragmentation of later students has persisted for a long time, ever since the separation between Chan and Vinaya. Once separated, [the truth became obscured].
To be bifurcated leads to injury on both sides. When the ancients studied the Way, they necessarily proceeded through gradual practice until they reached thorough enlightenment;
there was never a distinction of priority or sequence. This is because essence is not separate from function, and function is not separate from essence; essence and function are mutually integrated.

Thus, the Sūtras are the Buddha’s words, the Vinaya is the Buddha’s conduct, and Chan is the Buddha’s mind—so how could there be a division between Chan and Vinaya? Indeed, the four seasons have their cold...
The seasonal movements of the sun and moon are the laws of Heaven’s operation. If even Heaven does not violate these, how can humans do so?

To move, pause, turn, or stop without losing one's rectitude is the law of humanity; to maintain and practice this is what is called "precept" (*śīla*). Yet, names arise from their underlying meanings.
Those who are ignorant of the Way cling to the names alone, thereby becoming like those who sit waiting by a stump, mired in stagnation. I [have been] thus since my youth.

This year I took refuge in the Buddha Vehicle. While awaiting my punishment in the eastern provinces, I was able to hear that the Venerable Master Dinghu’s observance of the precepts is most rigorous and his understanding of the doctrinal teachings profound;
I have long been devoted to him in both thought and aspiration. Recently, having read the sutras and vinaya commentaries annotated by the Master, my worldly anxieties have suddenly vanished.

He was called Xinjinxi (Cessation of Mental Exhaustion). Therefore, I received from him the Eight Precepts of the Upavāsa fast. As for the Master’s spiritual practice, I truly could not fathom its loftiness or depth;
yet in his teaching of others, whenever he spoke of the Sūtras and Vinaya, he invariably included Chan, and whenever he spoke of Chan, he invariably included the Sūtras and Vinaya.
I have observed that those who study Chan today often neglect the Sūtras and Vinaya, much like the Confucians...
These individuals merely discourse upon the meanings of the scriptures without engaging in personal practice. The rise and fall of the world’s fortunes are met with corresponding human affairs;

this is likewise brought about by the force of destiny and the cycles of qi. The Master, out of profound compassion and earnest concern, contemplates emulating the conduct of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of antiquity.
He exhorted all later students and sought to turn back the declining winds of the final age. Whenever I recite his work, I cannot help but feel boundless admiration and veneration.
Now that this commentary on the sutra has been divided into sections and explained in detail, it causes the single pearl of the Brahmajāla Sūtra to illuminate all other pearls.
I am about to return to the capital. Therefore, I have composed this preface and returned [the manuscript] to you.
Written on a summer day in the Jiwei year of the Kangxi era by Sun Tingduo, disciple under the eightfold precepts and Magistrate of Nan’en.

A Brief Commentary on the Structural Outline (Concluded) The Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground Chapter, Part Two, of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha Volume One of the Brief Commentary Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty (Note: The provided text contains only the title and bibliographic information for the first volume of a commentary; it does not include the actual exegesis.)
Composed by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Baoliang Forest, Guangzhou.
Now, this sutra is explained. The major outline is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the scriptural text.
First, the explanation of the title (divided into two parts): First, the direct explanation of the scriptural title; second, the explanation of the names of the translators.
◎ First, the direct explanation of the scriptural title:
*The Buddha-Spoken Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
"Spoken by the Buddha" means that it was personally proclaimed by Śākyamuni after [the teaching of] Samantabhadra.
"Brahmajāla" refers to the time when the Buddha was in the palace of Mahesvara, the Great Brahmā Heavenly King;
he spoke while observing the Indra-net banners atop that celestial palace. Those net-banners were composed of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of *maṇi* jewels.
It was thus formed. Yet the light and color of each individual jewel were distinct and different from one another; they reflected one another and mutually encompassed one another.
Consequently, every single jewel contained the colors of all the other jewels. Their patterns and textures were layered upon one another without any mutual obstruction.
Because of this, the Buddha used it as a metaphor to explain that immeasurable worlds are like the mesh of a net, with each individual world being likewise.

Each is distinct. The Buddha’s teaching methods are likewise so. By this principle, it is demonstrated that the establishments of the worlds throughout the ten directions are each immeasurable and different.
The teaching methods established by the Buddhas of the ten directions are also immeasurable and not the same.
The practices, realizations, and attainments of the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions who rely on these teachings are likewise infinitely varied.

Each is distinct. Therefore, the *Brahmajāla* (Net of Brahmā) is used as a metaphor for the title of this scripture. This great original version of the sutra consists of one hundred and twelve fascicles;
it is like a single mesh of that net. The present "Chapter on the Mind-Ground" (*Cittabhūmi*) is merely like a single pearl within that net.
Regarding the term *sūtra*: the Sanskrit word is *sūtra*, which here is translated as "Sutra of Accordance" (*qijing*). "Accordance" (*qi*) means that it accords with the [truth] above...
The principle of the Buddha accords with the capacities of sentient beings below. "Sūtra" (sūtra) means to penetrate and to gather and transform.

It penetrates the meanings that ought to be known and gathers and sustains the sentient beings to be transformed. Furthermore, it is said that "sūtra" means "constant. Although past and present differ, the path of awakening does not change;
it cannot be thwarted by the various heretics, nor can it be altered by the multitude of sages. Therefore, it is called "constant."

Furthermore, according to various sūtras and vinayas, some are titled by means of a person and a dharma; some are designated by means of a dharma and a metaphor; some are titled by means of a person, a dharma, and a metaphor;
and some are designated by a single person, a single dharma, or a single metaphor. This present sutra is titled by means of a metaphor.
If one considers it together with its chapters, however, it is designated by means of a person, a dharma, and a metaphor: "Brahmajāla" (The Brahma’s Net) is the metaphor.
The Bodhisattva is the person; the mind-ground is the Dharma; the sutra is the teaching that expresses it; the Brahma Net is the Dharma expressed;
and the Buddha is the person who expresses it. If one discusses its fundamental tenet, essence and function, doctrinal characteristics, and what is subsumed under the provisional and the real:
the primary tenet is the true precepts of the source mind-ground; the ultimate goal is the realization of the fruit of the Samantabhadra Buddha.
Its essence is the mind-ground of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Its function is the cessation of evil and the practice of good. Its doctrinal aspect is the Mahāyāna Vinaya.
Among the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*), it is subsumed within the Vinaya Piṭaka; among the two collections of the Great and Small Vehicles, it is subsumed within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka;

and among the provisional and ultimate teachings, it is subsumed by both the provisional and the ultimate. The *Ābharaṇa-sūtra* states: "The precepts of all ordinary beings are entirely based upon the mind."
It takes this as its essence. Because the mind is inexhaustible, the precepts are also inexhaustible; therefore, it takes the ground of the mind of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as its essence.

(Regarding "essence" [*zong*]: it means "veneration," referring to that which is held in highest esteem by this sutra. Regarding "destination" [*qu*]: it is the ultimate point to which the essence returns. *Indra*: here it is called "Heavenly Emperor" or "Red Jewel.
Taken together, it refers generally to the Red Jewel Net Banner of the Great Brahmā King.)
Bodhisattva, Earth-Mind Chapter, Part Two.
In Sanskrit, the term is fully *bodhisattva*. *Bodhi* here means "path" (*mārga*) or "awakening" (*bodha*).
*Sattva* here means "sentient being" (*sattva*). This refers to one who transforms all sentient beings through the Buddha-path. It is also called "Awakened Sentient Being" (*bodhisattva*).
"Bodhisattva" has the meaning of "one who can awaken. "Sattva" has the meaning of "sentient being," signifying one who can cause all sentient beings to attain awakening.
Furthermore, because they seek the supreme above and transform those below, establishing great undertakings, they are called "Mahāsattvas" (Great Beings).

They are also called "Kais" (Opening Beings), signifying that they are able to open and transform all sentient beings. From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment until the final stage of Equal Enlightenment, [they...]
They are called Bodhisattvas. As for the "ground of mind," it is the fundamental source of all sages and ordinary beings.

When among ordinary beings, they are deluded regarding this mind, and thus they wander through the three realms, the six paths, and the four modes of birth. When among sages, they awaken to this mind.
Furthermore, it returns one to the fundamental source and cuts off the vast flow of birth and death.
Because Bodhisattvas wish to return to this source, they rely upon these correct precepts of the mind-ground as the supreme cause to realize the ultimate fruit of Samantabhadra.
"Ground" (di) is named metaphorically; it signifies that Bodhisattvas practice the six perfections and myriad deeds to teach, transform, and support all beings.
Toward sentient beings, neither hatred nor attachment arises. Through this, extraordinary causes and sublime fruits increase and flourish.

It is like the great earth, which bears and supports all things without disdain for the pure or the defiled; all things grow and develop because of it. The equanimity of the Bodhisattva’s mind is likewise so.
In the Sanskrit language, this is called *parivarta*; here it is translated as "chapter" (*pin*). A "chapter" refers to a collection.

This means that categories of meaning follow one another and are collectively gathered into a single cluster. According to the separate chapters of the original scripture, those sections still discuss the world at large;
this present chapter, however, emphasizes the cultivation of the teaching and clarifies the fundamental mind-ground. Furthermore, it is divided into upper and lower parts:
the upper part clarifies how Bodhisattvas, by the power of concentration and wisdom, cultivate and realize the stages of the Three Sages and Ten Stages. Now, as for this lower part:
It is specifically commanded that Great Beings rely upon the precepts of the Original Source Mind-Ground as the direct cause for concentration and wisdom;
therefore, from those of the Three Sages and Ten Sages up to the Stage of Equal Enlightenment, all are required to recite and uphold them.
II. Explanation of the Translator’s Name.
Translated by Kumārajīva, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Yao-Qin [Dynasty].
"Yao" is his surname; "Qin" is the name of the state. He was the sovereign of the Later Qin, surnamed Yao and named Xing. "Tripiṭaka" (Sanskrit: *tripiṭaka*)...
This refers to the Dharma Master, who was skilled in translating the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka—Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. Kumārajīva means "Child-Life" (Tóngshòu) in Chinese;
this indicates that even when the Dharma Master was at the age of childhood, his discernment and wisdom already surpassed those of the elderly.
His father was a man from India, renowned for his intelligence and wisdom. When the King of Kucha heard of him, he subsequently gave him his daughter in marriage.
From the day the Master was conceived, his mother’s own discernment and wisdom increased. At the age of seven, he left the household life;

by daily reciting a thousand verses, at nine years of age he debated with non-Buddhists, refuting their heterodox arguments and blunting their sharp points. The kings of India all honored and revered him as their teacher. [At that time,] Fu Jian...
Hearing that the Master’s virtue and character were extraordinary, he dispatched General Lü Guang with an army of seventy thousand to invade Kucha and invite the Master.
However, before the Master had even reached the halfway point, Yao Xing succeeded to the throne of Qin and welcomed him back to the kingdom.

It was not until the third year of Hongshi that he finally entered Chang’an. Emperor Yao Xing treated him with great courtesy and honor, inviting him to reside in the Ximing Pavilion and the Xiaoyao Garden.
He was accommodated in a separate hall and commanded to translate over fifty treatises and sūtras. This *Brahmajāla-sūtra* was the very last of these to be translated.

At that time, eight hundred wise śramaṇas consulted and received the Master’s teachings; together with three hundred śramaṇas of sharp intellect who had resolved upon the Great Vehicle, he conferred the Bodhisattva precepts.
This was the first instance of receiving the Bodhisattva precepts in the Eastern Land (China).
This is the beginning of the precepts. Tianren Luguan Chang replied to Vinaya Master Xuan, saying: "Master Shi’s rank is that of the Three Worthies (Tri-piṭaka).
Since the time of the Seven Buddhas, he has served as a master of scriptural translation.
'Translation' means to transpose those Sanskrit words from the Western Heavens into the Chinese language of this Eastern Land."
◎ Second, the explanation of the scriptural text (divided into three parts): First, the introductory section; second, the main body; third, the dissemination section.
According to various sutras, all are complete with these three divisions of introduction, main body, and dissemination. This "Chapter on the Mind-Ground" is extracted from the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
The original version of the *Brahmajāla* contains sixty-two chapters; this "Chapter on the Mind-Ground" corresponds to the tenth chapter therein. Therefore...

This scripture lacks the general introduction (sūtra-pūrva-nidāna) such as "Thus have I heard," and possesses only a specific introduction (viśeṣa-nidāna), as in the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, where each chapter begins with the words "At that time.
This present work is likewise so; thus, it comprises both the main teaching (bhūtārtha) and the dissemination (pravartana).
This also clarifies the nature, characteristics, phenomena, and principle of this single chapter; it is not the primary teaching or the dissemination section for the entire [Avataṃsaka Sūtra].
Therefore, the *Huayan jing shuchao* states: "When sages establish their teachings, there must be a gradual progression. When they are about to transmit the subtle words..."
First, the origins and causes are manifested. Once the origins and causes are manifested, those whose capacities are suited receive the Dharma; therefore, he bestows upon them the True Teaching.

Once the True Teaching has been set forth, the aim is to provide liberation and salvation; not only does it strengthen those present at this assembly, but it also ensures that its fragrance is transmitted to future generations.
May the lamp of the Dharma shine forever, its brilliance inexhaustible; therefore, it is entrusted for circulation.

This applies not only to this single section, but all chapters and sections alike are included herein. Now, in this commentary, I shall list only the major headings (*mahā-vibhāga*) and omit the sub-headings (*avāntara-vibhāga*), fearing that beginners might find them difficult and thus further increase their confusion. As for the other subtle and profound principles, they are as follows:
The stages of the Bodhisattva are fully recorded in the *Yishu* (Commentary on Meaning) and the *Fayi* (Unveiling the Hidden); one should consult them for oneself.

Regarding the division of the explanation of the sūtra into the Introduction (*nidāna*), the Main Body (*śarīra*), and the Circulation (*parivarta*): this practice first began with the Dharma Master Dao’an of the Jin dynasty. Subsequently, when the commentaries and exegeses of various Bodhisattvas from the Western Regions arrived, they all likewise divided [the sūtras] into these three parts. Only then did we realize that the Jin followed the Western exegesis; indeed, this is a constant rule that has remained unchanged through antiquity and the present.

"Introduction" (*xu*) means to introduce or narrate; it is also a "thread" (*xu*) and a "cause" (*zhi*). It refers to the causal basis of a single sūtra, which is both general and specific. As for the general introduction, as is the case at the beginning of all sūtras, there are always phrases such as: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was in a certain place, together with a great assembly..."

The "General Preface" (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*) refers to the assembly of the audience. The "Specific Preface" (*asādhāraṇa-nidāna*) refers to the fact that each discourse has its own distinct causal origin; thus, the specific preface provides the introductory context for a single sutra or a single chapter. The "Main Body" (*mūla-prakaraṇa*): "Zong" (宗) means primary or principal.

It signifies that when the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he invariably honors the meaning spoken for the sake of the specific occasion as the primary subject; this constitutes the central tenet of a sutra. The "Circulation" (*paryavasāna*): "Liu" (流) means not stagnating; "tong" (通) means not being obstructed.

Since the correct meaning has been set forth, it must be transmitted to future generations to benefit sentient beings, so that the source of the True Dharma may circulate without obstruction, spreading throughout the ten directions without end.
● First, the Introductory Section (divided into five parts): 1. The three Buddhas transmit the teaching; 2. Two Buddhas preach the Dharma;
3. One Buddha preaches the Dharma; 4. Verses in reiteration; 5. Narration of the establishment of the precepts.
I. The Transmission of the Teachings of the Three Buddhas (divided into three parts): 1. General Exhortation; 2. Specific Exhortation; 3.
Offering to the Principal Deity.
I. General Exhortation.
Regarding the three Buddhas: Vairocana, the Buddha upon the Thousand-Petaled Lotus, and the thousand, hundred, and ten billion Śākyamunis.

Śākyamuni transmits from the Thousand Buddhas; the Thousand Buddhas transmit from Vairocana; and Vairocana transmits from the Primordial Buddha. Nevertheless, all Buddhas possess the three bodies (*trikāya*):
that is to say, Vairocana is the pervasive radiance whose body is the True Dharma (*saddharma*), while Vairocana [as the response-body] is the perfection of practice.
The retributive fruit constitutes the body [of Śākyamuni]. The manifested traces of Śākyamuni constitute his body in response to the needs of sentient beings.

The Dharma-body is without form; it is perfectly luminous and shines universally throughout the ten directions. Vairocana possesses all ten thousand virtues, with eighty-four thousand marks and signs adorning his body.
The golden body of Śākyamuni is sixteen feet tall; he is endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs. In the Sanskrit language, this is called Vairocana.
This is called "pervading all places" and "the universal illumination of light. First, the light of the physical body illuminates the entirety of the dharma-realm as far as space extends.
Second, the light of wisdom illuminates the multilayered dharma-realms. It is also called "Mahāvairocana" (Great Sun).

Just as the sun in the world illuminates only one side while leaving another side in darkness, shines by day but not by night, and illuminates only one world while leaving other worlds in shadow; [the Buddha] is not like this.
The *dhātu* cannot be called "Mahāvairocana. Now, as for Vairocana, his *rūpakāya* and *dharmakāya* pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*, illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions.
A verse from the *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa-sūtra* says: "The *dharmakāya* body pervades all sentient beings;
Myriad virtues are凝然 (*niṣkampa*) and its nature is eternally abiding. Unborn and undying, without coming or going, Neither one nor [many]..."
It is distinct from, yet neither severed nor eternal. The *dharmadhātu* is all-pervading like space; it is that which all Tathāgatas have collectively cultivated and realized.
All conditioned and unconditioned merits rely upon the *dharmakāya*, which is eternally pure. The intrinsic nature of the *dharmakāya* is like space;

it is far removed from the six sense objects and remains unstained. The *dharmakāya* is formless and transcends all characteristics, being devoid of both the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*).
All are entirely empty. Thus, the wondrous Dharma-body of all Buddhas is the cessation of conceptual proliferation and verbal designations;

it is far removed from all discrimination, the sphere of mental activity is extinguished, and its essence is identical to Suchness (*tathatā*). This is for the purpose of cultivating and realizing the body of the Tathāgata.

The Bodhisattva skillfully cultivates the ten thousand practices; though the Dharma-body is without marks, it relies upon the two bodies of recompense and transformation. Thus, the *Cittaviveka-śāstra* states: "The first body serves as the support for the latter two."

At that time, Vairocana Buddha, for the sake of this great assembly, briefly opened up the "Earthly Ground" (*bhūmi*) within the Dharma-gates of the hundred thousand Ganges-sands of ineffable teachings, as much as the tip of a hair.
"At that time" refers to the time when Vairocana Buddha preached the Dharma. In Sanskrit, "Vairocana" means "Universal Radiance.
Internally, he illuminates the true *dharmadhātu* with the light of wisdom; this refers to his self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).

Second, externally, the body’s radiance responds to those of great capacity; this refers to the *paranirmāṇakāya* (the Body of Manifestation for Others) [where "great capacity" refers to Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas].
Furthermore, it is translated as "Pure and Perfect. Because all evils have been completely exhausted, it is called "Pure";

this is the retributive fruit of ceasing evil. Because all virtues are fully perfected, it is called "Perfect"; this is the retributive fruit of practicing good. These are mostly derived from oneself.
It is by virtue of being "enjoyed" that it receives its name. Its radiance shines everywhere; for the most part, it is designated as the *paranirmita-sambhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body for Others).

According to the *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa-sūtra* (Heart Ground Contemplation Sutra), the *dharmakāya* is also called the *svabhāvakāya* (Self-Nature Body). It is without beginning and without end, free from all marks, and transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
It is all-pervasive and boundless, remaining eternally and immutably present—this is termed the *dharmakāya*. As for the *sambhogakāya*, there are two kinds.
The marks [of the Buddha-body] are twofold: first, the body of self-enjoyment; second, the body of enjoyment for others. As for the body of self-enjoyment:

having cultivated the myriad practices over incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings, one reaches the fulfillment of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), transcending the triple world (*tridhātu*).

Dwelling in a pure and wondrous land, seated upon a great jewel lotus flower, surrounded by an immeasurable ocean-like assembly of bodhisattvas who offer him worship, respect, reverence, and praise—this is called the benefit of future retribution. At that time, the bodhisattva...
Entering the Vajra-samādhi, one eliminates all subtle cognitive and afflictive obstructions and attains unsurpassed bodhi.
Such a wondrous fruition is called "present benefit" and is the true saṃbhogakāya.

Having a beginning but no end, its lifespan lasts for the duration of kalpas without limit, reaching to the furthest reaches of the future. Its faculties and marks of excellence pervade the entire dharma-realm.

The four wisdoms are perfected, and he enjoys the bliss of the Dharma. Possessing eighty-four thousand gateways of wisdom, all such meritorious qualities as these are called the Tathāgata’s Body of Self-Enjoyment. This is the Tathāgata’s Body of Enjoyment for Others.

Endowed with eighty-four thousand marks and signs of excellence, he dwells in the truly pure land and teaches the Dharma of the Single Vehicle, causing all bodhisattvas to enjoy the subtle and wondrous joy of the Mahāyāna.

To transform the assembly of bodhisattvas on the ten stages, all Tathāgatas manifest ten kinds of enjoyment bodies for others (*para-sambhogakāya*). The first Buddha body sits upon a hundred-petaled lotus flower.
For the sake of Bodhisattvas on the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), he teaches the "Gate of Illumination into the Hundred Dharmas" (*śatadharmavidyāmukha*).

Once the Bodhisattva has realized this, he gives rise to great supernormal powers and transformations that fill a hundred Buddha-worlds, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to countless sentient beings. This is the second Buddha-body.
Seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus flower, he expounds the "Thousand Gateways to the Illumination of Dharmas" for the sake of Bodhisattvas on the second bhūmi.

Once the Bodhisattvas have attained realization, they manifest great supernormal powers and transformations that fill a thousand Buddha-worlds, bringing benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings.
The third Buddha-body sits upon a ten-thousand-petaled lotus flower and expounds the "Ten-Thousand Gateways to the Illumination of Dharmas" for the sake of Bodhisattvas on the third bhūmi.

Gate. Having realized this, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great supernormal powers and transformations that fill ten thousand Buddha-lands, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to countless sentient beings.
In this manner, the Tathāgata gradually increases [in stature] until reaching the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).

There, in the body of enjoyment for others (*para-sambhogakāya*), he sits upon an ineffable, wondrous jewel lotus flower and, for the sake of the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, expounds the ineffable.
The Gate of Illumination of All Dharmas. Having realized this, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great supernormal powers and transformations that fill unspeakably many subtle and wondrous Buddha-lands.
They bring benefit, peace, and happiness to unspeakably, unspeakably many, immeasurable, and boundless classes of sentient beings.
Thus, these ten bodies all sit beneath the king of bodhi trees made of the seven treasures and realize [enlightenment].
Attaining unsurpassed bodhi (this is called the *saṃbhogakāya*). Each petal of every flower constitutes a separate trichiliocosm, each containing ten billion Mount Sumerus and four great continents.
In each of these Jambudvīpas, there is a Vajrāsana and a king of Bodhi trees. Under each of these trees, the various emanation Buddhas defeat the armies of Māra. One...
At that time, they realize unsurpassed bodhi. Each of these bodies of emanation-buddhas is fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
For the sake of bodhisattvas, followers of the two vehicles, and ordinary beings, they preach the wondrous Dharma of the three vehicles according to what is appropriate.
All such emanation-buddhas are called the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) of the Buddha. These are the two kinds of *nirmāṇakāya*.
Although the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha manifests parinirvāṇa, this Buddha-body remains in continuous, eternal presence. As the verse says:
"To transform the Bodhisattvas of the bhūmis, a single Buddha manifests ten kinds of bodies; appearing in accordance with their capacities, each is distinct."
Increasing exponentially until reaching the infinite, ten such Buddhas thus attain perfect enlightenment, each sitting beneath a bodhi tree made of the seven precious gems.

As the preceding Buddha enters nirvana, the succeeding one attains enlightenment; they do not differ from the transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*) who appear throughout the kalpas (referring to the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, specifically the thousands of billions of transformation bodies).

When it is said that they increase exponentially to the infinite, how could it refer merely to thousands of billions? Therefore, the text states: "From hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands, up to the unspeakable. These great and small transformation Buddhas each sit [beneath their respective trees].

The Bodhi tree refers to what is stated in the *Prasāda-prakaraṇa* (the section on the dissemination of the sutra): "The Buddhas of worlds as numerous as motes of dust. The phrase "for this great assembly" points to the Buddhas upon the thousand-petaled lotus.
As for the thousands, hundreds, and billions of Śākyamunis, according to the *Shangpin* (Upper Chapter):
at that time, Śākyamuni received the great assembly of this world, returning them to the Lotus Treasury World (*Padmagarbhalokadhātu*) to behold Vairocana Buddha.

There, the Buddha extensively revealed and taught the Dharma-gates of the Three Sages and Ten Holy Ones, which serve as the fundamental source for entering the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus, it is known that there are not merely a thousand Buddhas, but rather thousands, hundreds, and billions.
"For the sake of the great assembly, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges": the river is located in Central India; it is forty *li* wide, and its sand is as fine as flour.
The number of grains of sand in a single river is already infinite, let alone the number of grains of sand in hundreds of thousands of rivers—how could that ever be exhausted?
Therefore, it is called "unspeakable" (*anabhilāpya*). "Unspeakable" is also the ninth of the ten great numbers. This is because...
The Dharma-gate of metaphors is vast, inexhaustible, and boundless. Now, from within this inexhaustible Dharma-gate, I shall briefly explain the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.
It is like a mere hair-tip’s breadth—no more than a single grain of sand out of hundreds of thousands of grains of sand in the Ganges River.
Although the Dharma-gates are extensive, they do not transcend the Mind-Ground. To cite the Mind-Ground is to encompass all phenomena; thus, it is by means of the few.
This is a summary of what is extensive. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Buddha was in a grove and took up a few tree leaves. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
'That which I have realized regarding all phenomena is like the grasses, trees, and leaves of the great earth;
that which I have taught to sentient beings is like the leaves in my hand. This is also the same metaphor."
This has been taught by all Buddhas of the past, will be taught by the Buddhas of the future, and is being taught by the Buddhas of the present.
Bodhisattvas of the three periods have studied it, will study it, and are studying it now.

"Buddha" (佛) is the abbreviated form of the Sanskrit term *Buddha*, which means "Awakened. This awakening possesses three meanings: first, self-awakening, like waking from a great dream, which distinguishes him from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);
second, awakening others, which distinguishes him from those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); and third, the perfection of awakening, which distinguishes him from Bodhisattvas.
Because his practice is complete and his fruition is perfected, he is called a Buddha; that is, both afflictions and karma are exhausted, and merit and wisdom are fully realized.
"Full" (pūrṇa) is a term for completion. Past, future, and present constitute the three periods of time.

What is now spoken by Śākyamuni, though said to be "not even as much as a single hair-tip," is in fact spoken by all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time and studied by all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
Why is this? The mind is the source of all dharmas; when the mind is raised, all dharmas are exhausted. Therefore, the Buddhas speak in unison and the Great Beings study together.
I have cultivated this ground of the mind for a hundred kalpas, and thus I am named Vairocana. You Buddhas, turn my [teachings]...
What has been taught is the opening of the path to the mind-ground for all sentient beings.
"I" refers to the true self (*ātman*) of the Tathāgata’s eightfold mastery; it is not the deluded self of ordinary people that clings to the body and mind of the five aggregates (*skandha*).
As for "kalpa," in the Sanskrit language it is fully called *kalpavastu*, which means "great period. It is exceedingly...
It is of such great duration that it cannot be known by mere years or months. As the *Yingluo benye jing* (Sutra on the Original Acts of the Garland) states:

"Suppose there is a stone one *li*, two *li*, or even ten *li* in length and breadth. Using a celestial robe weighing three *zhu*, and wiping this stone once every three years according to the human reckoning of days, months, and years, when this stone is completely worn away, it is called one small kalpa (*kṣudra-kalpa*). If [the stone is] one *li* or two..."
A distance of one *li*, up to forty *li*, is also called a minor *kalpa*. Furthermore, there is a stone eighty *li* in length and breadth, likewise [in size].

With a Brahmā-garment weighing three *zhu*, and using the hundred-jeweled radiant pearls within the Brahmā-heaven as the measure for days, months, and years, if one brushes this stone once every three years until it is completely worn away, it is called one intermediate *kalpa* (*antarakalpa*). Furthermore, there is a stone eight hundred *li* in length and breadth...

The same applies to the others. Using a garment from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven weighing three *zhu*, and using the light of a thousand-jeweled mirror from within the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens as a measure for days, months, and years, one wipes this stone once every three years. When this stone is exhausted, it is called one *mahā-asamkhyeya-kalpa*.
If stones measuring one *li*, two *li*, or even ten *li* are exhausted in this manner, they are called a one-*li* kalpa, a two-*li* kalpa, and so forth.
When the stones of fifty *li* are exhausted, it is called a "fifty-*li* kalpa. When the stones of one hundred *li* are exhausted, it is called a "hundred-*li* kalpa.
When the stones of one thousand *li* are exhausted, it is called a "thousand-*li* kalpa. When the stones of ten thousand *li* are exhausted, it is called a "ten-thousand-*li* kalpa.
All worthy sages enter these numerical measures; they cultivate all dharma-gates for periods of time long or short until they attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Such is their number.
After one hundred *kalpas*, one attains equal enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). If all sentient beings were to enter this count, they would attain Buddhahood before long;
if they do not, they cannot be called Bodhisattvas. Now, while it is said here that one practices for one hundred *kalpas*, the previous chapter states "one hundred *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
This may be an abbreviated text; according to other sutras, it is generally stated that the Tathāgata [attained enlightenment] after three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

He practiced for *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. After passing through three great *kalpas*, he further cultivated the causes for the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) during one hundred *kalpas*;

hence, it is said to be "one hundred *kalpas*. Tiantai cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and other treatises, stating that from the ancient Śākya [Buddha] up to Śikhin Buddha, the Tathāgata encountered seventy-five thousand Buddhas; this is called the first *asaṃkhyeya*.
(He was not Śikhin among the seven Buddhas). From Śikhin Buddha to Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he encountered seventy-six thousand Buddhas;
this is called the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, during which he received the prediction of enlightenment and was named Śākyamuni.
From Dīpaṃkara Buddha to Vipaśyin Buddha, he encountered seventy-seven thousand Buddhas; this is called the completion of the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa. From the beginning until...

Having completed the cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), he further dwelt for a hundred kalpas cultivating the causes for the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśanmahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) and the eighty minor marks (*aśītyanuvyañjana*).
Thus, the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* (*Xiányújīng*) records that the Buddha said: "For three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I practiced with diligent asceticism;
for a hundred kalpas, I cultivated merit. During the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, I made offerings to eighty-eight thousand Buddhas; during the middle asaṃkhyeya..."
For one *kalpa*, he made offerings to ninety-nine thousand Buddhas. Then, during a subsequent incalculable *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*, he made offerings to one hundred thousand Buddhas, World-Honored Ones.
He left the household life and maintained the precepts, fully perfecting the vehicle of the *śīla-pāramitā* and the chariot of the six perfections.
Donning the armor of patience, he sat beneath the Bodhi tree upon the diamond throne (*vajrāsana*), subdued the Māra kings, and attained the Way of Buddhahood.
According to the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing), when the Buddha first resolved his mind, he aspired to seek the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas.

He dwelt in quietude for forty-four billion kalpas during which time there were no Buddhas, Dharma, or Sangha. After seventy kalpas within that period, he encountered the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, who expounded the Mahāyāna;
he then developed faith and understanding and established meritorious deeds. Furthermore, after nineteen kalpas had passed...
A great king, who had made offerings to the pure assembly and provided for the poor and destitute, renounced his throne to leave the household life.
Dwelling in tranquility and practicing silent contemplation, his mind gradually grew weary from coming and going through birth and death and receiving countless retributions.

Because his intention lacked a great vow and he merely sought to escape his own suffering, another sixty kalpas passed until he encountered the Buddha Ratnamālā. This was the One Vehicle, the non-dual path. Not...
Upon hearing the name of Kṣudrakavīrya, I first conceived that intention; my heart of great vows was difficult to thwart.
From that time until today—seven hundred million asaṃkhyeya kalpas—I have protected and followed the True Dharma. Only now have I attained self-awakening.
One must know that prior to those seven hundred million kalpas, although I practiced the Way with diligent effort, I lacked firm vows and could ultimately not achieve Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
According to this, even one hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas would still be insufficient; this too is taught according to the capacities of sentient beings.

The provisional and the real, as well as the two vehicles of the Great and Small, differ in their methods of transformation. Now, Vairocana [reveals] the dharma established through the verification of his own cultivation and realization.
Thus he spoke to them, causing others to give rise to faith so that they might practice and realize according to this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground.
You, all Buddhas, who transmit what I have spoken—while previously I taught the Dharma for the sake of the great assembly at large, now I entrust the Seal of the Mind;
as it is not something other persons are capable of bearing, I specifically charge the thousand Śākyamunis to transmit my words as Vairocana Buddha’s speech and reveal them to all beings.
It has arisen so that [the Dharma] may be received from above and spread below; the transmission of the Dharma has its own origins.

To open the path of the mind-ground for all sentient beings: although the minds of sentient beings are fundamentally empty and penetrating, they have been obstructed and closed off by deluded emotions and karmic afflictions since beginningless kalpas.
Therefore, Śākyamuni entrusted this Great Path of opening the mind-ground to me through the thousand Buddhas.
This Dharma gate causes all sentient beings to suddenly and fully penetrate their own original mind. This is now briefly described;
it will be shown in detail in the following sequence.
II. Specific Entrustment.
At that time, from the Lion Throne of radiant celestial light within the Lotus-Womb World, Vairocana Buddha emitted rays of light.
The light addressed the Buddhas upon the thousand petals, saying: "Take this 'Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground' and depart. Furthermore, transmit it [to others]."
The thousand, ten-thousand, and hundred-million Śākyamunis, as well as all sentient beings, shall sequentially expound for you this chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Superior Ground-Mind.
You should receive, uphold, read, and recite it, and practice it with single-minded devotion.
The "Lotus-Womb Treasury World" (*padmagarbhalokadhātu*) is precisely the "Flower Ornament Ocean-Treasury World.
"Treasury" (*garbha*) takes the sense of containment, for the dharma-realms of the ten directions are all contained therein. The remainder is explained as in the subsequent verse section.
Regarding the "majestic celestial light lion throne," this refers to how this throne emits light that is lofty, brilliant, manifest, and blazing, just like...
It is like the light of heaven shining universally and brilliantly. When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma of fearlessness, all non-Buddhists and Māras submit and surrender;
it is like the roar of a lion, at which all birds and beasts crouch in hiding.
Therefore, every seat upon which a Buddha sits is called a "lion throne" (*siṃhāsana*), and is also called the "throne of the emptiness of phenomena" (*dharmasūnyatā-āsana*); this also symbolizes—
Fearlessness means that because the Tathāgata has attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), he is without anything to fear. As stated in the *Shangpin* (Chapter on the Superior):

"Sāṃyakṣambuddha resides within a palace of hundreds of thousands of millions of purple-gold vajra-lights, seated upon hundreds of thousands of millions of lotus flowers and a majestic seat of radiant light.
This refers to that very state. When the Light addresses the Buddhas upon the thousand petals, it indicates that the Tathāgata’s mind-ground is fundamentally beyond names and words.
Regarding sound and form: now, wishing to manifest the True Dharma of the Mind-ground, one performs Buddha-work by means of the radiance of the mind.
Therefore, it is not proclaimed through words, but proclaimed through light. This is how Śākyamuni’s light proclaims to the thousand Buddhas;
those thousand Buddhas, in turn, transform into a thousand billion Śākyamunis; and these Śākyamunis, in turn, preach for all sentient beings. Thus it is taught in successive order.

Regarding the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gates of the Superior Ground-Mind": this refers to the exposition of the various dharma-gates of the ground-mind—such as the ten stages of departure (*daśa-prasthāna*)—which the bodhisattva cultivates and realizes in successive order within the superior ground. This encompasses the precepts of the inferior ground-mind within this chapter.

When these are internalized in the mind, they constitute "upholding" (*dhāraṇā*); when expressed through the mouth, they constitute "recitation. Since the cultivation of mind and mouth are non-dual, it is said: "with a single mind."
Practice.
○ Third, making offerings to the Honored One.
At that time, the Buddha of the Thousand-Petaled Lotus and the hundreds of thousands of myriads of Śākyamunis [emerge] from the World of the Lotus Flower Treasury, majestically...
Rising from their lion seats, they each took their leave. From every part of their bodies, they emitted inconceivable light, and this light transformed into immeasurable Buddhas.
Simultaneously, with immeasurable flowers of blue, yellow, red, and white, they made offerings to Vairocana Buddha.
Having completed the reception and upholding of the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" as explained above.
Vairocana entrusted the Dharma to the Thousand-Flower-Top Buddha; those thousand Buddhas, in turn, entrusted the Dharma to the hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis.
Each received and upheld it, and thus each took their leave. As for "the entire body emitting inconceivable light":
the light of the Buddhas consists of both constant light and emitted light. Constant light is the perfect clarity of original enlightenment (*mūla-jñāna*), which shines universally.
The Dharma-realm: the emission of light is precisely the supernatural power (ṛddhi) that arises from it, manifesting in manifold ways.

Yet all these manifestations emerge without departing from the fundamental source—the precept-body of the mind-ground. Since this is the precept-body of the fundamental source, it transcends the paths of speech and thought;
therefore, it is called "inconceivable. As for the light transforming into immeasurable Buddhas, "immeasurable" likewise does not depart from the mind-ground.

This is the *samantabhadra-citta-bhūmi* (the ground of the mind of Samantabhadra). It transforms into a thousand Buddhas; the thousand Buddhas transform into a thousand times ten million (*koṭi*) Buddhas;

the thousand times ten million transform into the infinite. They further transform into infinite wondrous flowers, which are returned as offerings to the Buddha of the original source-ground of the mind.

This also symbolizes that a Bodhisattva, relying on the essence of the precepts of the mind-ground, cultivates both merit and wisdom together, thereby perfecting the myriad virtues, and then [returns them to...]
The adornment of the self-mind with myriad virtues.
○ Second, the Buddhas preaching the Dharma (divided into two parts): first, the Buddhas upon the thousand-petaled lotuses preach;
second, the two thousand and ten billion Śākyamunis preach.
○ First, regarding the Buddhas upon the thousand petals as described in the Sūtra:
I shall first describe how these Buddhas on the thousand petals manifest their bodies and preach the Dharma in ten locations;

subsequently, I shall describe how the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis likewise manifest their bodies and preach the Dharma in ten locations. As for the ten locations: first, the Vajrāsana and the Wondrous...
1. Hall of Light (Ābhāsvara); 2. Palace of Śakra; 3. Yāma Heaven; 4. Tuṣita Heaven; 5. Nirmāṇarati Heaven; 6.
Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven; 7. First Dhyāna Heaven; 8. Second Dhyāna Heaven; 9. Third Dhyāna Heaven; 10. Fourth Dhyāna Heaven.
This is the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), the Fourth Dhyāna, at the summit of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven; above this, there are no further heavens. [Question:

Since there are no further heavens above the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, where do the four heavens of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) reside? [Answer: Those four heavens of the Formless Realm constitute a body through the four aggregates (*skandhas*) of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

They possess no material substance; they are like the azure void to humans, and their realm is like empty space. Therefore, they have no fixed location. Rather, wherever a person cultivates and realizes the four formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*), that place is designated as a heaven of the four formless realms. Because these concentrations transcend the Four Dhyānas, they are listed above the Fourth Dhyāna.

Each of them vanished from this Lotus-Womb World. Having vanished, they entered the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of Essential Nature and returned to their original source world, Jambudvīpa, to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Its essential nature is without marks; therefore, it is called "empty space. This is precisely the original ground of the mind. The ground of the mind inherently possesses the function of wisdom.
Thus, although the substance of the mind is empty, it is fully endowed with the wondrous functions of the ocean-like sands of virtuous qualities and the light of nature.
Therefore, it is called the "Flower-Light of Essential Nature. Furthermore, the samādhi of the Tathāgata is fundamentally neither entering nor exiting; hence it is said that the Nāga is ever-present.

It is fixed; there is no time when it is not fixed. Furthermore, it is said: "Without arising from the samādhi of cessation, one manifests all modes of deportment and displays the forms of the ten dharma realms to guide and benefit sentient beings.
What is now called "entering and emerging" refers to the fact that essence and function are darkly unified; therefore, it is called "entering."

The essence and its function are fully manifested; therefore, it is called "emerging. This refers to the hundreds and thousands of gates of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) all returning to a single stillness, and the boundless ocean of wisdom never departing from its original source.
Guifeng said: "To cease all conceptual discrimination so that wisdom merges with principle is called 'entering'. This is precisely what is meant.
*Samādhi* is translated here as "right concentration" (*zhèngdìng*) and also as "right reception" (*zhèngshòu*). However, the name and essence of *samādhi* are extremely... [text truncated]
There are many; the practices and realizations are not uniform. For example, all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) are called both "concentration" (*samādhi*) and "meditative absorption.
Here, the phrase "the essence-nature of the Flower Radiance" is used to distinguish it from other samādhis. Jambudvīpa is translated here as "State of Superior Gold.
This refers to the fact that to the north of this southern continent, there is a great tree named Jambu. Beneath the tree is a river, and in the river is purple-gold.
Because of this sand, it was given that name. Thus, the tree took its name from the river, and the continent (zhou) derived its designation from the tree.
This is what is now called Jambudvīpa. Bodhi means "the Way" (mārga); as it is the ultimate of all ways, it is termed Bodhi.

This is the Way of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*). Originally, the tree was named *piṇḍa-bhāra*; because the Buddha sat beneath this tree and attained the Way of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), it is called *bodhi*.
It stands several hundred feet high, with a trunk that is yellowish-white and branches and leaves that are lush green.
They do not wither in winter or summer, remaining radiant and unchanged. On every fifteenth day of the second month, when the Tathāgata enters *nirvāṇa*, [the tree sheds its leaves].
One day, all the leaves withered and fell. After a short while, they returned to their former state. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Bodhi tree is lofty, prominent, and extraordinary;
its trunk is made of diamond (*vajra*), its main stem of lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*). Its branches and twigs are composed of various exquisite jewels.
Precious leaves spread out luxuriantly, casting a shade like clouds. Jeweled flowers of variegated colors cast shadows from their spreading branches. Furthermore, it is adorned with *maṇi* gems..."

It serves as their fruit. This is the *sāmbhogika-kāya* (enjoyment body) of Śākyamuni, which is the realm of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and cannot be seen by ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Nevertheless, it also manifests the light of wisdom from the Buddha’s samādhi and supernatural powers, appearing as an adornment within the mental ground (*cittabhūmi*), just like the Flower Light [Buddha] who is of the same essential nature (*tathatā-svabhāva*). Because Śākyamuni cultivated the path through this, it is called "returning."

In the world of the primal source, beneath the Bodhi tree, he emerged from the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of the Void Nature of Essential Substance. Having emerged, he then sat upon the Vajra Throne of the Thousandfold Radiant King.
And at the Hall of Wondrous Light, he taught the ten oceans of worlds. Again rising from his seat, he went to the palace of Śakra and taught the ten abodes (*bhūmi*).

Again rising from his seat, he went to the Yāma Heaven and taught the ten practices (*caryā*). Again rising from his seat, he went to the fourth heaven (*Tuṣita*) and taught the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*).
Again rising from his seat, he went to the Nirmāṇarati Heaven and taught the ten meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). Again rising from his seat, he went to...
In the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, he taught the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). Then, proceeding to the First Dhyāna, he taught the Ten Vajras.
Then, proceeding to the Second Dhyāna, he taught the Ten Patiences (*daśakṣānti*). Then, proceeding to the Third Dhyāna, he taught the Ten Vows (*daśapraṇidhāna*).

Then, proceeding to the Fourth Dhyāna, in the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, he taught the Heart of the World of the Lotus-womb Treasury (*padmagarbha-lokadhātu*), which is the source of my own being, as spoken by the Buddha Vairocana.
The Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Grounds.

Previously, it was explained that the thousand Śākyamunis and the hundreds of thousands of billions of Śākyamunis all first received the Bodhisattva-piṭaka of precepts before Vairocana, and then entered samādhi to return to their original source worlds. Now, it is explained that they emerge from samādhi and manifest.

He preached the Dharma from his body at the Seat of the King of a Thousand Rays, located in Central India, two hundred li west of Rājagṛha in the kingdom of Magadha, beneath the Bodhi tree. When this world was first formed, the seat arose together with the great earth;
it occupies the center of the trichiliocosm, reaching down to the Golden Wheel and extending upward to the surface of the earth.

It is composed of vajra and measures over one hundred paces in circumference. The thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa all sat upon this seat to enter the vajra-samādhi and attain unsurpassed enlightenment;
therefore, it is called the Vajra Thousand-Rays King Seat (*Vajra-sahasraraśmi-rāja-āsana*).
It is the place where the Tathāgata cultivated and realized the holy path, and is also termed the *bodhimaṇḍa*. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "That ground is firm and solid, composed of vajra."
Supremely exquisite jewel wheels and various precious flowers, adorned with pure maṇi gems, manifest as boundless oceans of diverse forms and appearances.
Furthermore, by the spiritual power of the Tathāgata, all the adornments of this site of enlightenment are reflected therein.
The palaces and multi-storied towers where the Tathāgata resides are vast, magnificent, and beautiful, pervading the ten directions.
It was square in shape, composed of *maṇi* jewels of every hue, and adorned with various precious flowers.
Its halls, pavilions, towers, balconies, staircases, thresholds, doors, and windows—all such features—were fully and magnificently adorned. Its lion throne was lofty, vast, and exquisite;
its dais was made of *maṇi*, its canopy of lotus flowers, and its wheels were fashioned from pure and wondrous jewels.
This is not something that can be perceived by those who lack the great capacity of a bodhisattva;

ordinary beings and followers of the two vehicles see only a wooden Bodhi tree, with a seat measuring over a hundred paces in circumference and a golden body sixteen feet tall. As for the Hall of Sublime Light, it is adorned with various precious jewels.

Therefore it is called "Sublime. Because the precious radiance illuminates one another, it is called "Light. It is also named the Hall of Universal Light, and is further known as the Hall of Universal Radiance.
Located not far to the west of the Bodhi tree, this hall was established by Brahmā with the seven treasures when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment;
Śakra established a throne of the seven treasures there, which emitted extraordinary light.
It illuminates the Bodhi tree. When the Buddha sat upon his seat, he emitted light for seven days;
now the jewels have transformed into stone. This is what is described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "In the Hall of Universal Radiance, he sat upon the Lotus-Treasury Lion Throne.
Regarding the ten world-oceans, they are detailed in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. To summarize: first, the world-ocean; second, the assembly [of worlds].
1. The ocean of birth; 2. the ocean of the establishment of the three realms of existence; 3. the ocean of Buddhas; 4. the ocean of the Buddhas' pāramitās; 5.
the ocean of the Buddhas' liberations; 6. the ocean of the Buddhas' transformations; 7. the ocean of the Buddhas' expositions; 8.
the ocean of the Buddhas' names and titles; 9. the ocean of the Buddhas' lifespans. "Ocean" signifies depth and vastness, referring to all the dharmas taught by the Tathāgata.
These ten encompass everything without exception. The *Necklace Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) states:

"When the Buddha first attained the Way beneath this tree and preached the Dharma-gate of the Ten World-Oceans, eighty thousand stainless Bodhisattvas (Equal-Enlightenment Bodhisattvas) manifested their bodies and attained Buddhahood.
It further states: "There were nine billion people who entered the Gate of Illumination of the Six Entrances, and subsequently reached the Universal Radiance Dharma."
In the Hall, he preached on the ten Buddha-lands. There were hundreds of billions of people who entered the gate of illumination of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

... [and so on] ... up to the Maṇi Hall of the Sixth Heaven, where he preached on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). There were as many people as the sands of ten million *Gaṅgā* rivers who entered the gate of illumination of the six sense-bases.
The Palace of Śakra. In Sanskrit, it is fully called Śakradevendra; here it is translated as "The Lord of Devas Who is Able."

This refers to his ability to act as the lord of the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa). His palace is named the Palace of Supreme Excellence (Vaijayanta), situated on the summit of Mount Sumeru;
this is the second heaven of the desire realm, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"At that time, by the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual authority, within every single Jambudvīpa among all the four continents in every world throughout the ten directions, [the assembly] beheld [him] in their entirety."
The Tathāgata sat beneath each tree, and in each place there were bodhisattvas who, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, expounded the Dharma;
none of them failed to consider themselves as being constantly in the presence of the Buddha. At that time, the World-Honored One did not depart from beneath any of those bodhi trees.
He ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru and proceeded toward the palace of Śakra. Each of the others likewise ascended in this same manner. The Commentary states:
"The Tathāgata does not move from the Bodhi tree, yet he ascends to the realm of the Śakras. His essence and function are without fixed direction, responding to the desires of sentient beings.
It is like the single moon in a clear river being observed by three boats: one boat remains stationary, while the other two..."
South and north: those in the south see the moon and follow it for a thousand *li* to the south; those in the north see the moon and follow it for a thousand *li* to the north.
Yet when one stops their boat and looks at the moon, it does not move. This is called the moon not leaving the middle of the stream while traveling to the south and north.

The manifestation of the Tathāgata may be understood by analogy with this. It is the function of the essence itself, universally pervasive in all things. Departure and abiding depend upon conditions; such is the Buddha.
There is neither movement nor stillness; it is unmoving yet pervasive, responding to the capacities of others. Thus, a sutra says:

"The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, appearing universally before all sentient beings. Responding to conditions and meeting with responses, there is nowhere it does not reach, yet it ever remains upon this seat of Bodhi.
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not arise from the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), yet he brings universal benefit to all living beings. 10.
Regarding "abiding": the Bodhisattva progresses through the stages of practice from the shallow to the profound, taking wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) as the ultimate fruit.
This process must necessarily be preceded by the ten levels of faith (the ten faiths will be explained later), for it is through faith that one enters into wondrous enlightenment.

"Entering" means being able to abide. Below this are the four stages of abiding, practice, orientation, and realization (*caryā-vihāra-pratipatti-bhūmi*). The enumeration of their names varies slightly across various sūtras;

they correspond to the "Ten Minds of Initial Aspiration" (*daśa-prasthāna-citta*) within the "Stage of Firm Faith and Patience" (*adhimukti-kṣānti*) at the beginning of this sūtra’s chapters: first, the mind of relinquishment (*tyāga-citta*); second, the mind of precepts (*śīla-citta*).

3. The mind of patience; 4. The mind of diligence; 5. The mind of concentration; 6. The mind of wisdom; 7. The mind of aspiration; 8. The mind of protection; 9. The mind of joy; 10. The mind of the summit.

According to the *Yingluo benye jing* (Sutra on the Original Acts of the Garland), these correspond to: 1. The dwelling of the initial arousal of the mind; 2. The dwelling of the mind that cultivates the ground;

3. The dwelling of the mind that practices; 4. The dwelling of the mind born of nobility; 5. The dwelling of the mind fully endowed with skillful means; 6. [The dwelling of the mind of non-retrogression].

The Stage of Abiding in the Rectified Mind; the Seventh, the Stage of Abiding in the Non-retrogressive Mind; the Eighth, the Stage of Abiding in the Childlike Mind; the Ninth, the Stage of Abiding in the Mind of a Dharma Prince;
the Tenth, the Stage of Abiding in the Consecrated Mind. ○ *Yāma* (Flame Heaven). In Sanskrit, it is called *Yāma*, or sometimes *Niyama*; this is translated as "Time-portion.
It is the third heaven of the Desire Realm. Its palace is named the Jewel Hall. Regarding the "Ten Practices," they arise from the preceding ten...
Abiding [in this stage], one’s cultivation of merit reaches fulfillment; one has personally attained one's own benefit, yet the practice of benefiting others is not yet perfected.

Therefore, one extensively performs acts of benefit, accords with sentient beings, and causes them to rejoice. This occurs within the stage of firm dharma-patience (*dharmakṣānti*), wherein there are ten ways of nurturing the mind.
1. The mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*). 2. The mind of compassion (*karuṇā-citta*). 3. The mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā-citta*). 4. The mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*).

5. The mind of giving (*dāna-citta*). 6. The mind of goodness (*śubha-citta*). 7. The mind of benefit (*hita-citta*). 8. The mind of sameness (*samatā-citta*). 9. The mind of concentration (*samādhi-citta*). 10. The mind of wisdom (*prajñā-citta*). The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (瓔珞經) states: 1. The practice of the mind of joy; 2.
The practice of the mind of benefit; 3. The practice of the mind free from anger and resentment; 4. The practice of the inexhaustible mind; 5. The [mind] free from...

1. The mental activity of deluded confusion; 2. The mental activity of the six sense-bases; 3. The mental activity of non-attachment; 4. The mental activity of reverence; 5. The mental activity of wholesome dharmas; 6. The mental activity of the six sense-bases;
7. The mental activity of non-attachment; 8. The mental activity of reverence; 9. The mental activity of wholesome dharmas; 10. The mental activity of reality. The Fourth Heaven:
This is the Tuṣita Heaven of the Desire Realm. In Sanskrit it is called Tuṣita, which here means "Contentment. Its palace is named the Hall of Dharma-Light. The Ten Dedications.
When the merit of the ten practices is fulfilled, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
One redirects the goodness of the ten practices toward three destinations: first, toward the reality-limit of true suchness (*tathatā-bhūtakoṭi*), because it is that which is to be realized;

second, toward unsurpassed bodhi, because it is that which is to be sought; and third, toward all sentient beings, because they are those who are to be delivered. Furthermore, by means of this capacity to redirect...
The mind [of these ten vows], along with the virtuous deeds dedicated toward those myriad classes of beings, fulfill the ten thousand practices and enter equally into the Dharma-realm;
this is the superior grade. Within the firm cultivation of patience, there are the ten adamantine minds: first, the mind of faith; second, the mind of mindfulness; third, the mind of dedication;
fourth, the mind of penetration; fifth, the mind of rectitude; sixth, the mind of non-retrogression; seventh, the Mahāyāna mind; eighth, the mind free from conceptualization...
The mind: ninth, the mind of wisdom; tenth, the indestructible mind. The *Ratnavyuha Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) states:

first, the mind of dedication that rescues all sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of a "sentient being"; second, the indestructible mind of dedication; third, the mind of dedication equal to all Buddhas;
fourth, the mind of dedication reaching all places; fifth, the mind of dedication to the inexhaustible treasury of merit; sixth...
1. The mind of dedication that accords with roots of goodness in equality; 2. The mind of dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings;
3. The mind of dedication to the mark of true suchness (*tathatā*); 4. The mind of dedication to liberation without bondage; 5.
The mind of dedication entering the immeasurable realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). ○ The Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*) is the fifth heaven of the desire realm. 10.
As for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is also called the ten great samādhis. Only the great bodhisattvas are able to skillfully enter them.

Upon entering these samādhis, they obtain the power of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) which is inexhaustible; they attain the rank of Dharma King with immeasurable sovereignty; they are born into the family of the Tathāgata;
and they manifest various kinds of vast supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). These are: first, the Samādhi of Universal Radiance; second, the Samādhi of Sublime Radiance.
1. Samādhi; 2. Samādhi of successive universal travel to all Buddha-lands; 3. Samādhi of the practice of the pure profound mind;
4. Samādhi of knowing the treasury of past adornments; 5. Samādhi of the treasury of the light of wisdom; 6.
Samādhi of thoroughly knowing the Buddha-adornments of all worlds; 7. Samādhi of the differentiated bodies of sentient beings.

The ninth is the samādhi of mastery over the nine dharma-realms; the tenth is the samādhi of the unimpeded wheel. These are seen in detail in the "Chapter on the Ten Samādhis" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
However, the *Avataṃsaka* was compiled after the [Daśabhūmika] *Sūtra*. ○ The Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) is the sixth heaven of the desire realm.
The name of that palace is Maṇiratnagarbha (Jewel-Treasury). Regarding the "Tenth Ground" (*bhūmi*): it means that when a bodhisattva realizes this tenth ground, it is like the great earth;
all Buddha-dharmas arise in dependence upon it. The *Ratnavyūha Sūtra* states: "Ground" (*bhūmi*) means "support," for it supports all hundreds of thousands of koṭis of asaṃkhyeyas of merit.
It is also called "birth," for it gives birth to all causes and effects. Therefore, it is so named.

The Grounds: namely, within the superior grade of the noble patience of firmness (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), there are ten grounds: first, the ground of the equality of essential nature; second, the ground of excellent wisdom of essential nature;
third, the ground of luminosity of essential nature; fourth, the ground of suchness-flame of essential nature; fifth, the ground of wisdom-illumination of essential nature;
sixth, the ground of flower-radiance of essential nature; seventh, the ground of fulfillment of essential nature; eighth, the ground of the Buddha’s roar of essential nature.

The Grounds: 1. The Ground of the Essence of Adornment; 2. The Ground of the Essence of Entry into the Buddha-realm. The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states: 1. The Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*); 2. The Ground of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*); 3.
The Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*), also called the Ground of Emitting Light; 4. The Ground of Blazing Flames (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), also called the Ground of Blazing Wisdom;

5. The Ground Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*); 6. The Ground of Manifestation (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*); 7. The Ground of Far-reaching Travel (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*); 8. The Ground of Immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*).

The Ninth is the Stage of Sublime Wisdom (also called the Stage of Excellent Wisdom). The Tenth is the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (*Dharmameghā-bhūmi*). (In the *Yingluo jing*, the Buddha explains in great detail the dharma-gate of the six stages:

Abiding, Practice, Orientation, Ground, Equal Enlightenment, and Sublime Enlightenment. 1. The First Dhyāna: This refers to the first dhyāna heaven within the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the "ten vajras":
According to the upper fascicle of this sutra and the subsequent text of this chapter, these are the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

However, since the ten dedications were already explained while [the Buddha] was in the fourth heaven, the names are identical but the meanings differ. Now, following the *Avataṃsaka*, I shall set forth the ten adamantine minds (*daśa-vajracitta*).
Indeed, this original sutra and the *Avataṃsaka* were taught simultaneously; it was later compilers who divided them into two sections.
That is to say, the bodhisattva’s mind of aspiration is firm and unshakable, like a diamond. These are: first, the mind that awakens to all phenomena;
second, the mind that transforms and delivers sentient beings; third, the mind that adorns the world-realm; fourth, the mind that dedicates roots of goodness;
fifth, the mind that serves the Great Master; sixth, the mind that realizes all phenomena in truth; seventh, the mind that extensively practices patience; eighth, the long...
At that time, there is the mind of cultivation. Ninth, the mind of fulfilling one’s own practice; tenth, the mind of causing others’ vows to be fulfilled. ○ Second Dhyāna:
This refers to the second dhyāna heaven within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the ten kinds of patience (*kṣānti*):

by attaining these patiences, one reaches the stage of all Bodhisattvas known as the "Stage of Unimpeded Patience" (*asaṅga-kṣānti-bhūmi*), wherein one realizes all Buddha-dharmas, which are unimpeded and inexhaustible. This is [the state of] equality.
This is the realization attained by the Bodhisattva’s final mind, having severed all subtle ignorance. It consists of: first, the patience of a single sound;

second, the patience of conformity; third, the patience of the non-arising of phenomena; fourth, the patience of being like an illusion; fifth, the patience of being like a flame; and sixth, the patience of being like a dream.
7. The patience like an echo; 8. The patience like a shadow; 9. The patience like a transformation; 10. The patience like space (for details, see the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*). ○ Third Dhyāna:
This refers to the third dhyāna heaven within the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding the ten vows: the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* enumerates two sets of ten vows. As for the first ten vows: 1.
To vow that one will bring sentient beings to maturity without ever becoming weary; 2. To vow that one will fully practice all... [text continues]
1. To purify all world-systems; 2. To serve the Tathāgatas with constant reverence through three vows; 3.
To protect and uphold the True Dharma, not sparing even one’s own body or life; 4. To observe with wisdom and enter all Buddha-lands; 5.
To become of one and the same essential nature as all Bodhisattvas; 6. To enter the gateway of the Tathāgata and fully comprehend all dharmas; 7. [The eighth vow: ... [to be fulfilled].
Those who see them will give rise to faith; there are none who do not obtain benefit. Ninth, may the power of these vows cause me to abide in the world throughout all future kalpas.
Tenth, may I fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra and purify the gateway to all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*). Regarding the subsequent ten vows: first, the vow to pay homage to all Buddhas;
second, the vow to praise the Tathāgatas; third, the vow to extensively cultivate offerings; fourth, the vow to repent of karmic transgressions.

The vow to remove obstacles; fifth, the vow for the merit of sympathetic joy; sixth, the vow to request the Buddha to turn the wheel of Dharma; seventh, the vow to request the Buddha to remain in the world;
eighth, the vow to always follow and learn from the Buddha; ninth, the vow to always accord with sentient beings;
tenth, the vow of universal dedication. ○ The Fourth Dhyāna: this refers to the fourth dhyāna heaven within the Realm of Form (rūpadhātu). Maheśvara: this is translated as "Great."
He is sovereign, having attained the eight masteries. He delights in liberation, his radiance surpasses all, and he dwells at the pinnacle of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
As the lord of the great trichiliocosm, he is a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (daśabhūmi), named Weilingdi.

While previously situated below the fourth dhyāna before the Buddha, he expounded various Dharma-gates such as the stages of abiding, practice, and orientation; now, for the final time, he resides in the fourth dhyāna and expounds the Mind-Ground (cittabhūmi).
This Dharma-door, this fourth dhyāna, is the ultimate pinnacle of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
This celestial palace of the Heavenly King lies above the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*); there is no other heaven superior to this.

Therefore, within the teachings of the Three Vehicles, it is established as a Pure Land, the dwelling place of the Reward Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya-buddha*). The Esoteric Section states that beyond the Five Pure Abode Heavens, there exists...
This is the palace of Vairocana. It also symbolizes the ultimate point where all phenomena converge within the single mind;
it is most honored and unsurpassed, for there is no phenomenon higher than the mind.
This present source, the unconditioned and signless Dharma, cannot be fathomed by the consciousnesses of ordinary beings on the lower stages; only Buddha after Buddha can know it.
...thus it is. ○ Two thousand billion Śākyamunis speak;
the remaining two thousand billion Śākyamunis are likewise thus—without duality and without distinction—as described in the "Chapter on the Worthy Kalpa" (Bhadrakalpika-parivarta).

It is said that the thousand Buddhas of the past have thus repeated and expounded this *Śākyamuni’s Mind-Ground Dharma Gate* (*Xianshou Xindi Famen*). Now, the hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas likewise repeat and expound it;
therefore, it is said to be non-dual and without distinction. This is from the "Chapter on the Worthy Kalpa" (*Xiánjiè Pǐn*) in the Great Version (*Dàběn*).
The above scriptural passage constitutes the concluding words at the end of the "Chapter on the Summary" (Jiepin).

Ancient commentaries place it at the beginning of the following chapter to manifest the fundamental and manifested traces of Śākyamuni, enabling people to understand them as clearly as looking at their own palms; therefore, we have retained this ancient arrangement here.
*Foshuo Fanwang Jing Pusa Xindi Pin Xia Lue Shu*, Scroll One: *Yinyi*. "Yin" (sound) refers to the phonetic transcription;
it is also a transmission and an interpretation. It is the mutual interpretation of the linguistic sounds of two countries, transmitted and proclaimed for others.

According to the *Zhouli* (Rites of Zhou), the *Wangzhi* (Institution of the King) was charged with mastering the languages of the four quarters. Each direction had its own *xiangxu* (elephant-mouthed interpreters) as official translators.
Those of the East were called *ji*; they were able to transmit and lodge the differences of local customs here. Those of the South were called *xiang*;
this meant they could imitate and represent the differences of customs there. Those of the West were called *didi*; this meant they could distinguish the differences in dress and adornment.
