Since the Buddha himself recited it, all bodhisattvas of the past who sought great enlightenment have already studied within it; future bodhisattvas shall study it, and those of the present [should likewise do so].
A bodhisattva in training should revere [this] with a sincere heart, receiving and upholding it upon the crown of the head, never allowing even a moment’s forgetfulness or loss.
II. Separate Enumeration.
○ First, regarding the precept against killing:
Śrāvakas loathe and fear birth and death, and thus regard self-benefit as their primary concern; for this reason, the precept against sexual misconduct is established as the foremost.

This is because sexual desire is the root of saṃsāra and the source of birth and death. Bodhisattvas, however, do not fear birth and death, as they take the benefit of sentient beings as their priority.

This is a matter of primary importance; therefore, the precept against killing was established first. Furthermore, killing severs the seed of the Buddha-nature and violates the fundamental vow of compassion.
For through loving-kindness one can bestow happiness upon sentient beings, and through compassion one can extract the suffering of those who possess feeling.
This is the practice of the Great Being in delivering sentient beings and the virtue of accomplishing the Dharma-body. As for "killing":
all sentient beings take the five aggregates as their body and mind; if one gives rise to anger and malice, destroying those five aggregates, it is therefore called "killing."

The Buddha said: "O sons of the Buddha, whether one kills by oneself, teaches others to kill, employs means to kill, praises killing, rejoices upon seeing it being done, or even kills through incantations—"
"If" (*yadi*) is a term used for hypothetical illustration; in one version of the text, the character "if" is absent, which would then directly refer to a specific individual—this is incorrect.
"One who kills by oneself" refers to performing the act of killing with one's own body. "One who instructs another to kill" refers to verbally commanding another person to commit a slaughter.
"Killing by means of skillful methods" refers to using various ingenious and expedient means to ensure that death occurs.
"Praising the act of killing" refers to extolling someone's virtues in the presence of one who desires to die, saying such things as: "You have already performed many meritorious deeds;
having been born, you suffer, but upon dying you shall be reborn in heaven and experience inexhaustible bliss. In this way, [one induces them].

If one causes another to die by means of one's own death, or by verbal instruction, or by manifesting signs of praise through the body, or by sending someone to speak on one's behalf, or by sending someone with a letter to cause them to die—
and if one rejoices upon seeing this being done— then one commits the act of killing through both bodily and vocal karma.
Now, rejoicing in this is a mental action (*manas-karman*). That is to say, when one sees another person committing killing, the mind follows along with them and gives rise to joy.
The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) is an expression indicating that the list is not exhaustive; it means that since the instances of killing therein are numerous, they cannot all be cited.
For example: some create fire pits or traps to cause others to fall into them; some set mechanical devices to cause death; or some set snares.
Setting traps, or using snares, or administering poison, or causing abortions, and so forth—killing through incantations also belongs to the karma of speech.
This refers to using malevolent spells to curse someone until they die. In foreign lands, there exists the spell for raising the corpse-demon (*vetāla*).
He was named Vīra. He took an intact corpse that had not yet decayed and used a mantra for summoning spirits; after chanting it for twenty-nine days, he caused the corpse to rise.
He washed it and dressed it in clothes, gave it a sword, placed it upon a carriage, and instructed it to go and kill people.
In this region, there are also non-Buddhist practitioners who possess malevolent spells capable of causing death. Within the Vinaya, suicide is categorized into three types.
The first involves using one's own physical form—namely, by means of the hand, the foot, the head, or any other part of the body—to take another's life.
Second, employing external matter: this refers to hurling objects such as wood, stones, swords, spears, bows, or arrows at another person from a distance.

Third, employing both internal and external matter: this refers to striking another with one's own hand while grasping wood, stones, swords, or similar items. Apart from these three types of matter, [there is no other].
That which can cause a person to die includes such things as pits, traps, mechanical devices, and even malevolent incantations.
These constitute the cause of killing, the conditions for killing, the method of killing, and the karmic action of killing.

The initial arousal of the intent to kill serves as the cause (*hetu*). The subsequent continuity of that intent, which assists in the completion of the act of killing, serves as the condition (*pratyaya*).

The deliberation and preparation of the means and instruments serve as the method (*dharma*). When life is severed, the karma is established. The first sprout of a single thought of killing is termed the "affliction-obstruction" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The completion of the act and the severance of life is termed the "karmic-obstruction" (*karmāvaraṇa*). That which summons and brings about the suffering of the three evil realms in the future is termed [the retribution-obstruction].
The retributive obstacle (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*). These constitute the three obstacles, all of which arise from the initial arising of a single thought of unwholesomeness.
If that initial thought is extinguished and the subsequent thought does not continue, then there will be no volitional deliberation or action, and the karma of killing will not be established;
thus, the retributive obstacle cannot come to pass. The nine subsequent precepts should be understood according to this principle. As for the term "accessories and implements" (*upakaraṇa*):
This refers to using internal form, external form, or both internal and external form; methods such as digging pits or setting traps, and so forth. The *Yi-shu* (Commentary) states:

"The immediate cause is proximate while the conditions are remote. The primary cause is the murderous intent, which acts as the cause; the other factors that assist in its accomplishment act as the conditions.

The 'proximate' refers to the actual commission of the act, which invites and brings about future retribution, following it like a shadow follows a form. The 'conditions' are remote because they merely assist in its accomplishment. Regarding these causes and conditions:
To "perform" (kṛ) is the meaning of karma. There are four factors that constitute the completion of an act of karma: first, a sentient being; second, the perception of a sentient being;
third, the act of killing; and fourth, the severance of life. If any one of these is missing, the karma is not completed.
"Up to and including all living beings, one must not intentionally kill. Regarding "up to and including":
this refers back to harming human beings above and extends downward to include even the most minute forms of life. Regarding "all": this excludes only those of the human realm.
This refers to other beings such as ghosts, animals, insects, and so forth. "Those who possess life" refers to all sentient beings;

the continuous succession maintained by the six sense organs and six consciousnesses is called "life-span. The severance of this succession is termed "death. Therefore, "killing" means having the intention to take life;
it does not refer to unintentional or accidental killing. Although killing animals and the like may be subject to repentance, [it remains a grave offense].

One must behold auspicious signs for one's offenses to be extinguished. The Bodhisattva thoroughly understands the nature of karma and regards all sentient beings with equanimity, making no distinction between great and small, high and low.
Because of wholesome karma, they are born in the realms of humans and devas; because of unwholesome karma, they are born within the paths of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Since all equally possess the nature of consciousness, there is no difference between suffering and pleasure; therefore, [the Bodhisattva] does not kill any.
In all such cases, one incurs sin. Furthermore, all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; they share a single source.
To kill another is thus to harm oneself, as well as to harm the Buddhas of the future.
If this bodhisattva, who ought to give rise to a mind of constant compassion, a mind of filial obedience, and skillful means to rescue and protect all sentient beings,
instead kills living beings with a self-indulgent and pleasure-seeking mind, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that bodhisattva.
It is eternally abiding; it is precisely the original source-ground of the mind. Since this ground of the mind is neither born nor extinguished, how could there be any arising?

This refers to the arising of function from essence. Above, it accords with all Buddhas in their identical power of compassion; below, it accords with sentient beings in their identical yearning for pity.
Therefore, it is said that one "arouses the mind of compassion. If one is not filial and obedient, one is in opposition to the original source-ground of the mind.
How much more so for all sentient beings, who have all been one's own parents throughout many lifetimes; therefore, one ought to be filial toward them.

How could one ever kill them? Even if one does not kill them oneself, when seeing another killing, one must still employ various skillful means to rescue and protect them, enabling them to escape their peril;
only then is one acting in accordance with filial piety and not violating the Great Being’s fundamental vow to benefit living beings. One should not act as follows:
This initial preparatory effort already deviates from the Bodhisattva’s original intention; yet, instead of restraining the mind, one indulges it and finds pleasure in committing this evil deed.
Because the evil karma has been completed, one immediately incurs the offense of *pārājika*. *Pārājika* is a Sanskrit term with many meanings, and thus there is no direct translation for it.
However, it is an extremely grave and heavy offense, like a capital punishment in the secular world. It may also be translated as...

It means "to abandon. One abandons all merit entirely; because there is no longer any portion of the fruit of the Path, one is forever cast out from the pure assembly and may not dwell with them, just as the great ocean does not harbor a corpse. Alternatively, it is translated as "defeat" (pārājika).
This means that they have been utterly defeated by the thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, it means they have been utterly deceived by other practitioners of purity.
Alternatively, it is called "falling into an undesirable state," meaning that upon death, one immediately falls into the hells and other evil destinies (*durgati*).

This is not a *pārājika* offense for a *bhikṣu*; therefore, it is said to be a *pārājika* for a bodhisattva, because for a bodhisattva, this [offense] is more grave than [the gravity of a *bhikṣu*'s].
This is because they are bhikṣus. To say that [killing] is an ultimate evil to be abandoned would mean they have forever lost their mind of compassion, filial piety, and protection.

Question: Those who have left the household life distance themselves from harmful intent, and thus the precept against killing is easy for them to maintain. However, kings and ministers exclusively hold the authority over the power of killing.
If one does not punish those who have committed crimes, how can the state be brought to peace? Answer: Sometimes by killing one person, one saves an entire village;
by killing many people, one saves an entire district or a nation. This is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of a Bodhisattva, which may be employed upon perceiving the appropriate opportunity.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "The skillful means of a Bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting others, [may involve] seeing a robber or thief..."

Out of greed for wealth, he wishes to kill many people, or perhaps intends to harm a virtuous one—a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or a bodhisattva—or else intends to commit multiple acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma). Having observed this situation, the bodhisattva reflects:
"If I were to take that evil person's life, I would fall into hell; yet if I do not take it, his karma of immediate retribution [will ripen]."
It is established that one shall undergo great suffering. It would be better to fall into hell oneself than to cause another to suffer the pains of the Avīci Hell.
With a virtuous mind and a compassionate heart, if one takes the life of such a person, there is no transgression of the precepts. Furthermore, the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra* states:
"If one sees someone committing the five crimes of immediate retribution, slandering the Mahāyāna sūtras, or acting in rebellion against their sovereign..."
Regarding those who disrupt the True Dharma, one should give rise to a mind of compassion and perform rites of subjugation. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"In the distant past, during a long-forgotten kalpa, there was a king named Śīlavat (Possessing Virtue).

He heard that certain evil bhikṣus, out of a heart of hatred, were brandishing swords and staves with the intent to harm the Dharma Master Bodhivṛddhi (Awakened Virtue). The king, in order to protect the True Dharma..."
Therefore, he immediately renounced the five precepts and engaged in battle with various wicked bhikṣus. At that time, the king was wounded, his entire body covered in injuries.
Later, when the king passed away, he was reborn in the eastern land of Akṣobhya Buddha (A-mi-tuo Fo) as that Buddha’s foremost disciple.
The Buddha said: "The king at that time was none other than myself; the bhikṣu Dharma Master was [the other]."
That was Kāśyapa Buddha. Today, I have attained various marks and signs to adorn myself, and have accomplished the Dharma-body and the indestructible body.
To protect the True Dharma, I have obtained such immeasurable fruits of merit as these.
Furthermore, in the past, a Tathāgata was a great king named Śānta (仙豫), whom [Kāśyapa] loved, cherished, and revered.
Having served the various Brahmins for as long as twenty years with everything they required, according to the Mahāyāna sūtras, he addressed them, saying:
"Teachers, you should now resolve to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta. They replied:
"Great King, the nature of bodhi is non-existent; the Mahāyāna sūtras are likewise so. Great King, how can this be?"
He wished to cause others to become like empty space. At that time, the king’s mind was deeply set upon the Mahāyāna;

hearing that [the Brahmins] were slandering the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, he immediately took their lives. When those Brahmins reached the end of their lives, they were reborn in the Avīci Hell, whereupon they realized for themselves that because they had slandered the Mahāyāna scriptures and lacked faith in the principle of causes and conditions, they had been killed by the king and had consequently come to be born there.
Having understood this, he conceived a heart of reverence and faith toward the Mahāyāna sūtras.
He passed away shortly thereafter and was reborn in the world-system of the Tathāgata Amṛtadundubhirāja. There, his lifespan lasted for ten full kalpas, as described in the sūtra.
A Mahāyāna bodhisattva, out of a heart of compassion, benefits sentient beings without a single thought of anger, malice, or self-interest. If...
There are those who do not comprehend the intent of the scriptures; for the sake of their own self-interest, they harbor a mind of anger and harm others.
Not only is this of no benefit to others, but they themselves will fall into the Avīci Hell from which there is no prospect of escape.

Nevertheless, when Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings, they may also do so by transforming and subduing them through wholesome dharmas. For example, in the past, King Prasenajit had two great generals; one took refuge in the Dharma and...
A bhikṣuṇī practiced the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta-bhāvanā*). All her weapons were made of bamboo and wood.
Later, when the border regions rebelled, the King ordered her to go and subdue them. Upon reaching that border, she immediately entered the samādhi of loving-kindness.
The rebels all saw the Four Heavenly Kings leading immeasurable celestial armies filling the void; they subsequently surrendered. Furthermore, in the past...
In Central India, King Śīlāditya ordered all his soldiers to hang water bags from the tips of their bows;

even for the horses' drinking water, they were required to filter it using these bags. Consequently, all the kingdoms submitted to him. Thus, whether in times of conflict or submission, one must grasp the other's intent;
if one errs in judgment, calamity will descend for ten thousand kalpas. One must not fail to be cautious.
○ Second Precept on Stealing:
The preceding precept harms the internal life-force of another’s primary retribution; this precept harms their external life-force as it relates to their secondary retribution.
Since material wealth can nourish the physical body, it is categorized as external life. The Vinaya states: "Objects belong to others and are guarded by them."
To take what is not given is called theft. "Not given" means that it has not been bestowed by another.

If a disciple of the Buddha, whether taking for oneself, inciting others to take, or employing expedient means to take—whether by means of spells, the causes of theft, the conditions of theft, the methods of theft, or the karmic acts of theft—[commits such an act].
The Vinaya states: "There are briefly five types of theft: first, taking by force in the presence of the owner; second, taking by secret pilfering;
third, taking by trickery; fourth, taking what was entrusted; and fifth, taking back after having given. These five types are all considered the act of a thief.
'Stealing by oneself' refers to taking by one's own person. 'Teaching another to steal' refers to instructing another verbally, or dispatching a messenger to take it."

To steal by making signs so as to let [the owner] know; to steal by means of expedients, using various clever devices and deviousness to deceive others into ignorance, even down to the smallest measures of *gui*, *he*, *zhu*, and *liang*, deceiving them in every matter, such as shifting boundary markers or encroaching upon land—this refers to these acts. To steal by means of incantations (*dhāraṇī*):
to use the heterodox arts of non-Buddhists to summon those objects through incantation so that they come of their own accord, or to incantate and summon ghosts and spirits, causing the ghosts...
This refers to theft. Regarding the karma of the dharma of dependent origination: the initial arising of a thieving mind constitutes the cause;

the subsequent continuity of that thieving mind and the various factors that assist in accomplishing the act of theft constitute the conditions; the deliberation on the method of stealing the object constitutes the mental formation (*dharma*);

and the object’s removal from its original location completes the karma. As the Vinaya states: "With respect to property belonging to another, forming the perception that it belongs to another, one lifts it and removes it from its original place."
If one forms the notion that the object belongs to oneself, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) immediately upon moving it from its original place.

If one employs the means to lift it but does not yet succeed, or even if one touches it, shakes it, or turns it over, as long as it has not left its original place, one incurs a light offense of defilement (*duskṛta*).

If it leaves its original place, but one subsequently gives rise to a mind of regret or a mind of fear and returns it to its original place, one likewise incurs a grave offense (provided there was seed in the original place).
The distinctions between these types are recorded in detail in the *Bhikṣu-vinaya* and the *Upāsaka-pañcaśīla-sūtra*.

Regarding everything from ghosts and spirits to property belonging to others, the goods of bandits, and all manner of wealth— even a single needle or a blade of grass— one must not intentionally steal them.
Regarding "the spirits and deities who have a master" and "the property of bandits," this refers to the owners to whom those goods belong.
In discussing persons, there is a distinction between great and small, superior and inferior; in discussing objects, there is a differentiation between light and heavy.

Those at the highest level are the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, sovereigns, parents, and teachers; those in the middle are officials and commoners; and those at the lowest level are spirits, deities, bandits, and beasts. However, as for objects...
"Owner": To know in one's own mind that something has an owner is the perception of ownership; stealing it constitutes an offense. "All property, even a single needle or a blade of grass":
this refers to the relative gravity of the objects. "Property" (*dhana*) refers to gold, silver, coins, the seven precious gems, and so forth.
"Objects" (*bhāṇḍa*) refers to clothing, food, drink, copper, iron, bamboo, wooden utensils, and the like. "Needles and grass" refers to minor items.
Even taking what is not given when it is of the smallest and lightest degree still constitutes the karma of theft; how much more so in the case of heavy objects?

According to the Vinaya, the determination of the offense is based on the weight of the object. How does one incur a grave offense? In all nations, the laws of Madhyadeśa (Central India) and Magadha are considered authoritative.
If one steals five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it constitutes a capital offense. The Buddha, following the laws of the land, [established this] in general.
Within Jambudvīpa, in places where the Buddha-dharma exists, stealing five *kārsāpaṇas* constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
If it concerns other goods, the offense is established by calculating their value. A "coin" refers to a large coin; one large copper coin is equal in value to sixteen small copper coins.

According to the *Arthaviniścayasūtra-ṭīkā*, if a Bodhisattva steals two coins or more, it immediately becomes a grave offense, because the precepts of a Great Being are more weighty than [those of ordinary beings].
Regarding "the property of the Śrāvakas": this refers to when a Mahāsattva practices the *dāna-pāramitā* and gives to sentient beings, yet in doing so, he instead causes harm to others;

therefore, it is considered grave. Regarding "the property of the Buddha": this refers to items used for offerings to Buddha-stūpas and images, ranging from incense, flowers, and ritual implements down to the surplus provisions provided by donors for the Buddha.
Regarding "the property of the Dharma": this refers to items for making offerings to the scriptures, or for the production of scriptures.
Regarding material wealth, the Vinaya states that stealing scriptures constitutes an offense based on their calculated value.

As for monastic property—meaning items offered to the Sangha, whether belonging to the *pratyutpanna-saṃgha* (the present community) or the *sthāvara-saṃgha* (the permanent endowment)—if one takes such things, the resulting retribution is like that suffered by the blind dragon girl or manifested as the immediate karmic fruit experienced by Gao Fayǎn.
The *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhi Sūtra* states that stealing property belonging to the permanent endowment is worse than [stealing from]...
The sin of killing eighty-four thousand parents. The Vaipulya Sūtra states:

The Bodhisattva Puṣpaketu said, "I am able to save even those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and the four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*); however, I cannot save those who steal the property of the Sangha.
The *Yaoji* asks: "For what reason is the crime of misappropriating the property of the Sangha particularly grave? The answer is: "When a donor originally relinquishes a single [item]..."
A single grain of incense is intended as an offering to the ten directions; the first toll of the bell and drum is heard alike by those far and near.

Both the holy and the mundane partake of it, and all together accomplish the work of the Path. It provides secret support for the donor, resulting in boundless merit. Since the accumulation of goodness is so great, how could the transgressions incurred be anything but few?
"The Ruler’s Property" refers to items belonging to the King, down to the theft of taxes or the illicit crossing of passes and ferries. (According to the Vinaya...)

It is said: If one carries one's own goods to a customs station and causes another person to pass them through, one incurs a grave offense. If one conceals them in the mouth, wraps them in clothing, or takes a detour to avoid the road, one likewise incurs an offense.

However, if one carries goods belonging to the Three Jewels or to one's parents past a customs station, one should extol the merits of the Three Jewels and speak of the profound kindness of one's parents for the sake of the tax official; if they do not take the tax, there is no offense. Thus it is said.

If one borrows items belonging to relatives—meaning the property of one's parents—and the parents permit their use, and if one gauges the feelings of those close to them and finds they would also rejoice, there is no offense.
In the first year of the Longshuo era of the Tang dynasty, Li Jiaowei of Luzhou went to the market in Huazhou.
She saw a solitary pig whose four legs had already been bound, and it was about to be slaughtered. When the pig saw the woman, it spoke to her, saying:
"You are my daughter, and I am your grandmother. Originally, because your family was poor, your mother repeatedly begged me for grain.
Your eldest son would not permit it. Out of pity for you, mother and child, I secretly evaded my son and gave her five *sheng*."
"He has now been made into a pig to repay his debt for theft; why did you not save me? When the magistrate heard this, he immediately ransomed and released the pig from the butcher.
The pig ran on its own toward a nearby temple’s sanctuary for releasing living beings. The magistrate returned to his home province to inform his mother.
Later, the mother came in person to see the pig; when mother and child met, they both wept at once. In the first year of the Linde era, the pig was still alive.

Because household property belongs to the children, a mother who steals her child's belongings receives such retribution. As for a child stealing the wealth of their parents, how could one possibly measure the resulting retribution?
Furthermore, during the Sui dynasty, there was a woman named Zhang, the mother of Geng Fusheng from Jizhou. To avoid her husband, she gave two bolts of silk to her daughter.
Later, when the mother died, she was transformed into a sow. These two accounts of evidence are recorded in detail in the *Fayuan zhulin*. Master—
"Objects" refers to things more precious than even one's own kin, because such objects are what have been bestowed through the faithful devotion of a *dānapati* (donor).
"Official objects" refers to the property belonging to the nine ranks of the bureaucracy. "People’s objects" refers to the property of the common people.

"Objects of spirits and deities" refers to the ritual implements within shrines and temples that are guarded by humans, or those guarded by the spirits of mountains and forests themselves. [To seize] these is *kṣaya* (plundering).
Regarding "stolen goods": this refers to property that has been plundered by thieves; once it has been seized, the property belongs to the thieves.

If one's own property is stolen by thieves and one has already formed the intention to relinquish it, the property then belongs to the thieves and may not be reclaimed. To reclaim it constitutes an offense, for this would be "a thief robbing a thief.
Even if those brave and capable thieves subsequently seize it back from him, although he does not regain the property himself, he still incurs the offense of double theft.

It is an offense. If one asks for the object back, there is no offense. If one has not yet formed the intention to relinquish it, and subsequently sees the object and takes it back, there is no offense.
Regarding the property of birds and beasts—down to the six domestic animals, birds, mice, and so forth—if they are holding something in their beaks or mouths, one must not snatch it away.

According to the *Wujiexiang jing* (Sūtra on the Characteristics of the Five Precepts): "If one steals a bird with an owner, it constitutes a grave offense; if it is a bird without an owner, it constitutes a light offense.

If one steals a four-legged beast, whether by lifting it up or driving it away, once it has moved more than four double-steps, it constitutes a grave offense because it has been removed from its original location;

if it moves more than two double-steps, it constitutes a light offense. If one steals a person, once they have moved more than two steps, it constitutes a grave offense. [This applies even if] the person is being carried on one's shoulders or back."
If both feet leave the ground, it constitutes a grave offense. Regarding "not intentionally stealing": "intentionally" means it is not an act committed through lack of mindfulness or by mistake.

Furthermore, a Bodhisattva should give rise to a mind of filial piety toward the Buddha-nature, a mind of compassion, and should constantly assist all people so that they may generate merit and happiness.
To instead steal another's wealth and property is a *pārājika* offense for a Bodhisattva.

The Buddha-nature is the original source, the ground of the mind. Since this nature is fundamentally characterized by filiality and compassion, that which is said to "arise" refers to the manifestation of function from the essence.
Therefore, through the two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—one constantly assists others in generating merit and happiness.

To instead steal another's property is to oppose the original source and contradict the fundamental nature; it is to fail to practice the two kinds of giving and, conversely, to cause others to suffer.
Poverty and suffering arise from committing evil and destroying the wholesome; therefore, one incurs the offense of *pārājika*.
○ Third, the precept against sexual misconduct:
In both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, this precept is termed "non-Brahmacarya. *Brahma* means purity; since the conduct is not pure, it is so named.
Thus, it defiles one’s own nature and also defiles the minds of others; therefore, it contradicts the pure Dharma and the person. The *Yi-shu* states:

"The five groups of the ordained community are all subject to this prohibition. For the two groups of the laity, however, only sexual misconduct is prohibited; that is to say, with the exception of one's own wife or concubines."
To externally violate any man or woman is entirely termed "deviant.
If you, O disciples of the Buddha, engage in sexual misconduct yourself or teach others to do so—even with any woman—you must not intentionally commit sexual acts or provide the causes for such acts.

The conditions for sexual misconduct, the nature of sexual misconduct, and the karma of sexual misconduct—the offense is the same whether committed by oneself or incited in another. Since a Great Being should bestow pure dharmas upon others to deliver them, one ought not instruct them in defiled actions.
As for "all women," this includes those of high or low status, beautiful or ugly, old or young, and those who are kin or strangers.
Therefore, it is said "up to and including. Regarding "one must not engage in intentional sexual misconduct": how could there be such a thing as unintentional lust?

If one encounters difficult circumstances and is forcibly coerced, or is seized by an evil person, if there is a mind that experiences pleasure, one commits the offense. What is meant by experiencing pleasure?
It is like obtaining food when hungry, or obtaining a drink when thirsty. What is meant by not experiencing pleasure? It is like eating excrement, or like [touching] hot iron.

This pertains to the body. The initial arising of a lustful thought constitutes the cause (*hetu*). The subsequent continuity of that lustful thought, which assists in its completion, constitutes the condition (*pratyaya*).
The application of skillful means constitutes the phenomenon (*dharma*). The accomplishment of the act constitutes the karma (*karman*).
"Even unto female animals, female devas, female spirits, and sexual intercourse via improper orifices. Regarding "even unto":
this refers to human men, women, eunuchs, and those with both sexual organs, down to female animals, female spirits, and so forth, as well as improper orifices.
As for "improper orifices," [intercourse via] the anus or the mouth constitutes a grave offense; as for the rest of the body...

[This constitutes] a division. One incurs a light offense. As prescribed in the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*, even with one's own wife, one is prohibited from [sexual intercourse] at improper times or in improper places.

"Improper time" refers to when she is pregnant, after childbirth, while nursing, or during her menstrual period. "Improper place" refers to non-vaginal orifice. In all such cases, one incurs the offense of impurity and the transgression of intentional action (*kṛta-āpatti*).
Yet a bodhisattva ought to give rise to a heart of filial piety and obedience to save and deliver all sentient beings and bestow the pure Dharma upon others;

yet instead, they further give rise to lust for all people, making no distinction even among animals, down to their own mothers, daughters, sisters, and other members of the six types of kin, engaging in sexual misconduct with them.
To lack a heart of compassion constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
That which should be generated refers to the great function of giving rise to filial piety and compassion within the fundamental essence of the mind-body in order to deliver sentient beings.
However, in saving sentient beings, one must preach for them the Dharma of detachment from defilement and the joy of purity; only then does it constitute self-benefit and the benefit of others.
How could one instead give rise to lustful thoughts? Therefore, one incurs a grave offense. Regarding the six relations (*ṣaḍbandhu*), four have already been mentioned in the sutra;
one should complete the number of six by including the wives of one's brothers. To commit an unlawful act among these six relations is what the world...
How rare! I fear that those with false views might claim that one has no fault in committing an offense against one's own kin.
For example, there was once a son who intended to commit an unrighteous act upon his mother’s body; as he approached her bedside, the earth suddenly split open and he fell into hell.
His mother hurriedly grasped at him in desperation, catching only a handful of hair, while his body had already sunk away. [Thus one must] receive the precepts.
How can one not be fearful?
○ Fourth, the precept against false speech:
knowing for oneself that it is untrue, yet deceiving and confusing another; because the mind and mouth are at variance, it is called "false speech."

If a Buddha’s disciple speaks falsehoods themselves, teaches others to speak falsehoods, or employs skillful means to speak falsehoods; or if they provide the causes for speaking falsehoods, the conditions for speaking falsehoods, the methods for speaking falsehoods, or the karmic actions of speaking falsehoods.
Regarding "lying by oneself": it means speaking to others oneself, saying, "I have attained the state of a superior person" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*). Regarding "inciting others to lie":

it means instructing another to speak to others, saying, "I have attained the state of a superior person," or instructing another to speak to others, saying, "I myself have attained the state of a superior person.

If the resulting fame or profit does not enter one's own possession, it constitutes a light offense. What is meant by the "state of a superior person"? It refers to that which is cultivated and realized by the noble ones (*ārya*).
Regarding the Dharma of realization: that which is cultivated consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and various dhyānas and samādhis;
that which is realized consists of the stages of the three levels of worthies (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages of sages (*daśārya*).

Because this Dharma is the most honored and supreme compared to all the tainted (*sāsrava*) dharmas of ordinary worldlings, it is called the "Dharma of Superior Persons" (*uttara-pudgala-dharma*). Regarding "deceptive speech through expedient means": [desiring...]
To utter false speech: first employing various kinds of clever words to cause another to believe and accept them; or sending a messenger to speak for one; or sending a letter;
or making gestures of understanding—if the other person comprehends these, one incurs a grave offense in all such cases.

Or, if one borrows the words of another to praise someone while secretly extolling oneself, this also constitutes an offense. The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* states: "If a bodhisattva, for the sake of others..."
Regarding what is praised as these "Ten Abodes," if an Arhat or similar practitioner accepts them in silence, they incur an offense.
If it is one of arrogant conceit who lacks a deceptive intent, they likewise commit a minor transgression;

because they have attained a small measure of realization and claim it to be actual proof, they give rise to pride in their mind regarding the superior supramundane dharmas, yet do not intentionally delude others.

For this reason, one does not incur a grave offense. The initial arousal of a deceptive mind serves as the cause; the continuity of deceptive thoughts that assists in accomplishing the deceptive act serves as the condition;
the employment of various deceptive methods and clever speech serves as the means; and the understanding and acceptance by the other person completes the karma.
"Even to claiming to see what one has not seen, or to claim not to see what one has seen—this is false speech of body and mind.

Regarding the term "even to" (*nāyattvā*): it refers back to the aforementioned great false speech and so forth, extending down to the minor false speech of claiming to have seen what one has not seen.
Although all six consciousnesses are capable of manifesting falsehood, here only the three of seeing, body, and mind are cited; this is an abbreviation. [From the] Vinaya.
The six consciousnesses are grouped into four: namely, seeing, hearing, touching, and cognizing. Seeing belongs to the visual consciousness; hearing belongs to the auditory consciousness;
and touching belongs to the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body, which are grouped together as one because these three are dull.

Cognizing is the mental consciousness. Thus, there are eight types of false speech in total: namely, saying one has seen what was not seen, saying one has heard what was not heard, [saying one has touched what was not touched,] and so forth.

To say one has touched when one has not touched; to say one knows when one does not know; to say one has seen when one has not seen; to say one has heard when one has not heard; or to say one has not touched when one has touched;
to say one does not know when one knows—engaging in any one of these is termed false speech.

However, if it is for the sake of saving the lives of sentient beings, or to benefit another person through skillful means, this is the great being’s mind of sacrificing oneself to benefit others; there is no offense. It is just as...
Although it generates much merit,
if a bodhisattva constantly produces right speech and right view for themselves, yet also produces right speech and right view in all sentient beings,
and then conversely gives rise to wrong speech, wrong view, and wrong action in those very sentient beings, this constitutes a pārājika offense for that bodhisattva.

"Sin. "Constantly arising" refers to not forgetting [the truth]. This means that a Bodhisattva, within the essence of the fundamental source-mind, constantly gives rise to right speech and right view;
they do not erroneously call the ordinary person a sage, nor mistake the false for the true, and they likewise cause all [beings] to do so.
Sentient beings give rise to the sublime causes of right speech and right view; this is the Bodhisattva’s fundamental aspiration to benefit living beings.

Yet, if one instead causes them to produce wrong speech and wrong views, thereby committing wrong actions so that they never obtain pleasant retributions throughout their lives and suffer endless bitter fruits, this greatly violates the Bodhisattva’s vow of conduct to benefit beings. It harms both oneself and others, and thus incurs grave transgression.
○ The fifth precept concerns the selling of intoxicants.
"Selling" refers to buying and selling; it includes either brewing and selling them oneself or purchasing goods to resell. Alcohol is a toxic drug that deludes people;

in the present life, it ruins one's affairs and endangers the body, while in future lives, it causes the loss of the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*). A Mahāsattva is dedicated solely to benefiting sentient beings.
It is solely due to the mind that wisdom is produced; therefore, drinking for oneself constitutes a light offense, while selling it constitutes a grave offense.
O disciples of the Buddha: to sell alcohol oneself, to teach others to sell alcohol, or to engage in the causes, conditions, methods, and karmic actions of selling alcohol—[these are all prohibited].
If one sells oneself, this is an act committed by oneself; if one instructs another to sell oneself for one's own profit, it is an act caused by another to be done for oneself.
Since the benefit accrues to oneself, both constitute a grave offense (*pārājika*). If one instructs another to sell themselves [for their own benefit], the offense is lighter.

However, since the Great Being takes the salvation of sentient beings as his primary purpose, although the profit goes to the other, the fact that it harms the body and destroys wisdom is equivalent [to harming oneself]; thus, he too should incur a grave offense, as it binds the minds of sentient beings in perversion.

This is an offense. It is not a formal act (saṃghāvaśeṣa) committed for the sake of profit. The initial arising of the intention to sell is the cause. The subsequent continuity of that mind which assists in accomplishing the act of selling is the condition.
Skillful craftsmanship is the constituent factor (dharma). The completion of the sale is the action (karman).
One must not sell any kind of alcohol. Such alcohol is a causal condition for the arising of transgressions.
"Any kind of alcohol" refers to that which is fermented from the five grains, or concocted from roots, leaves, medicinal herbs, various flowers, or fruits—whether raw or cooked.
It includes anything possessing the color of alcohol, the fragrance of alcohol, or the taste of alcohol, even if one of these is lacking.
Two items are omitted. Whether it be yeast or dregs, anything that can cause intoxication may not be sold. The *Yi-shu* (Explanatory Commentary) states:
"Although medicinal liquor may involve the pursuit of profit, there is no offense if it does not cause intoxication.

Since medicine can cure illness and bring peace to the body, how much more so when one cannot drink much of it and thus lacks the affliction of intoxication and confusion; therefore, there is no offense. This refers to a lay bodhisattva’s governance [of such matters].
It is opened for those who support their families; it is not permitted for those who have left the household life, as [drinking] constitutes a wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
Regarding the causes and conditions for the arising of offenses: all sinful evils and transgressions arise from alcohol;
thus it is said that "alcohol possesses thirty-six faults. This is what is meant.
If a bodhisattva should instead give rise to the perverted mind of all sentient beings, when they ought to have given rise to the clear and penetrating wisdom of all sentient beings,
this constitutes a pārājika offense for that bodhisattva.

Regarding "the wisdom of clear penetration": it is called "clear" (*ming*) because wisdom can shatter the dark alleys of affliction; it is called "penetrating" (*da*) because it reaches directly to the fundamental source, the mind-ground.
A Great Being should employ various skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to inspire sentient beings and cause them to give rise to wondrous wisdom;

therefore, it is said they "should produce" it. Because they fail to distinguish between the two paths of the heterodox and the orthodox, they are deluded regarding the truth and pursue the false; therefore, it is said:
To be inverted: to fail to enlighten them with sublime wisdom and instead bestow upon them delusion—this is called "producing perversity.
It causes sentient beings to fall into inversion and lose their life of wisdom; therefore, one incurs a grave offense.
The sixth is the precept concerning the proclamation of the faults of the fourfold assembly.
To expose the transgressions of others gravely harms the Dharma-gate, diminishes the virtue of those who came before, and cuts off the hopes of sentient beings.
It profoundly contradicts the Great Being’s fundamental vow to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma, and greatly violates the Bodhisattva’s compassionate mind that benefits living beings.
Because the Śrāvakas prioritize their own benefit, they distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles; since transgressions vary in severity, they impose formal disciplinary measures accordingly.

For a Bodhisattva who prioritizes the benefit of others, however, if one speaks with a malicious intent, the offense is grave regardless of its magnitude, and in all such cases, a heavy transgression is incurred.
If a disciple of the Buddha, whether a lay bodhisattva or a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, personally speaks of the transgressions of others, or teaches others to speak of their transgressions—
their causes of transgression, their conditions for transgression, their methods of transgression, and their karmic actions of transgression.
The renunciant bodhisattva refers to the five groups of renunciants who have received the *cittabhūmi* precepts.
The lay bodhisattva refers to the two groups of upāsakas and upāsikās who have received the *mahāsattva* precepts.

The bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs refer to those who have received the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) but have not yet received the bodhisattva precepts; these constitute the fourfold assembly within the Dharma.

"Transgression" refers to the fault of violating the precepts. Whatever one says that causes harm to oneself, distresses sentient beings, or impairs the fundamental source of one's own mind-ground is such a transgression.
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "All speech by those who have left the household life should be for the sake of benefit;
one must not privately speak of others out of resentment. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "It would be better to destroy a stupa..."
Do not disparage images. Do not speak of the faults or evils of bhikṣus to others; if one speaks of their transgressions, it destroys the Dharma-body of the Buddha.
As for teaching others to speak [of such faults], this may be done by verbal instruction, by signaling with gestures, by sending a messenger, or by sending someone with a letter.
If a Mahāsattva sees that the assembly of the Dharma has faults, he should immediately regard them with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of compassion, and protective mindfulness.
With a sincere mind, one should encourage and earnestly admonish them to repent and reform. One must not harbor private motives to ruin another's reputation or interests;
by doing so, one will personally avoid the enmity that lasts for ten thousand generations and further escape the fault of defiling the True Dharma.

If they do not change after three admonitions, one may report the matter to the assembly of monks. Acting with a heart of compassion and a desire to protect the Dharma, one commits no offense. If one speaks as previously described...
If a person holds wrong views, they do not incur an offense, even though they may still generate much merit. Why is this?

It is because the conduct of a Great Being (Mahāsattva) for the benefit of sentient beings requires that the heterodox and the orthodox be distinguished; one must not lead many people onto a false path.
If one has been appointed by the Sangha and speaks with a public mind rather than with a private mind, there is no offense, as in the case of Devadatta.
He committed a heinous offense (*ānantarya-karma*). The Buddha ordered the Saṃgha to perform a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) and dispatched Śāriputra to a layperson’s home to preach.

This is it. Taking the initial arising of the intention to speak as the cause, and the subsequent mental assistance that brings about the act of speaking as the condition, employing various skillful means of eloquent exposition as the method, the listener’s comprehension constitutes the completion of the karma. The *Yi-shu* states: "There are two ways of speaking: first, to lead [the listener] into error..."
The first is the intent to cause another to lose reputation, profit, and so forth. The second is the intent to subject another to imprisonment and the like.
These two states of mind constitute the primary factor for the offense. Regarding the determination of the gravity of the offense:
one view holds that it depends on the person; the other holds that it depends on the verbal karma. If it depends on the person, then speaking toward a single individual constitutes one grave offense.
Regarding offenses: for every word that issues from the mouth, one incurs a grave offense.

However, when a Bodhisattva hears heterodox practitioners or those of the two vehicles speak what is not the Dharma and not the Vinaya within the Buddha-dharma, they should always give rise to a mind of compassion and teach these wicked people, causing them to develop wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna.
"Non-Buddhists" (tīrthika) refers to the ninety-five types of heterodox followers in India and the secular teachings of the various schools and masters in this land [China].
Because their teachings stop at cultivating the self, regulating the family, and governing the state, they are called "external.

The sacred teachings of the Three Vehicles instruct one to still the delusions of the mind and awaken to the fundamental ground of the mind; therefore, they are called "internal. Non-Buddhists do not believe in their own minds.
This Buddha originally possessed the virtues of his nature, yet he became deluded regarding the truth and pursued the false, taking the deviant for the correct and creating unwholesome karma;

therefore, he is called an "evil person. Those of the Two Vehicles do not know the source-ground of the mind; they loathe the five aggregates of body and mind, sever the afflictions of views and thoughts, and realize the principle of partial emptiness.
Remaining alone beyond the three realms, they lack the heart to save and deliver others; they, too, are called "evil persons."
That which is neither Dharma nor Vinaya refers to the Dharma and Vinaya of the Source-Mind Ground (*cittabhūmi*) of the Mahāyāna;

it is not like the heterodox teachings of external paths that deny the causes and effects of the three periods of time, nor like the worldly laws and codes that disparage and reject one's own mind and self-nature.

The false claim that "qi gives rise to qi" is a mistaken view. It differs from the approach of those of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas), who cultivate the Dharma of the Four Truths and the Vinaya of the Five Sections and Seven Groups out of their aversion to suffering and aspiration for tranquility; therefore, that statement is incorrect.

Furthermore, this refers to beginners among those of the Two Vehicles, not to those who have realized the fruits of the Two Vehicles. Those who have realized the fruits know for themselves that they possess the Great [Vehicle].
Riding upon the Dharma and Vinaya, one realizes that by one's own power alone it cannot be practiced; therefore, this is not what they [the Hinayanists] teach.
It is intended to give rise to wholesome faith in the Mahayana, leading one to believe that the great precepts of the mind-ground are inherently possessed by both oneself and others.

There is no evil that is not ceased, no good that is not cultivated, and no sentient being who is not delivered. The Buddhas are those who have already attained Buddhahood; you are a Buddha who has not yet attained it. Just so...
It is for the sake of those with good faith.
Yet, if a Bodhisattva instead speaks of the faults and transgressions within the Buddha-dharma himself, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for that Bodhisattva.
A Great Being should even teach others not to speak of such things, as their mind is intent on bringing peace to all beings; to do the opposite and speak of them oneself is to cause one's own ruin.
Those who come before [us] have deeply harmed the True Dharma and brought ruin upon their own virtue; where, then, is the conduct of a Bodhisattva?

When people today wish to speak of the faults of others, those faults are few indeed, yet the speaker incurs a karmic offense with every word spoken. How can the gravity of such offenses be described?
It is only because they do not fear the causes and effects of sin and merit that they speak of others' faults out of a heart of private resentment.
They utter venomous words, fearing only that they are not deep enough; they raise their voices to proclaim faults, desiring them to pervade the entire earth.
They seek only immediate gratification, caring nothing for the calamities that follow after death—the plowing of their tongues by the plowshare. Question: Does the Buddha-dharma tolerate such flaws?
Answer: The Buddha commanded that every half-month the *poṣadha* (confessional assembly) be held to examine the three types of action (*trikarma*).

If one has committed an offense, one must disclose it to eliminate the transgression; if there is no fault, one may cultivate pure virtue. If one does not confess of one’s own accord, those who witness it shall admonish them in private.

For minor offenses, one is made to repent and eliminate them before another person; for grave sins, one is made to see auspicious signs. If one still refuses to speak of them, then [the confession] is performed before the assembly.
The community shall deliberate. If one does not acknowledge their transgression, the Sangha shall subject them to the *karmavācanā* rite for "not seeing one's fault" to discipline them.
If a disciple commits an offense, the teacher should instruct them well to reform; if they do not see their fault, the teacher shall expel them and not dwell with them.

This is how the purity and turbidity of the Buddha-dharma distinguish themselves; how could it be like using a private mind to broadcast evil, only then claiming that others' faults cannot be tolerated?
Yes. The rest is as clarified in the precept on not instructing others to repent for their offenses.
○ Seventh, the precept against self-praise and disparaging others:
extolling one’s own merits is called "self-praise," while reviling the faults and evils of others is called "disparaging others. This [precept] protects oneself and benefits others, concealing...
To suppress evil and promote good is the fundamental practice of a Mahāsattva for benefiting sentient beings. To praise oneself and revile others benefits oneself while harming others;
this is not the compassionate mind or the virtuous mind of a Bodhisattva.

If a disciple of the Buddha praises themselves and disparages others, or likewise teaches others to praise themselves and disparage others— whether through the causes for disparaging others, the conditions for disparaging others, the methods for disparaging others,
or the karmic actions of disparaging others.
To praise oneself and disparage others is to simultaneously elevate oneself and suppress another; when both these acts are present, it constitutes a grave offense.
There are two ways of instructing others: first, instructing them to praise oneself and disparage others—either by manifesting such intent directly, or by sending a messenger with a letter;
second, instructing them to praise their own virtues while belittling and disparaging others. In each case, the initial arising of the intention to praise and disparage serves as the cause.
Next, the continuity of the mind acts as a contributing condition. By means of various skillful methods of praise and censure, one takes this as the dharma;

when the other person understands and accepts it, the karmic action is established. Among these four phrases, only the censure of others is mentioned, while self-praise is not explicitly stated because it would merely be a matter of literary style.
Furthermore, the mindfulness of self-praise is slight, whereas the malicious intent in censuring others is particularly heavy; therefore, the heavier case is cited to encompass the other.
This is frivolous.
Yet a bodhisattva should, on behalf of all sentient beings, undergo abuse and humiliation; they should direct evil toward themselves and give good to others.
If one were to extol one's own virtues, conceal the good deeds of others, and cause others to suffer disgrace, this is [frivolous].
Regarding the *pārājika* offenses of a bodhisattva:

herein it is revealed that one must be able to undergo [the consequences] on their behalf so as not to let them suffer humiliation. One draws evil toward oneself; one must never engage in self-praise.
One dedicates excellence to others, ensuring by all means that no one else suffers disgrace. "To manifest" (*yang*) means to extol; "to conceal" (*yin*) means to hide.
To conceal one's own faults is to fear that others may surpass oneself; to hide the virtues of others is to worry that they may excel me.
To know only how to benefit oneself and not consider harming others is not the mind of a Great Being who turns evil toward themselves and pushes goodness toward others.

To praise oneself and disparage others is precisely the work of the "house-owner" (the karmic master), and thus incurs grave retribution. If it is for the purpose of luring others away from heterodox paths...

They return to the True Path. While they disparage the Two Vehicles to bring them into accord with the One Vehicle, their speech may seem like censure, yet their heart is truly one of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
This is the compassionate mind of a Great Being (*mahāsattva*) who pities sentient beings and propagates the teaching; it is the great vow that establishes the banner of the Dharma.
How could such a person be compared on the same level as those who argue over self and other, or over victory and defeat? The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* says:

If one disparages non-Buddhists in order to praise the Buddha-dharma, or uses skillful means to subdue them so that those without faith may gain faith and those with faith may increase and expand it, there is no offense.
○ The eighth is the precept against stinginess and malicious disparagement.
To refuse to give wealth or the Dharma when requested is called "stinginess. To respond with anger, resentment, and verbal abuse is called "malicious disparagement.
This greatly violates the Way of compassion and profoundly contradicts the intention to benefit all beings.

If a disciple of the Buddha is stingy themselves, teaches others to be stingy, or engages in the causes of stinginess, the conditions for stinginess, the methods of stinginess, or the karmic actions of stinginess—then they have failed in the practice of a Great Being.

A Great Being practices the *dāna-pāramitā* (perfection of giving) by not discriminating between the close and the distant; they give everything to those who ask, never distinguishing between what is good and what is bad.
If one fails to give and instead inflicts abuse, it constitutes a profound violation of the Bodhisattva’s Threefold Pure Precepts. As for being stingy oneself:
whether by speaking with the mouth, displaying signs of stinginess, or remaining hidden to avoid giving wealth or the Dharma; or by saying "I have none," or driving others away with a staff.
Or by using harsh words and insults; or by teaching others to be stingy, such as instructing them to keep wealth and the Dharma secret rather than giving them away;
or by instructing them to inflict harm; whether through verbal instruction or by sending a messenger with a letter to give such instruction.

The initial arising of the mind of stinginess serves as the cause, while the subsequent mental factors that assist in completing that stinginess serve as the conditions. These include various skillful words and methods of parsimony.

Dharma. The preceding person understands this; its function is the accomplishment of stinginess. Regarding these four phrases, the reason it does not mention "adding insult to injury" is that such insult follows first from stinginess.
If there is insult alone without stinginess, it belongs to the minor defilement precept.
The *Upāli-paripṛcchā-sūtra* asks: "Among the root offenses, which is the most grave? The Buddha said: "Abiding in the Mahāyāna Bodhi..."

Sā. Suppose one were to commit as many offenses of greed as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; when compared with a single offense of anger, between these two offenses, anger alone is the more serious.
Why is this? One who manifests anger abandons sentient beings, whereas one who manifests greed loves and protects sentient beings, and thus does not become a source of affliction.
Consequently, for a bodhisattva, there is no fear of calamities or misfortunes. Therefore...
The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* asks: What is the meaning of anger (*dveṣa*)? It refers to one who, by their very nature, commits great transgressions and fails to give rise to skillful compassion.
To act with malice and wrath is not beneficial; rather, it nourishes afflictions (*kleśa*), diminishes compassion, and constitutes a grave fault.
This precept concerns stinginess: thus, out of parsimony regarding wealth, one inflicts harm and disparagement. If one were greedy yet capable of giving, [it would be different].
Thus, there will be no further faults such as disparagement or anger. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:

"If one has previously contemplated giving even slightly but ultimately does not give, one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). If one speaks of giving but does not give, one falls into the realm of hell (*naraka*).
How much more so regarding unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), which involves making a complete vow to give to all sentient beings in all worlds without exception."
Yet, when a bodhisattva sees any poor person or beggar, they should give them everything according to that person's needs.
However, if with an evil mind or a mind of anger, they do not bestow even a single coin, a single needle, or a single blade of grass;

or if there is one who seeks the Dharma, they do not explain for them even a single word, a single verse, or a fragment of Dharma as small as a mote of dust, but instead further revile and insult them.
This constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
"All" refers to monastics and laypeople, both male and female. There are two kinds of poverty: first, physical poverty, which requires material wealth and should be met with the giving of wealth;
second, mental poverty, which requires the Dharma and should be met with the giving of the Dharma. Therefore, it is said that one should provide everything according to what is required.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-sūtra* states: "A lay bodhisattva should practice two kinds of giving: first, material wealth; second, the Dharma.
A renunciant bodhisattva should practice four kinds of giving: first, paper; second, ink; third, pens; and fourth, the Dharma.
Because renunciants possess no material wealth, these items—paper, ink, and pens—are few and easily obtained; since they facilitate the transcription of scriptures, these are also termed 'Dharma.'"
Regarding giving: a Bodhisattva who has attained forbearance practices three kinds of giving: first, the royal throne; second, wife and children; third, head, eyes, skin, and bones.
An ordinary person Bodhisattva should give according to their power and as is appropriate. There are, however, certain things that are not fit to be given.
Alternatively, if their faculties are dull and inferior; or if they are not vessels for the Dharma; or if, upon hearing the profound Dharma, they instead give rise to slander;
or if a woman seeks the Dharma but lacks a male relative by her side—then it is inappropriate to preach it to them. As for those to whom wealth should not be given:
if giving wealth might cause them to commit evil, or lead to calamity through that wealth, even to the point of endangering their lives, then one should not give it.
One should practice giving. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* asks: "How can a bodhisattva obtain immeasurable fruit from a small root of goodness?
This bodhisattva instructs inferior sentient beings to give even a small amount of material wealth to an inferior field of merit, or even to offer a single morsel of roasted flour to an animal.
Having given, they dedicate the merit toward unsurpassed enlightenment; by the power of this dedication, [immeasurable fruit is obtained].

One attains immeasurable fruits. Regarding "and so forth" (*paryanta*): in terms of material wealth, it ranges from the most abundant down to the very least—a single needle or a single blade of grass.
This refers to those who possess no wealth and are thus unable to give as they wish. In terms of the Dharma, it ranges from extensive expositions.
Even if one possesses only the very minimum—a single phrase or a mere speck of dust—one is called "of meager knowledge and unlearned," for one cannot explain extensively.
If there is truly no Dharma, one must not falsely boast of one's ability; to speak erroneously and mislead others incurs no small transgression.
To possess [the Dharma] yet refuse to bestow it, while instead adding insults and abuse, is to possess both stinginess and slander; this is precisely karma.

Master, one thus incurs a grave offense. There are, however, cases where no offense is committed: for instance, if one perceives that by means of reproach the person will repent, or through subjugation they will reform their evil ways;
and if one has no personal malice or anger, but acts for the benefit of others according to their capacity—this is the sublime and skillful application of the Great Being’s expedient means.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra* states: "If one knows that not speaking [the truth] will cause them to be tamed; if one knows..."
The former person is unable to show respect; or if their deportment is disordered; or if they possess dull faculties and, upon hearing the profound and subtle Dharma, give rise to a mind of fear;
or if it is known that after hearing it, their wrong views will increase; or if, having heard it, they will revile it and fall away.
Or, having heard [the transgression], one speaks of it to an evil person to destroy the True Dharma; in such cases, there is no offense.
○ Ninth: The precept against receiving an apology with a mind of anger.
Whether another has offended oneself or oneself has offended another, that person recognizes their fault and seeks [forgiveness] with a sincere heart.
Confession. Yet, the bodhisattva harbors anger within while outwardly manifesting an appearance of not accepting it.
O disciples of the Buddha, whether one is angry oneself, teaches others to be angry, or engages in the causes of anger, the conditions for anger, the methods of anger, or the karmic actions of anger.
Regarding "one who is angry": internally harboring resentment and anger, one externally manifests this through body and speech. Teaching others [to do so] is explained as before in the precepts.

Taking the initial arousal of the mind of anger as the cause (*hetu*), the subsequent continuity of that mind as the contributing condition (*pratyaya*), the various methods of beating and reviling as the phenomenon (*dharma*), and the actual performance of these acts as the karma (*karma*).
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "When a single thought of anger arises, a million gates of obstruction open."
Kai said: "One should know that even a single initial thought is already like this; how much more so when conditions continue in succession? If karma is not formed, there will be no retribution;

but once karma is formed, calamity descends and one sinks into the depths of samsara. Enmity becomes bound for ten thousand generations, never to be resolved from life to life. How can one not be cautious?"

Furthermore, a bodhisattva should give rise to the roots of goodness in all sentient beings and engage in matters free from contention. They should constantly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, as well as a mind of filial piety and obedience.
Although the ground of the minds of all sentient beings is fundamentally good, it is obscured and obstructed by ignorance and afflictions. Great...
A practitioner should, with a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, give rise to the roots of goodness of compassion, pity, and equanimity toward sentient beings;
thus, there will be no occasion for strife. How much less should one refuse an apology and instead incite further contention?
Constantly regarding all sentient beings as one's own infant, how could one bear to insult or humiliate them? This is what is meant by a mind of loving-kindness and compassion. Always...
To regard all sentient beings as one’s own parents—how could one dare to act in opposition to them? This is the mind of filial piety and obedience.
Yet, on the contrary, one further reviles and insults all sentient beings, even those who are not sentient beings, with harsh speech;

moreover, one strikes them with the hand or attacks them with knives and staves, without ceasing in intent. Even when the other person seeks reconciliation and offers sincere words of repentance, [one remains unyielding].
If one repents yet remains angry and does not resolve it, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.

Since a Mahāsattva is able to generate the roots of goodness in sentient beings and is further constantly compassionate and filial, there would be no reason for him to instead oppress or afflict them.
"Non-sentient beings" refers to the noble ones of the Three Vehicles and manifested beings (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*). To revile or insult them...
This constitutes verbal karma; striking with the hand constitutes physical karma; and not ceasing [the offense] constitutes mental karma.

By inflicting affliction through these three types of karma, which is more severe than that of wolves or tigers, and because one does not cease or resolve [the transgression], one incurs a grave offense. One who does not commit [this offense] is as follows:
perhaps the other person’s heart of repentance is not sincere, or their thought of apologizing is not earnest; thus, the Bodhisattva, out of a heart of compassion, ultimately desires...
Causing them to profoundly reform their past transgressions so that they shall not commit them again, he then manifests an appearance of wrath.
Or, he may subdue unruly sentient beings—those shameless, evil-natured, and heterodox individuals. While outwardly displaying majesty, his heart is truly compassionate;
while verbally rebuking and censuring, his thoughts are filled with pity. This is the Great Being’s method for taming sentient beings who are stubborn and fierce.
This is a great function; how could it be compared with those who possess the three poisons? The *Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra* states: "Regarding 'not committing an offense':
if one employs skillful means to subdue them, or if they do not repent according to the Dharma and their mind is not impartial such that they do not accept the repentance, there is no offense."
○ The tenth precept concerns slandering the Triple Gem.

This refers to slandering and confusing the True Dharma through one's own false views; it does not refer to the act of reviling or abusing it. Even if one were to revile it, the offense could still be repented of.
Therefore, the *Śīlasūtra* calls this the "precept against slandering and confusing the True Dharma," and it is also termed the "precept against slandering the Bodhisattva-piṭaka."
Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha: to personally slander the Triple Gem, to teach others to slander the Triple Gem, to slander its causes, its conditions, its teachings, and its karma;

to take what is false for what is true, and what is true for what is false; and to revile and slander the sūtras and vinaya of the Bodhisattvas, saying they were not spoken by the Buddha—this is [a grave offense].

To denigrate the World-Honored One is to slander the Mahāyāna sūtras; this is to slander the Dharma. To claim that those who receive, uphold, read, and recite [these teachings] are not disciples of the Buddha is to slander the Saṃgha.
Alternatively, one may personally give rise to false understanding and establish erroneous doctrines, claiming them to be correct;
or, having received erroneous speech from a false teacher, one composes false books—such as equating the words of Laozi and Zhuangzi with those of the Buddha.

These teachings on the arts of governing the world, when compared to the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, confuse and delude the hearts of people, mislead later students, cause them to lose the Right Path forever, and lead them to fall into heterodox ways.

Because these have been propagated to posterity and spread without ceasing, they leave behind calamities for ten thousand kalpas and sever the seeds of Buddha-nature. The sins incurred by this are not merely those of an icchantika; there is no place [to escape them].

It is possible [to commit this offense]. Taking the initial arising of a mind of false interpretation as the cause (*hetu*), the continuity of that false mind which assists in accomplishing the act of slander as the condition (*pratyaya*), and skillfully explaining the methods of false views as the means (*dharma*), the person before one understands and accepts it, thereby completing the karma.
If one intends to speak but has not yet uttered the words, the grave offense is not yet incurred. However, if one speaks the words oneself toward that person, or causes another to speak them...
According to tradition, if a person accepts false teachings, they incur one grave offense for each word they follow.
If they compose false writings, those who read and understand them incur a grave offense for every single word.
If a bodhisattva sees a non-Buddhist or an evil person utter even a single word of slander against the Buddha’s voice, it is as if three hundred spears were piercing his heart;

how much more so if they themselves slander him with their own mouths? If such a person fails to give rise to faith or a heart of filial obedience, and instead assists that evil person or heretic who slanders, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for the bodhisattva.
Those followers of heterodox schools in India and in this land—even those who seek dharmas outside the mind of a Bodhisattva—are all termed "outsiders" (tīrthika).
Because they do not believe in the Mahāyāna or the eternally abiding Triple Gem, they abandon the great precepts of the mind-ground and instead study the heterodox teachings of false paths.
By repudiating the karmic retribution of good and evil, they are called "evil persons. As for the phrase "a single word," it is because...
At the very least, it is like three hundred spears piercing one's heart; how much more so when such words are spoken at will and the sound of slander spreads abroad.

How could the mind of a Great Being endure this? It is truly out of compassion for those with false views who have sunk themselves into the mire of hell and further lead immeasurable sentient beings to fall mistakenly into the currents of suffering.
Thus, it is as if spears pierce his heart; it does not mean that he harbors anger toward those who slander and defame the Three [Jewels].
Cherish this thought. The essence of the Three Jewels is like the sun and the moon; it cannot be obscured by a single finger.
It would be like throwing an axe to strike the heavens and instead injuring one's own body. A Great Being originally receives these true precepts through faith and filial piety;
they should always revere and comply with the Three Jewels without opposition or contrariness. How could one, on the contrary, further side with those of evil views and heterodox followers?
If one delights in being a follower of external paths (tīrthika), one will forever lose the great precepts of the Bodhisattva’s mind-ground and no longer bear the name of a Buddha-son.
If one has not yet turned away from the correct path to return to the heterodox, one has not yet lost the precepts. One might even think and say: "The Three Jewels are not equal to external paths."
The Mahāyāna does not equal the Two Vehicles; when one’s deliberations are not yet perfected, one commits a minor offense (*laghu-āpatti*).

Although one believes in cause and effect, the Three Jewels, and the Mahāyāna, yet further believes that non-Buddhist deities and spirits possess power, efficacy, and inspiration, and consequently imitates their talismans, documents, and ritual offerings to exorcise demons and malevolent spirits—or even encourages others to believe and accept such things—one commits a minor offense in every instance. Or, if one clings to the Great...

Furthermore, to slander the Hīnayāna by claiming that there is no Hīnayāna at all, but only Mahāyāna, and that the four Āgamas and the Prātimokṣa Sūtra were not spoken by the Buddha—this is to slander the Śrāvaka Piṭaka and constitutes a secondary offense (light defilement).

How can one know that the Buddhas of the three periods appear in the world and establish teachings according to the capacities of sentient beings, teaching all three vehicles? The four fruits of the Śrāvaka are indeed the means for transcending the world.

The sages and worthies are the field of merit for humans and devas; how can they be treated with such levity? It is only because they lacked the intention to benefit living beings that the Buddha rebuked them.
Nowadays, beginners cannot even distinguish between millet and wheat; their understanding of Chan and the Teachings remains muddled.
