They flaunt their shallow knowledge and indulge in their own erroneous words, claiming that observing the precepts is merely clinging to signs, and thus they abandon them without receiving them. The Buddha calls such people "shaven-headed dwellers."
A practitioner may accept [the precepts] but fail to uphold them; the Vinaya calls such a person "a worn-out bag in the ocean of suffering.

If one despises and abandons the complete precepts, claiming they need not be received, one incurs a minor offense of defilement (*āpatti*). These ten grave precepts are all natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).

In the Hīnayāna, alcohol is considered a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*); however, for a Mahāsattva, benefiting sentient beings is the primary aim. Since alcohol causes others' minds to become deluded, [it is prohibited].
It is also categorized as a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) refer to the eight types of ethical conduct (*śīla*) of body and speech—namely, the three of the body and the four of speech—with the addition of abstaining from alcohol to guard the mental ground and thereby ensure a pure livelihood."

That is to say, among the ten wholesome paths of action, these correspond to the latter three mental actions (*manas-karman*). Although their enumerations differ, their meaning is no different. Regarding what is called a "natural offense" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*):
it is so named because it is inherently evil by its very nature, independent of any prohibition established by the Buddha. The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā-śāstra* states:

"As for natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*), regardless of whether one has received the precepts or not, to violate them constitutes an offense; to observe them, whether one has received them or not, constitutes merit."
Excellent. If one receives the precepts, maintaining them generates merit, while violating them incurs guilt. If one does not receive them, there is no merit;

yet if one violates them, there is no offense against the precepts, only the fault of misconduct and the guilt of a karmic path. To say that one incurs guilt by violating what has been received refers to offenses regarding natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Furthermore, it constitutes a transgression that further violates the precepts. ○ Third, the summary:
"O virtuous students, you noble ones, this is the Bodhisattva’s ten Pratimokṣa; you should train yourselves therein. Within this, do not...
One should not commit even a single transgression as small as a mote of dust, let alone committing all ten precepts in their entirety.
To practice without contradicting the fundamental source, the mind-ground, is called "skillful training. A person who brings benefit through compassion is called a "benevolent one" (*renzhe*).
These are the honorable titles by which the Tathāgata praised those who train in and uphold the precepts; he exhorted that they should be studied and maintained. If...
If one violates it, one immediately incurs the extremely grave offense of *pārājika*, which will bring about the retribution of suffering in the Avīci Hell.
To uphold it is itself a sublime cause; one shall realize *mokṣa* (liberation) and secure the ultimate fruit of deliverance.
Because this fruit is supreme, it is not called *pārājika*, but rather *prātimokṣa*. This is precisely the fruit.
The cause is explained within the fruit. The cause is the functional activity of *prajñā*-wisdom; the fruit is the quiescent essence of *tathatā*.

Because function arises in accordance with the essence, ignorance is extinguished and the original *dharmakāya* is perceived; this is what is meant by "explaining the cause within the fruit. Guifeng said:

"By relying on *tathatā*, one gives rise to wisdom, severs delusions, realizes the essence, and manifests its function. If one does not rely upon it, then one grasps at a self and what belongs to a self."

Since there is no means by which the characterized [phenomena] can be cultivated or realized, we know that the myriad virtues and myriad practices are all the functioning of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, they are able to give rise to the earnest aspiration for the fruit in a beginner and ensure that the resolve to strictly uphold the prohibitive precepts is firm;
this is also explaining the cause within the context of the fruit. "Among them" refers to among the ten grave precepts. "Even so much as a speck of dust" refers to...
This cites a small case to illustrate the many. If one who has committed even a minor offense is no longer called a bodhisattva, how much more so for one who fully violates the ten precepts?

Such a person loses the primary cause and the ultimate fruit, and will surely experience endless retribution for their evil deeds. Therefore, the following passage demonstrates these gains and losses.
If there are those who commit such offenses, they shall not be able to give rise to the bodhicitta in their present bodies;

they shall also lose the rank of a king or the rank of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), and they shall likewise lose the status of a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, as well as the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, and the ten adamantine stages.

The ten stages, the Buddha-nature, and the eternally abiding wondrous fruit—all will be lost. One will fall into the three evil realms for two or three kalpas, during which time one shall not hear the names of father, mother, or the Triple Gem.
For this reason, one must not commit any of these transgressions one by one.
Violating the precepts is like cutting off the head of a tree; the sprout of Bodhi has already withered, and therefore it can certainly not sprout in this present body.
A king is the lord of one realm, while a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) is the lord of four, three, two, or one world-system.
Both such kings have attained these superior rewards through maintaining the precepts over many lifetimes. Now, if...
If one accepts [the precepts] and yet violates them, then the virtue and status of one's nobility will diminish daily, and the superior retribution of future lives will be lost.

For both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it is fundamentally by means of the precepts that they receive their names; if they violate this Prātimokṣa, not only will they lose the title of "Mahāsattva," but their original names will also be forfeited.
It is not merely that they lose their titles and positions, but even the [stages of] the Three Worthies and Ten Sages...
The Buddha-nature and the eternally abiding wondrous fruit are both lost. As for the "wondrous fruit," it refers to the fruit of Buddhahood of wondrous enlightenment.
It is not merely that one loses the great benefits mentioned above forever; after this body perishes, one will fall into the three evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Once fallen into these evil realms, one cannot be liberated for thousands of births or ten thousand ages. Therefore, for two kalpas—
For three kalpas, one shall not even hear the names of worldly parents; if their very names cannot be heard, how could one cultivate the filial path of reverence and obedience?
Furthermore, since the names of the Three Jewels that transcend the world cannot be heard, how can one recognize the practice for realizing the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood?
Such a great loss exists; therefore, one must firmly uphold each precept, even to the point of breaking them [to pieces].

The physical bones [of the Buddha] must not be treated with even the slightest disrespect. As the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) states: "If one violates the ten precepts, it cannot be rectified through repentance;

one enters the *pārājika* [offense]. For ten kalpas, one undergoes suffering for a single day; eighty-four thousand extinctions and eighty-four thousand births [result from this]. Therefore, they must not be violated.
[This applies to all stages], from the three levels of the worthy (*sādhaka*) and the ten stages of the sage (*ārya*), up to the stage of awakening (*bodhi-bhūmi*). All...
All are lost. Therefore, this precept is the root of the practice of all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas.
It is impossible that any Buddha or Bodhisattva could attain the fruit of a noble one (ārya-phala) without relying on this dharma-gate of the ten precepts.
All you bodhisattvas—those who are now training, those who shall train, and those who have already trained—should train in these ten precepts;
you should respectfully uphold them. The eighty thousand categories of dignified conduct shall be explained in detail.
This precept is that which the Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time have studied together, maintained together, and jointly realized as the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood.

For this reason, the Tathāgata has exhorted us with repeated earnestness to study and maintain it. If one wishes for a detailed elucidation of the nature and characteristics of its observance and transgression:
This should be examined in detail within the "Chapter on the Eighty Thousand Modes of Conduct" in the latter section of the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra].
What is now being explained is merely a brief outline of the ten inexhaustible treasuries of precepts.
In the third fascicle of the *Brief Commentary on the "Bodhisattva’s Ground" Chapter of the Buddha-spoken Brahma-net Sūtra*, regarding the phonetic gloss for "ji-bō" (機撥):
it refers to a mechanical device (*kìguān*) that causes objects or people to lean and trigger movement; it is synonymous with being bound and falling into [rebirth].
The upper character of "jiāng" (弶) is pronounced qiáng (強) with the departing tone; it refers to setting snares on roads. The lower character is pronounced háng (杭);
it refers to using wooden restraints to clamp the feet, twist the hands, and place a yoke around the neck.
The upper character of *pāśa* (羂索) is pronounced as *jiān* with the third tone; it means a net. The lower character is pronounced as *sāng* with the fourth tone; it refers to a rope or cord.
These two great generals were named Shanjian (善劍, "Skilled Sword") and Shanggong (善弓, "Skilled Bow"). Of these two, Shanjian took refuge in the Dharma and became a bhikṣuṇī.
Their weapons were all made of bamboo and wood. At that time, the king ordered them to go and suppress the rebels on the borders.
Upon arriving there, he immediately entered the Samādhi of Loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta-samādhi*). He then led his military forces and recited the sutras throughout the night.

By virtue of the merit of these recitations, he dedicated it to the various devas. The Four Great Heavenly Kings (*catur-mahārāja*) then commanded the celestial armies and the eight classes of *nāga* spirits to fill the air.
When the rebels saw this, they hurriedly left the city to surrender.

The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra on the Blind Nāga Girl* states: A certain blind nāga girl addressed the Buddha, saying, "In a previous life on the causal ground, I once went to a forest grove near a monastery and stole ten mangoes to eat. Due to the karmic conditions of this act, I suffered in the hells;
as my evil karma was not yet exhausted, I have now become a starving nāga, constantly being devoured by various insects and consuming pus and blood."

The suffering was unbearable, so he sought refuge in the Buddha’s liberation. The Buddha said to the dragon: "This karma is extremely heavy, even greater than the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*).

Why is this? If one misappropriates the property of the permanently resident Sangha from the four directions, or the property of the *saṃmukhībhūta* Sangha, or items given out of devout faith—such as flower gardens, fruit orchards, food, drink, medicinal decoctions, bedding, mats, or any other necessities—"
To spend it for one's own use, or to take it and give it to acquaintances, relatives, or laypeople—this sin is heavier than that of the Avīci Hell.
The Buddha spoke in verse: "It would be better to swallow a great, glowing red iron ball, causing flames to burst forth from one's mouth,"
All food, drink, and utensils belonging to the Sangha must not be used privately for external purposes.

It would be better to slaughter oneself with a sharp knife and eat one's own flesh, skin, and membranes than to do so. Laypeople among the laity must not take or receive the miscellaneous food of the Sangha.
The *Zhao fa yao ji* (Essential Collection of Various Scriptures) states: "Now we see foolish people who, greedily coveting meritorious objects, intend to use them..."
They provided for their own bodies: some consumed the food of the Sangha; some made use of its flowers and fruits; some rode upon the mounts kept by the Sangha;

some followed along with the slaves belonging to the Sangha; some privately borrowed monastic property and failed to return it; or they used their official authority to lie in wait and seek out the faults of the Sangha.
Such harms as these could not be fully enumerated even if listed together. Reflecting quietly upon these transgressions, how could one not feel heartache? Now...

Regarding the protection of those who do not give: this is not out of stinginess or a refusal to bestow gifts; rather, it is out of compassion for laypeople, considering that they might suffer in the future.
If one were to give [the items] away, it would not only harm the laity but also burden the administrators, such that in future lives they would share in the same retribution.
As seen by the bhikṣu Puṇyavardhana, one must surely fear the insects gnawing at the great tree.
The āmra fruit resembles a peach but is not a peach; it resembles a crabapple but is not a crabapple. It is difficult to distinguish whether it is ripe or unripe.
Its leaves resemble willow leaves but are a foot long.

*Niàng* (upper tone *niáng*, departing tone): to brew wine. *Yùn* (lower tone *yùn*): long-term fermentation.

The Four Noble Truths are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Suffering is the fruit of suffering; its origin is the cause of suffering;

The four Āgamas—translated here as "Dharma Returns"—are the *Ekottarika Āgama*, the *Madhyama Āgama*, and the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
The *Saṃyukta Āgama* (Contained Sūtras) consists of four sections totaling one hundred and ninety fascicles.
There are four types of wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*): first, the gold-wheel king, who rules over the four great continents;

The Caturdvīpaka [ruler]. There are four types of Iron Wheel-turning Kings who preside over the southern continent. All four possess a wheel-treasure that appears in the void;
they travel by flying according to the wheel. Therefore, they are called "Flying Emperors."

*Niraya* (mud-ni-li) is translated here as "Non-existence" (*wu-you*), which refers to the hells. This means that once one has fallen into the hells, there is no sense of joy, pleasure, or beneficial purpose.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) consist of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*).

The five faculties (*pañcendriya*), the five powers (*pañcabala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) together constitute the thirty-seven [limbs of enlightenment].
These represent the various categories according to the shallow or deep stages of entering the Path, as detailed elsewhere.
Slander of the Triple Gem. In Chang’an County, Yongzhou (present-day Xi’an), there was Gao Fayǎn. He was the great-great-grandson of Gāo Yǐng, the Minister of the Interior during the Sui dynasty.
On the twenty-fifth day of the first month in the third year of the Longshuò era, he went to the Zhōngtái to register for official service.
At noon, he returned home. His residence was in the Yìníng Fāng ward, situated in the southern corner with its gate opening toward the street. [He resided at] Huàdù Monastery.
To the east of the temple was the Gao family residence. He intended to exit through the Xunyi Gate on the western side of the city wall.
As he reached the gate, he encountered two men on horseback pursuing him from behind. Once outside the city walls, they drew closer and pressed upon him.
Outside the gate, to the north of the road, lay Puguang Temple. One of the men spoke to the riders, saying: "Run and seize the gate of Puguang Temple; do not let this man—"
When people enter the temple, it is difficult to apprehend them. Following these instructions, the man galloped to guard the gate.
Fayen was terrified and could not enter the temple, so he fled toward the west. He arrived at the southern gate of the Jincheng Ward on the West Street.
To the west of the road was Huichang Temple. He added four more horsemen and told the two men ahead who were riding horses, "Guard Huichang [Temple] urgently!"
The gate of Changsi Temple. Following these words, the man ran and seized the temple gate.
Fearing for his life, Fayen immediately said to the mounted man, "Who are you that dares to press me? The mounted man replied, "The King has sent me to take Fayen.
Fayen asked, "Why did the King send you? The mounted man replied, "King Yama has sent me. Fayen—
Having heard that the messenger of King Yama had arrived, he recognized him clearly as a ghost and immediately resisted him together with his companions.

The ghost became violently enraged and cried out, "Quickly cut off my hair! Another ghost then seized a blade and cut off both topknots of the Dharma-eye, which fell to the ground along with the flesh.
He then reached the western street, where he fainted and fell from his horse; he died suddenly and was unconscious. Having reached the main road at the crossroads, [the events unfolded].
While he was hesitating, more than a thousand people gathered to watch him. At the head of the West Street was a grand residence;
he immediately called his family members to carry him toward the house. He did not regain consciousness until dawn, at which point he spoke to those in his household, saying:
"I entered hell and saw King Yama. He ascended a great high throne and rebuked me with anger, saying: 'For what reason did you go to Huadu Monastery to see Mingzang?'"
Because he ate the fruits belonging to the permanent monastic community within his master’s quarters, he was made to swallow four hundred red-hot iron balls.
As he swallowed them, his throat constricted and closed; his body became scorched and shriveled, turning crimson. Only after swallowing them all did he regain consciousness.
When he had awakened on the twenty-sixth day, various ghosts came again to seize Fayuan and take him away.
He went before the King. The King said to him, "For what reason do you fail to revere the Triple Gem and speak of the faults and evils of the Saṃgha?

You must swallow iron balls until they are exhausted; it is fitting that you receive the plowing of your tongue with iron plows. On the twenty-ninth day of the first month, having finished swallowing the iron balls, he regained consciousness.
At dawn on the thirtieth day of the first month, he died again and returned to hell, where he once more underwent [suffering].
An iron plow shall plow his tongue. He sees his own tongue for himself; it is several li in length.

A bystander sees him spit it out, and it is over a chi long. The king speaks again to the wardens: "Because this man has spoken ill of the Triple Gem, cut off the root of his tongue with a great iron axe.
The wardens strike it, but they cannot sever it. The king speaks again, saying: "Mince his tongue finely with an axe."
He was about to be placed in a boiling cauldron to be cooked, yet he did not soften despite the boiling. The King again marveled and asked for the reason.
Fayen replied to the King, saying, "I have previously read the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The King still did not believe him and ordered an inspection of the records of his meritorious deeds.

Seeing within the files that there was one volume of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* read by him, the King verified the truth of it and finally released him from prison. That man appeared [before the King].

Those who observed him were as numerous as a marketplace; those who saw him conceived the aspiration for enlightenment. The entire family came to believe and revere him, exerting themselves with diligence, maintaining sincere caution without weariness.
This was known to both the clergy and the laity throughout the capital; there is no need to cite further evidence. [This account] appears in the *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma).

II. Forty-eight Minor Precepts (divided into three parts): 1. General Statement; 2. Detailed Enumeration;
3. Summary. 1. General Statement:
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "The ten *pratimokṣa* have already been explained. Now, the forty-eight minor precepts..."
It shall now be explained.
Regarding "light defilements": although these offenses are lighter than the ten grave [offenses], they can nonetheless defile the fundamental ground of the mind.
If one does not urgently seek repentance, they will act as an obstruction to the ground of the mind, making it difficult to achieve the fruits of sainthood. However, one must recognize this.

Regarding the characteristics of these offenses: their roots, their origins, and the distinctions between those arising from others and those that are independent. If one follows the ten heavy categories mentioned previously, when one intends to commit an act but has not yet completed it, the heavy offense is not yet incurred;
however, there is a light secondary offense consisting of the preliminary preparation for the act. This is called "originating from [the primary]."
If an action arises independently, not originating from among the ten grave offenses, it is called a "solitary light offense" (*duotou qinggou*).
Within these current fundamental light offenses, there are further transgressions such as those committed intentionally or through negligence.
If one commits an act intentionally within the fundamental section of the forty-eight precepts, it constitutes a light offense requiring confession; it should be treated as a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

Regarding the confession of an offense committed intentionally: because it was done deliberately, one further commits the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) and the *duṣkṛta* of improper conduct (*anācāra*).
If it was committed through negligence, one commits only the *duṣkṛta* of mental reproach (*cittānuśaya*). Thus, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* states: "This is an offense arising from defilement."
This constitutes an offense arising from non-affliction; one should perform the repentance for a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Failure to repent obstructs the bodhisattva precepts.
At the time of repentance, one must consult those who know the Dharma, and only then will the offense be extinguished. Thus, the *Bodhisattva-upāsaka-pañcaśīla-vinaya-sūtra* states:
"If there is an offense, one should immediately repent according to the Dharma. One should perform the repentance for a *duṣkṛta* and inquire of a Great Being."
Those of the Hīnayāna who are able to explain and accept repentance may perform *pratideśanā* according to the Dharma.

As for the method of repentance for a *sthūlātyaya* or a *duṣkṛta* (the latter translated as "evil deed"), it shall be explained below; each individual precept must be distinguished on its own, so I shall not list them here at length. (Duṣkṛta means "bad action.")
II. Detailed Enumeration.
I. The First Precept: Disrespecting Teachers and Friends.
Teachers are the compassionate models for humans and devas, the excellent paradigms for transcending the world. They give birth to our body of precepts and nourish our life of wisdom. All...

This is due to the power of the teacher; therefore, one ought to be respectful and compliant without opposition. Yet, if you instead act with arrogance, will you not fall into the profound and vast ocean of sin?
A friend can discern the character of others, assist in cultivating virtue, and aid in practice; through such a friend, all manner of goodness is accomplished and the myriad practices advance.
It is like crossing the great ocean, which requires both sail and rudder in mutual dependence; to neglect them is to sink by oneself.
They will seize and drown them; for this reason, the Tathāgata teaches that they should be revered as one would the World-Honored One.
If, O sons of the Buddha, you wish to receive the rank of a king, the rank of a universal monarch (cakravartin), or when officials receive their positions, [you must act accordingly].
One should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
This places the receiving of the precepts before the conferral of rank, so that one may first establish one's own virtue to invoke the protection of devas, nāgas, spirits, and deities.
When the king and ministers are at peace, the entire nation is at peace; when the king and ministers possess merit, the entire [nation] likewise possesses merit.
This is for the blessing of the nation. Thus, regarding the ten grave precepts, the exhortation to receive them begins with the king;
the final summary likewise prioritizes the king. Now, these minor defilements also begin and end with the king. This is truly because when the king is upright, the world is upright;
when the king is virtuous, the officials and commoners are virtuous. Therefore, the king possesses the power of transformation and instruction. [I] exhort...
This is the merit of goodness. If the King does not accept these precepts, he will personally lose the benefit of protection;
furthermore, by relying on his noble status, he will incur the harm of destroying the Buddha-dharma and will restrict his disciples, forbidding them from leaving home to cultivate the Way.

Once they have received the precepts, there is still fear that they might become arrogant and fail to show respect toward those of virtue; therefore, the Tathāgata specifically and emphatically exhorted them.

As for the five groups who have left the household life, each follows the disciplinary conduct and naturally knows the etiquette of respectful compliance; for this reason, [the matter] is omitted here.
All ghosts and spirits shall protect and guard the person of the king and the persons of his hundred officials. All Buddhas will rejoice.

Because the king and his ministers revere the Triple Gem and receive the precepts, ghosts and spirits will provide protection so that their bodies are healthy, the realm is peaceful and tranquil, the three calamities gradually subside, wind and rain are always regulated, and the myriad people receive benefit. Thus, the *Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa* (Heart-Mind Contemplation Sūtra) says:

The Sūtra says: "If there is a king who accomplishes right view and transforms the world according to the Dharma, he is called a 'Lord of Heaven,' because he transforms the world with the wholesome dharmas of the devas.
Consequently, the various celestial deities and the Four Heavenly Kings will constantly come to provide him with protection."
Because he guards the royal palace, although he dwells among humans, he cultivates the deeds of the devas.

Because his mind regarding rewards and punishments is free from partiality, such a holy sovereign is called a King of the True Dharma (*saddharmarāja*). A verse in the *Mahāsuvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* says:
"Because he is protected by the various devas, he is also named a Son of Heaven (*devaputra*). The Lord of the Thirty-three Devas shares his power with the human king, as do the hosts of stars."

The movements of the celestial bodies accord with their stations; the sun and moon do not deviate from their courses. Gentle breezes always respond to the seasons, and sweet rains fall in accordance with the time.
All the hosts of devas fill their respective palaces. Therefore, you, O King of Men, have sacrificed your own person to propagate the True Dharma.
Transforming sentient beings through the Dharma, one constantly causes them to attain peace and security.

One causes all those people to practice the ten wholesome deeds, so that the entire land is always peaceful and happy, and the realm attains tranquility. Regarding what is called "the joy of all Buddhas":

this Great Precept of the Mind-Ground has been transmitted by a thousand Buddhas, with the original aspiration that its transmission and reception would never cease. Now, the King and his ministers reverently uphold it.
If all under heaven were to follow this example, and every person practiced goodness so that each became a child of the Buddha, would one not feel joy?

Having received the precepts, one should give rise to a mind of filial piety and a mind of reverence. Upon seeing elders, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), instructors (*ācārya*), virtuous ones (*bhadanta*), fellow students, those of like view, or those of like practice, one should rise to welcome them, prostrate, and inquire after their well-being.
There are two kinds of *sthavira* (elders). The first is the *sthavira* among the Saṃgha, who is superior to all others because no one is more venerable than him;
therefore, he sits above his own *upādhyāya* and *ācāryas*. The second is one who received the precepts before oneself, even if only by a single moment or a single shadow;
such a person is an elder. King Bimbisāra addressed the disciples of the Buddha as [elders].
"Superior person" (*śreṣṭha-puruṣa*) refers to one who stands above kings, ministers, scholars, and commoners. In the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha said:

"A bodhisattva who practices for unsurpassed enlightenment with a single-minded focus, without allowing the mind to become distracted, is called a superior person. The term *upādhyāya* will be explained later.
*Ācārya* is translated here as "model" (*guifan*). "Model" carries the meaning of "teacher," referring to one who can instruct disciples in the rules of conduct.
Therefore, for the five groups of those who have left the household life, there are five *ācāryas*: first, one who bestows the ten precepts;

second, one who performs the *karmavācanā* when receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*); third, one who provides instruction; fourth, one who serves as a mentor (*niśraya*); and fifth, one who transmits the scriptures.
"Virtuous One" (*bhadanta*) is a term of respect, used because they possess virtue through their practice. "Fellow student" (*sabrahmacārin*) refers to one who shares the same teacher.
This refers to studying the Mahāyāna Dharma. "Same view" means that their minds share the same correct understanding of the Mahāyāna.

"Same practice" means that their persons engage in the same cultivation of Mahāyāna deeds and conduct. When such a person is about to arrive, one should immediately rise to welcome them; having welcomed them, one should prostrate.
Ritual (*li*) is principle; it is also treading. To advance and retreat with reverence, humility, and measured propriety constitutes its great principle. Bowing (*bai*) signifies submission.
The two bows of secular ritual take their model from the Two Polarities (*liangyi*); the four bows take their model from the Four Images (*sixiang*).
Buddhist ritual employs three bows to express the veneration of the Three Karmas and to take refuge in the Triple Gem, thereby attaining liberation from the Three Poisons.

As for "inquiring" (*kṣaṇa*), it means to question with words. Once the ritual is completed, one should relax the countenance and harmonize the expression, looking straight ahead with right mindfulness.
One should inquire, saying: "I trust you have little illness and little affliction; are you at ease in your daily life? The *Bhūmisaṃgraha-sūtra* says: "Is the road clear and peaceful?
Are the four great elements in harmony? Are you at peace when lying down and waking up? One should inquire accordingly according to the occasion; there is no fixed rule.
It is certain that these [beings] all revere the Dharma of the precepts and practice the way of filial piety and respect;

yet the Bodhisattva, on the contrary, gives rise to arrogance, pride, delusion, and anger, failing to rise to welcome or prostrate himself, and failing to provide each with offerings according to the Dharma.
Instead, he sells his own body, his kingdom, cities, men, and women, as well as the seven treasures and hundreds of other things, to make offerings.
One must provide these to them. If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

"Arrogance" (*māna*) refers to the unrestrained indulgence of body and mind; "conceit" (*mada*) refers to relying on oneself and looking down upon others; "delusion" (*moha*) refers to failing to distinguish between the honorable and the lowly;
and "anger" (*krodha*) refers to being resentful and hostile toward others. If one harbors any one of these four mental states within, one will consequently manifest a lack of respect outwardly.
Regarding these signs, he consequently did not rise to welcome him, nor did he receive him with a formal audience or prostration. As for "making offerings" (*pūjā*):

advancing in the practice of material giving is called "offering" (*pūjā*), while that which provides support is called "nourishment" (*bhojana*). Furthermore, offering what is below to what is above is "offering," and the veneration of the superior by the inferior is "nourishment."

One who sells their own body does so as the ultimate expression of reverence for the person and the honor accorded to the Dharma, and as the pinnacle of offering with total sincerity and exhaustion of one's resources.
For example, in the past, the Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita, in order to hear the Prajñāpāramitā, sold his own heart, liver, marrow, and bones to offer them to the Great Being Dharmodgata.
Furthermore, when Śākyamuni Tathāgata was on the path of practice and was a poor man, he [sold himself] in order to hear the Mahāparinirvāṇa...

Because of this sūtra, [the Bodhisattva] daily cut three *liang* of his own flesh and sold it to the sick to treat their illnesses. Having done this for a full month, he took the money to make offerings to the Buddha.
Although people today may be poor, surely they do not lack a few small things; yet they have not even reached the point of selling their own bodies, sons, daughters, and so forth.

This is because they value wealth and slight the Dharma, and thus they incur sin. As for the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, *musāragalva*, *aśmagarbha*, and *lohitamukti*.
"Vaiḍūrya," "musāragalva," and "red pearl. "Hundred things" refers to the great number of requisites for sustaining one's body.
If it is not so—that is, if one does not provide such respectful offerings as described above—one incurs a light offense of defilement.
As stated in the *Bodhisattva Upāsaka Pañcaśīla-Ācāra Sūtra*:
"If one does not listen to other talk when it is spoken, or if one does not answer truthfully when questioned, one commits a grave secondary offense (*gaurava-pāpaka*).

If there is no intention of pride, anger, or delusion, but one commits the act simply out of laziness, indeterminate state (*avyākṛta*), or a distracted mind, one commits a light secondary offense. However, if one is ill, or if one is listening [to something else], there is no offense."
Dharma. Teaching the Dharma. If one first converses with others, up to the point of protecting the minds of many people, this is called non-offense.
○ Second, the precept against drinking alcohol.
The previous precept prohibited the selling of alcohol; this present precept prohibits drinking it oneself.
O disciples of the Buddha, if one intentionally drinks alcohol, the transgressions arising from alcohol are immeasurable.
If one personally passes a vessel of alcohol to another person to drink, they shall be born for five hundred lifetimes without hands; how much more so if one drinks it oneself!
The faults arising from alcohol do not merely amount to thirty-six matters; therefore, they are said to be immeasurable.
If one pours wine from a jar or a cup into another vessel to give it to someone to drink, one still incurs the retribution of being born for five hundred lifetimes without hands;
how much more so for drinking it oneself—would that not evoke even heavier retribution? If one falls among the animals, one becomes an ignorant and deluded maggot, or even a leech or an earthworm.
Eels, loach, and other such handless creatures. The *Ghosts Question Maudgalyāyana Sūtra* states:
A certain ghost asked, "Since my birth, I have been dull-witted and ignorant; what sin has caused this? Maudgalyāyana replied, "When you were a human being..."

If one gives alcohol to others and further forcibly urges them to drink, causing them to become disoriented and lose their composure, they will receive this as a "flower reward" (an immediate retribution) now, while the "fruit" (the ultimate retribution) awaits in hell.

The *Saddharma-smṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "If one gives alcohol to an assembly of monks, to those who have received the precepts, to those who are tranquil, to those whose minds are extinguished in stillness, or to those who have attained meditative concentration—because it turbidly disturbs such persons—one shall fall into the Raurava Hell."
In the *Yù* (Treatise), it is asked: "The treatise states that when a Bodhisattva practices the *dānapāramitā*, even if there is one who begs for alcohol, he also bestows it upon them.

Why is this? The answer is: "When a Mahāsattva cultivates the six perfections and the myriad practices, and his practice of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is about to be fulfilled, he does not refuse the intentions of any who beg, because he desires to bring the *dānapāramitā* to full completion. It is as stated in the *Anuttara-śikṣā*:"

The *Sūtra on What is Asked* states: When a bodhisattva practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), if someone comes to beg for whatever they require, he should say, "Do as I instruct," and then provide it.
If the person is fond of alcohol, he causes them to give rise to right mindfulness and drinks with them;
subsequently, he causes them to renounce it. In this way, the bodhisattva is pure and skillfully embraces [the seeker] through expedient means (*upāya*).

If sentient beings cherish and do not wish to abandon [alcohol] within their hearts, the Bodhisattva will then, for their sake, describe in various ways the faults of alcohol as being like a sharp sword, so that they may certainly distance themselves from it and not continue in such behavior. Such is the giver.
Then there is no fault. This is what a Bodhisattva may do when perceiving the appropriate opportunity; it differs from the practice of the Śrāvakas.

As stated in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-vinaya-sūtra*: "For the sake of others, the robes that a Bodhisattva may accept—even up to hundreds of thousands—may be sought with all one's effort from a householder who is not a relative. Just as it is with robes, so it is with alms bowls; this is for the sake of others."

Because of this, [the Bodhisattva] should request thread and instruct weavers to weave [garments]. He may keep garments made of *kōśeya* silk and accept gold and silver, even in amounts reaching hundreds of thousands.
Such matters differ from those of the Śrāvakas; therefore, the *Vinayaviniścaya-sūtra* states:
To uphold the precepts of the śrāvakas is to break the bodhisattva precepts; to uphold the bodhisattva precepts is to break the śrāvaka precepts—this is so.
Or, driven by a private mind, one may imitate the Great Being’s skillful means of accumulating much, yet personally begrudge even a single coin and fail to give it away.
One may intend to study the practice of dāna until it is perfected, yet act contrary to the intentions of others and perform it falsely; such a person is like a monkey.
To wear pearl necklaces as an ornament is truly to invite one's own ruin; how much more so can one avoid the retribution of the deluded and the wailing of the damned?
Furthermore, one must not teach any person to drink, nor allow any sentient being to drink alcohol, let alone drinking it oneself.
No kind of alcohol may be drunk. If one intentionally drinks it oneself or teaches others to drink, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
"All people" refers to men and women, the young and the old, whether lay or ordained, and those from other regions or foreign lands.

"All sentient beings" refers to non-humans of various species, such as ghosts, spirits, and animals. To teach humans, non-humans, or to drink it oneself—in all three cases, one incurs a light offense.
All types of alcohol are explained as in the previous heavy precept. The Vinaya states: "To consume *mǔqū* (fermenting agent)."
As for fermented dregs that can cause intoxication, one incurs an offense with every swallow.

However, if there is a serious illness that cannot be cured by other medicines, and it must be treated with wine mixed with them to recover, the Tathāgata has permitted this for the sake of the disease, as clarified in the *Bhikṣu-vinaya* and the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*. Question: Since such faults are immeasurable, why does the commentary state:
[The questioner asks: "Are all transgressions permitted? [The Master] answers: "Since it is said that immeasurable faults arise, yet one is able to avoid such faults, they are therefore permitted.
For example, in the past, when King Prasenajit’s consort Mallikā had received the precepts from the Buddha, she encountered a situation where the king intended to execute a kitchen official.
The consort entertained the king with wine and exhorted him with mutual joy; the king was delighted with his consort."
By drinking alcohol, he forgot his fondness for killing, and the punishment for it was subsequently abolished. The lady then went to the Buddha to confess her transgression.
The Buddha said, "One who drinks in such a manner attains great and wholesome benefit; they do not violate the precepts.

However, were one to hear these words and, lacking the skillful means of Queen Māllikā, recklessly imitate her conduct, then the retribution would indeed be difficult to escape. It is also like the case of Qi...
The monk Tanxian once debated the Dharma with a Daoist while intoxicated; he was able to cause countless Daoists to submit to the Buddha-dharma, whereby the Buddhist teachings flourished greatly.
When he drank lethal poison, his urine caused the stones upon which it fell to shatter completely.
While satiated with wine and meat, he recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, completing sixty fascicles in a single night. If one can act in such a manner, then no transgressions will arise. However, if...
To lack this capacity is no small harm. Today there are those who practice "mad dhyāna," slandering the Vinaya as mere attachment to forms while they indulge their bodies and minds in license.

They eat without regard for day or night; how could they distinguish between ghosts, beasts, or carrion-eaters? They slander the precepts as being merely of the Hīnayāna, claiming that drinking alcohol carries no fault.
What fear do they have for the boiling excrement or the foolish maggots [of hell]? This has led ignorant followers to imitate them, blinding themselves and blinding others.

One will incur offenses and receive retribution, as clearly explained in the sutras. How could one not stand in awe? (The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* translated during the Jin dynasty consists of sixty fascicles; thus, it is divided into six bundles.)
○ Third, the precept against eating meat:
All meat originates from the taking of life. Yet, the Bodhisattva takes compassion as his foundation and the relief of others as his concern.
Compassion means to uproot suffering and bestow happiness; the desire to benefit means to extensively practice altruism. To eat meat [contradicts these principles].
Both [of these] courses of action are contrary [to the Dharma]. What further dharma could be called that of a Mahāsattva?
If, O Son of the Buddha, you intentionally eat meat, you must not eat the flesh of any sentient being. Now, those who eat meat sever the seed of the Buddha-nature of great compassion;
all sentient beings, upon seeing them, will abandon and depart from them.

Therefore, "eating" here does not refer to accidental consumption. Regarding the flesh of all sentient beings, it includes no more than those creatures that move through water, on land, or in the air—even including oysters, clams, mussels, and sea lizards; in short, anything that possesses life falls under this category.
The Great Compassionate One said: "The unsurpassed bodhicitta is it. To sever this mind is to sever the seed of buddha-nature.
Once the seed is severed, by what means can one achieve the foundation of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
When sentient beings see it and abandon it, their habituation to killing has not been eliminated; they remain terrified, like a pigeon flinging itself at Śāriputra."

Its shadow alone causes one to tremble incessantly; how much more so when its flesh is eaten? As for its form, color, and breath—those who see or hear them cannot fail to be struck with terror and flee in alarm.
Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "When hunters, butchers, fishermen, fowlers, and other such evil persons appear, dogs bark in alarm and wild beasts flee;
all sentient beings, whether flying in the air, dwelling on land, or moving in water, are likewise terrified."
Upon seeing him, they all had this thought: "This person's breath is like that of a rākṣasa; now that he has come here, he will surely kill us.
For the sake of protecting their lives, they all fled and avoided him; hence it is said that they saw him and departed.
For this reason, no bodhisattva may eat the flesh of any sentient being. To eat meat incurs immeasurable transgressions;
if one eats it intentionally, they commit a minor offense.

Regarding all Bodhisattvas: from the initial reception of the precepts until they have attained the stages (*bhūmi*), and even those who have already ascended to the stages, they themselves know the transgression of eating meat while maintaining the precepts.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "Even if a person who eats meat should attain an opening of the mind that resembles *samādhi*, they are all great *rākṣasas*; when their retribution ends, they will inevitably sink into the cycle of birth and death."
The ocean of suffering. How can such a person escape the three realms? The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

The Buddha told Mahāmati, "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have constantly been one another’s close relatives; having undergone various births, they receive the bodies of birds, beasts, and so forth.
How can you take them as food? When a Bodhisattva sees all sentient beings, they are all their own kin. Thus...
One should cultivate supreme compassion, regarding all beings as one's only child. All meats are produced from the impurities of semen and blood;

how could one who seeks purity take them as food? Whether one cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, maintains incantations, seeks liberation, or enters the Mahāyāna, none of these can be accomplished by eating meat. The devas will remain far removed.
One’s sleep and dreams will be restless; rākṣasas and evil ghosts will seize one’s spirit, increasing diseases and giving rise to all manner of evils, while destroying all meritorious virtues.
A verse says: Failing to liberate oneself from birth and death, One kills sentient beings for profit.
Using wealth as a net to capture their flesh— Both are evil karmas. Upon death, one falls into the Howling Hell; Therefore, it is said that one incurs immeasurable sin.
Thus it was. One ghost asked Maudgalyāyana: "Since my birth, I have had many sons, all handsome and pleasing to behold, yet they all died young.
My thoughts for them are severed; the pain is beyond words. By what sin has this been caused? Maudgalyāyana replied:

"When you were a human being, you saw your children kill living beings and you rejoiced in assisting them as they ate meat. Because of the killing, their lives were short; because of your rejoicing..."

Therefore, having experienced the bitter poison [of suffering] in the past, one now receives this provisional retribution; eventually, one will enter hell. If one witnesses an act being committed and rejoices in it, such is the retribution received;
how much more so for those who commit it themselves!
○ Fourth, the precept against eating the five pungent roots.
Generally, among things, there are those that have a pungent odor but are not spicy, such as asafoetida and the like;
those that are spicy but do not have a pungent odor, such as ginger and mustard; and those that are both pungent-smelling and spicy, namely the five pungent vegetables.
If a disciple of the Buddha, one must not eat the five pungent roots: garlic, leeks, scallions, onions, and asafoetida.
These five pungent roots must not be eaten among any foods whatsoever. If one intentionally eats them, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

Regarding the five pungent vegetables (*pañca-garaka*), they appear interchangeably in the Sūtras and Vinayas with varying names and species. Most accounts list them as onion, garlic, leek, scallion, and *hiṅgu* (asafetida).

In the present version of this sūtra, the onion is divided into three types to constitute the five; this is also due to differences in regional terminology and the distinct appellations used throughout antiquity and the present.
Garlic. Also known as *hú*. It was brought back by Zhang Qian when he was sent to the kingdom of Dàyuǎn (Ferghana). This is what people commonly eat today.
Some say it is the same as *húcōng* (Persian onion), claiming it is so called because it was brought from the lands of the Hu.

The *Běncǎo* states: "The *húcōng* resembles the common onion, but its stems and leaves are fine and short; like the *jīndēng*, it resembles garlic but is smaller in form. If this is the case, [it is indeed garlic].
This is not garlic (*laśuna*). It is *gecong* (wild onion), also known as mountain onion (*shanzhong*), which grows in mountains and marshes;

its stem is slender and its leaves are broad. It is also called *geshancong*. Some say it is identical to *xie* (shallot). There is also *cicong* (compassionate onion), which withers in winter and summer and flourishes in spring. There is also *lancong* (orchid onion).
This refers to *kṣudrārdraka* (small garlic). It is also called "wild-grown" (*yèshēng*). Some say it is simply leek (*jiǔ*).

However, as there are many varieties of onion, there are also wood-onion (*mùcōng*), large-official onion (*dàguāncōng*), water-onion (*shuǐcōng*), and tower-onion (*lóucōng*), also known as "dragon-use onion" (*lóngyòngcōng*) because its leaves have eight corners like dragon horns;
it is also called "dragon-claw onion" (*lóngzhuācōng*). Winter-onion (*dōngcōng*) is frozen onion (*dòngcōng*), which grows in both winter and summer.

The *cháng yǒng* (常永) is the Chinese onion (*Allium ascalonicum*). Its leaves and fruit are both stalky; the leaves wither in winter and it flowers at the end of spring, forming seeds that can be planted.
The *chūn cōng* (春葱) is the *jiū cōng* (茖葱). Some say *jiū* refers to the *cí cōng* (慈葱), because its stems and leaves are tender and supple.
*Xīngqú* (興渠) is a Sanskrit term, also called *xīngyí* (興宜); here it is translated as "little" (*shǎo*). This plant does not exist in this region. Its leaves resemble... [text fragment ends].
The *wúqīng* (mustard) has a root resembling that of the radish; in winter, both its stalks and leaves fall off, and it emits a pungent odor upon emerging from the soil.
Whatever is pungent and foul-smelling is forbidden to be eaten. It is incorrect for Daoists to consider *yúntái* (turnip) and *húsuǐ* (coriander) as "pungent" (*hūn*).
Regarding all foods that must not be eaten, this refers to the five pungent roots (*wǔxīn*); these must not be mixed into any food. Nor...

Regarding the consumption of food: the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that if there is a household in the Western Regions where food is being prepared, they are driven outside the city walls.
However, if there is a person with a serious illness and a physician instructs them to take the food, the Vinaya permits them to reside separately in a room outside the community.

After seven days have passed, they must bathe, change their clothes, and only then may they be permitted to rejoin the assembly. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that there are five faults in eating [impure] food; the first is that cooked food [prepared for oneself] gives rise to...

First, sexual desire gives rise to gluttony and increases anger. Second, even if one is able to proclaim the twelve divisions of the scriptures, the celestial immortals of the ten directions will loathe their foul stench and all distance themselves from them.
Third, various hungry ghosts will lick their lips and mouths; they will constantly dwell with such ghosts.
Fourth, their merit and virtue will diminish daily, resulting in a long-term lack of benefit. Fifth, the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions...

The various devas and benevolent spirits will not come to protect them; the powerful Mara King will find an opportunity to manifest in the form of a Buddha, coming to preach the Dharma for them, disparaging the prohibitions and precepts while praising lust, anger, and ignorance. At the end of their lives, they will naturally become the retinue of Mara;
once their demonic blessings are exhausted, they will fall into the Avīci Hell. Now, because they give rise to lust and increase their anger, they are defiled.

The state of mind [of such a person] is one from which the noble ones distance themselves; therefore, this constitutes a light offense. As for its retribution, one will ultimately fall into the Avīci Hell.
○ Fifth: The Precept Against Failing to Instruct Others to Repent Their Sins.
To conceal the transgressions of others and defile the Buddha-dharma is something even the Śrāvakas are forbidden from doing;
how much more so for a Mahāsattva who upholds the True Dharma, surpassing the Śrāvakas by hundreds of thousands of millions of times?

Furthermore, since one’s practice is dedicated solely to benefiting sentient beings, how could one see the faults of others and remain indifferent without exposing them, or fail to instruct them in repentance, thereby allowing evil to increase and bringing calamity upon both self and others? This would truly contradict the path of Bodhi.
This is the way of the Bodhisattva’s transformation of beings; it is the Great Being’s resolve to protect the Dharma.

O disciples of the Buddha, when you see any sentient being who has violated the eight precepts, the five precepts, or the ten precepts, or who has breached prohibitions, committed the seven heinous crimes, fallen into the eight difficulties, or committed any other offense against the precepts, you should teach them to repent.
"All sentient beings" refers to the eight classes of beings, including devas, nāgas, humans, non-humans, and others, who have received the Buddha’s precepts of either the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna.

Even those who have not received the precepts, yet commit evil deeds and engage in unrighteous acts, should be exhorted through skillful means to cease such behavior and repent their transgressions. As for the "eight precepts," they are the eight...

The method for observing the fast (*upavāsa*). Furthermore, the eight grave offenses (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* are: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, slandering, causing affliction, anger, and malicious speech.

The five precepts (*pañca-śīla*) refer to the five precepts of the male and female lay followers (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*). The ten precepts (*daśa-śīla*) refer to the ten precepts of the novice (*śrāmaṇera*), as well as the ten virtuous precepts (*daśakuśala-karma-patha*) consisting of three of the body, four of speech, and three of the mind.
Regarding "violation of prohibitions" (*śīla-vipatti*): "violation" (*hui*) means to transgress; "prohibition" (*jin*) refers to...

Prevention and restraint: The Tathāgata established the precepts to prevent and restrain the sense-gates of sentient beings and to admonish and constrain body and speech; thus, "prohibition" (jin) is identical to "precept" (jie).
Although the categories of precepts are numerous, they do not transcend the two vehicles of Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. The Mahāyāna consists of the three clusters of pure precepts (*tripuṇyaśīla*).
The Hīnayāna refers to the precepts obtained through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*. The seven heinous offenses (*ānantarya*) are as set forth below.
As for the eight obstacles (*aṣṭāv-antarāyāḥ*): first, the hells; second, the animal realm; third, the hungry ghosts; fourth, the long-lived devas;

fifth, the continent of Uttarakuru; sixth, being blind, deaf, or mute; seventh, possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence; eighth, being born before or after a Buddha. These eight all constitute hindrances.
Regarding the "difficulties": one cannot see the Buddha or hear the Dharma; therefore, they are called difficulties.

However, these eight matters may result from having violated the precepts in a previous life, thereby bringing about such difficulties; thus, one should be taught to repent so as to avoid further retribution.

Alternatively, if one violates the precepts and commits offenses in this life, one will certainly experience the retribution of these eight difficulties in the future; therefore, one must be taught to repent. As it is said: [as if making...]
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so forth, will inevitably result in retribution as hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals.

Cultivating the "attainment of non-conception" (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) of non-Buddhist paths results in rebirth in the Heaven of Long Life for five hundred kalpas. Failing to recognize the Triple Gem and performing only worldly merit results in rebirth in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru).
Giving rise to false views and feeling no joy upon hearing the Dharma results in the retribution of blindness or deafness. Not having faith in the Triple Gem [results in further suffering].

By slandering Dharma masters, one incurs the retribution of being mute and dumb. By disbelieving in the supramundane Dharma and indulging in worldly teachings, one incurs the retribution of possessing perverse intelligence and eloquence.
Because the karma is heavy while the conditions are thin, one does not encounter a Buddha, being born either before or after a Buddha’s appearance.
As the Sūtra says: "To slander the Triple Gem, to slight and disparage the Noble Path, to discuss the good and evil of others, and to seek out the faults of others..."

Briefly stated: those who falsely accuse the virtuous and harbor malice toward the worthy shall receive the retribution of being mute and unable to speak. The *Diyu Wen Jing* (Sutra on Inquiring about Hell) states:
"If one does not respond when called by one's parents or teachers, one will fall into the hell of the mute spirits (*mūka-preta*), where one is constantly burned with iron tweezers."

Their tongues shall be cauterized for two hundred years; thereafter, if they are reborn as humans, they will be mute. For this reason, one should instruct them in repentance (*pratideśanā*) to avoid retribution in the future.

Regarding "all" [offenses]: whether they are light or heavy, natural (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) or proscribed (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), one must instruct them all to feel shame and remorse, and to perform repentance according to the Dharma, so that their evils do not increase daily and lead them later to fall into the three miserable realms (*durgati*) and suffer humiliation.
This is contrary to the Great Being’s vast vow to benefit sentient beings and protect the Dharma.

If a Bodhisattva does not instruct [the offender] to repent, nor to dwell together, nor to share in the community's offerings, nor to participate in the communal *poṣadha*, nor to recite the precepts as part of the assembly,
and fails to bring their offense to light or instruct them to reform their transgression, they commit a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).
"Living together" means residing within the same great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*). "Sharing in gains" means sharing in the offerings made to the Saṃgha as a single unit.
"Poṣadha"—the full term is *poṣadha*; *poṣa* has the meaning of "nurturing," and *dha* has the meaning of "purifying.
This refers to the assembly of the community every half-month to recite the precepts, whereby one is able to nurture wholesome dharmas and purify one's own mind.

This excludes all that is unwholesome. Regarding "the community reciting the precepts together": this refers to the Saṃgha within a single boundary (sīmā) performing the *poṣadha* and reciting the precepts together every half-month.
Alternatively, within one great boundary there may be two residences that share the same recitation of the precepts but have separate offerings (*lābha*).
Since the present case is not like that, it is said they "share the same offerings. This is what is meant by "the community reciting the precepts together."

Furthermore, regarding those who do not expose transgressions: if one possesses the three bases of seeing, hearing, or suspecting, one must immediately expose the offense committed and instruct the offender to repent.
If one neither exposes nor instructs, they share equally in the community's offerings and improperly accept the faith-offerings of the laity;

this leads to the accumulation of even deeper karmic offenses. Moreover, it violates the mind of compassion, the mind of pity, and the mind of protection, whereby one incurs guilt oneself. — *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*

It is said: If there is a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts and protects the true Dharma, and upon seeing one who destroys the true Dharma, is able to expel them, rebuke them, and punish them, you should know that such a person attains immeasurable merit beyond calculation.

If, however, one leaves them be and fails to rebuke, expel, or bring their offenses to light, you should know that such a person is an enemy within the Buddha-Dharma. If one can expel and rebuke [the offender]...
Reproach. This is my disciple. The *Bodhisattva Upāsaka Pañcaśīla-Ācāra Sūtra* states:
"A bodhisattva who serves as a leader for many people, upon seeing that their retinue is engaged in unrighteous activities, ought to reprimand them or expel them.

If, out of a mind of anger or malice, they neglect to reprimand or discipline them, they commit a grave defiling offense (*gurutara-mala-pāpa*). If, however, they fail to instruct or reprimand them due to indolence or negligence [the fault is less severe]."

...one commits a minor offense. The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "It would be better to accept evil precepts for a single day and thereby sever the life-faculties of immeasurable sentient beings, than to ever harbor a corrupt and wicked disciple who cannot be tamed. Why is this?
Such a state of non-restraint brings calamity only upon oneself; one cannot instruct a wicked disciple, which instead leads [them] to..."
One may measure the evil deeds committed by sentient beings and their ability to slander immeasurable sublime dharmas. Furthermore, the *Śīla-sūtra* states:
"Even though outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) and butchers perform evil karmic actions, they cannot destroy the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, nor are they necessarily destined to fall into the three evil realms.
However, if one acts as a teacher yet fails to instruct and admonish their disciples, they thereby destroy the Buddha-dharma; this is certain."
One will fall into hell. However, when exposing the faults of others, one must not act precipitously; one must first do so before a person of virtue who maintains the precepts.
In the Vinaya, even when a bhikṣu wishes to expose the faults of another, he first seeks their permission.

A Mahāsattva should, with a mind of loving-kindness and gentle speech, instruct and admonish them so that they are brought to submission through a sense of shame. If it is not done in this manner, one will [fall into hell].
Tell him as before, in the sixth section. Therefore, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When accusing someone of an offense, one must not go toward that person to accuse them;

rather, one should speak to a virtuous bhikṣu. If that bhikṣu who has committed the offense is violent, or relies on the power of kings, ministers, or violent men, such that there arises a cause for taking life or harming one's own fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one should act as follows..."
This is the reflection: "The karmic actions of that person will inevitably have their own retribution; they themselves should know this. It is like a fire breaking out;
one should only save oneself—how can one concern oneself with other matters? At such a time, it is faultless to protect one's sense faculties accordingly. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"If a bodhisattva sees sentient beings committing evil deeds in this life or future lives, and due to a heart of resentment..."
If one speaks correctly, this is called an offense. However, there is no offense if one lacks wisdom oneself; or if one lacks the power [to speak]; or if one causes someone who has power to speak;
or if one uses skillful means to bring that person to subjection; or if, while speaking correctly, the other person harbors malice or resentment toward oneself;
or if they utter evil words and misunderstand [the teaching]; or if they lack affection and respect; or if the person's nature is stubborn and perverse. If one sees that... [there is no offense].
If one fails to censure those who should be censured, fails to punish those who should be punished, and fails to expel those who should be expelled, this is called an offense.
However, if the person is incorrigible, unfit for conversation, or unfit for instruction; if they frequently give rise to resentment;
if there is fear that a dispute will arise; if there is mutual litigation; or if it would cause the destruction of the Saṃgha and so forth—one should observe the proper timing and not act.
Offense.
○ The sixth precept: Not providing for those who request the Dharma.
While the first precept required respect for teachers and friends, this one specifically includes providing for those who request the teaching; thus, they are distinguished.
If, O sons of the Buddha, you see a Mahāyāna Dharma Master, or fellow students of the Mahāyāna who share the same views and practices,
entering a monastery, a private residence, or a city— whether they have come from a hundred *li* or a thousand *li* away— you must immediately rise to welcome them and escort them on their departure.

You should prostrate to them and make offerings, providing sustenance three times each day, including food worth three *liang* of gold daily, as well as food of a hundred flavors, bedding, seats, and medicine.
One should serve the Dharma Master, providing all that is required. First, the Dharma Master of the Mahāyāna is designated;
next, the fellow students and the three types of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) who practice the Mahāyāna are designated. This is done to distinguish them from teachers and friends of the Hīnayāna.
As for the Dharma Master, they must have a thorough mastery of the Mahāyāna sūtras, vinayas, and the characteristics of their nature (dharmatā-lakṣaṇa), and even be capable of transforming others.
This refers to those who guide sentient beings and cause them to enter the stage of Buddhahood. The mention of "a hundred li or a thousand li" expresses the distant to include the near;
that is to say, if one should offer and invite even those who are far away, how much more so those who are nearby? As for "making offerings at the three times": [text continues].
This refers to the time when the sun first rises—specifically at the end of the *chen* hour and the beginning of the *si* hour—as well as the time of midday.
Regarding the "three or two pieces of gold" and the "hundred flavors," these express the utmost sincerity in performing service, performed without a heart of stinginess or indolence.

Those who receive such offerings should give rise to a sense of shame and remorse; only then will they be able to digest the faithful alms. As the *Zongjing* says: "If one studies the Mahāyāna Buddha-dharma..."
If one were to receive the donor’s staple food, it would be like Mount Sumeru; if one were to receive the donor’s robes, they could be spread across the great earth.
If one is not yet a learner (aśaikṣa) and has not yet entered the ranks of the Saṅgha, there is nowhere in the ten directions where one might spit without desecrating the ground. Yongjia said:

"If one attains the power of inconceivable liberation, its wondrous function is as boundless as the sands of the Ganges. How could one dare to decline the toil of the fourfold offerings? Ten thousand catties...
Even gold would be insufficient; grinding one’s bones to powder would not suffice as recompense. A single phrase, when clearly realized, transcends billions [of worlds].
Nevertheless, even so, one must know contentment in its use; only then will one be free from transgression.

As for those who give everything away, this is the highest form of making offerings through one's own resolve, yet one may still fear it is not enough. Now, regarding what is required by teachers and friends, do not...

Do not go against their wishes; you should give them everything they ask for. This clarifies the diligence of serving [the Dharma teacher]. Below, it clarifies the tirelessness in requesting the Dharma.
One should constantly request the Dharma Master to preach the Dharma at the three periods of the day, prostrating three times every day, and never giving rise to anger or a mind of resentment.
For the sake of the Dharma, one should be willing to sacrifice one’s own body. One must request the Dharma without weariness. If one does not act thus, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

"Constantly requesting instruction" clarifies that this is not limited to a single day or a single moment. As for the "three times," these are the periods before noon, after noon, and at nightfall, when one requests further teaching.
Performing prostrations during these three times signifies a joyful devotion to the Dharma and diligent application without slackening.
One must not give rise to a mind of anger because the Teacher has committed even a minor transgression. Furthermore, one should not harbor a mind of distress due to the exhaustion of wealth;
for even the body may be abandoned or extinguished, so how could one allow a mind of retreat to arise out of a reluctance to provide service?
When the Tathāgata was on the path of practice, he sacrificed his entire body to seek half a verse, and gouged a thousand sores in his own flesh to light lamps.
"Please preach the Dharma. I shall offer my wife and children as food for the yakṣas; I wish to hear the essentials of the Dharma.

Thus, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva said to Sudhana: "Within this ocean of Dharma, there is not a single word or a single phrase that was not sought by relinquishing the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch and all that one possesses—how much more so those things external to the body?"
Ah! If one cherishes their own body and begrudges their wealth, this is not the practice and vow of a Mahāsattva who forgets themselves for the sake of the Dharma;
furthermore, it violates the fundamental mind of reverence and filial piety. Thus, one commits an offense. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* states:

"Sentient beings of the final age who wish to cultivate practice should, throughout their lives, make offerings to virtuous friends and serve spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*). When those spiritual teachers are about to come..."
When approaching others, one should sever arrogance; when distancing oneself from them, one should sever resentment.

Regarding the manifestation of favorable and adverse conditions as being like empty space, one thoroughly understands that one's own mind is ultimately equal, sharing the same essence as all sentient beings without distinction.

By practicing in this manner, one finally enters Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). The Commentary states: "When a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) guides others, they employ various skillful means (*upāya*) so that the minds of teacher and disciple may reach resonance;
only then can the intent of the Dharma be transmitted. Therefore, the teacher bends down to accommodate the capacities of beings and draws them close through mutual intimacy.
Yet, the ignorant lack discernment and thus give rise to arrogance. Once arrogance obscures the mind, one does not enter the Path. Hence it is said that one 'should sever' [it]."

Arrogance. Or, when encountering adverse conditions that cause one to be separated or estranged from others, one gives rise to resentment and anger, saying, "He distances himself from me and favors another," thus speaking of love and hate.
Once a single thought of anger arises, ten million hindrances manifest; this is not merely a matter of losing the Path, but one will also fall into the three miserable realms.
Therefore, it is said that one should sever resentment and anger. According to the *Upamāna-sūtra* and other scriptures, the Venerable Ānanda, in the past...
In a past age, he was once a young boy selling incense. He saw a śrāmaṇera begging for alms while reciting a verse from a sutra, and asked him the reason for this.
The śrāmaṇera replied, "My teacher practices the Way in the mountains;
he requires me to deliver one sheng of rice daily and, in addition, to recite one verse. He asked again, "If you were not required to deliver the rice, how many verses could you recite each day?"
The master replied, "You may recite ten verses. The youth said, "From now on, do not go begging again; I shall provide the rice in your stead.
The śrāmaṇera was delighted and was able to sit in quietude to study. This continued until he had provided nine *shu* of rice in his stead. Then, the śrāmaṇera was tested on the scriptures.

He became thoroughly proficient in all of them. By virtue of this karmic reward, in a future life he was born as a disciple of the Buddha, foremost among those of great learning (*bahuśruta*), endowed with the three types of higher knowledge (*trividyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and became the transmitter of the Buddha’s mind-seal (*cittamudrā*).

Thus one should know that if even a *śrāmaṇera* who maintains the sūtras receives such a superior reward for providing him with offerings, how much more so will the superior rewards obtained by those who make offerings to Mahāyāna teachers and friends who are able to preach the Dharma?
Who could possibly fathom this?
○ Seventh is the precept against indolence regarding not listening to the Dharma.
Regarding the previous precept: "When he comes here, I shall request instruction. Regarding the present precept: "When he is in another place, I should go there to listen. Only...
This is the distinction. If,
O disciples of the Buddha, there is anywhere where the Dharma, Vinaya, Sūtras, and Śāstras are being expounded— whether in a great house or wherever else the Dharma is being taught.

"Expounder of the Dharma" (*dharmabhāṇaka*) is a general term for one who preaches the Dharma and discusses its meaning. The Sanskrit term *vinaya* means "extinction" (*nirodha*), referring to the extinction of evil in body, speech, and mind.
It is also called "skillful governance," meaning that one is well able to govern oneself regarding lust, anger, and ignorance, and is likewise able to govern the evils of sentient beings;
these names are derived from its functional efficacy. However, these are not the primary translations. The primary translation is as follows: [the remainder of the text follows].

It is called *vinaya*. *Vinaya* means "dharma. This is a name derived from its function as a teaching; it refers to the adjudication of what is light or heavy, what is permitted or prohibited, and what constitutes upholding or violating the precepts.
It is not a non-dharma or something indeterminate. Furthermore, *vi* is said to mean "removal," and *ni* is said to mean "reality.

This signifies that one removes various forms of non-reality and proceeds toward reality—whereby "reality" refers to the fundamental source, the mind-ground. Thus, both the *sūtras* and the *vinayas* are collectively referred to as *vinaya*.
The *Sūtra* refers to the *Brahmajāla-śīla-sūtra*; the *Vinaya* refers to the *Cittabhūmi-vinaya* as well as the various *bodhisattva-śīla-piṭakas*.
Furthermore, because all Mahāyāna sūtras possess the meaning of extinguishing evil and generating goodness, they are likewise termed *vinaya*.
A newly initiated bodhisattva should carry the scrolls of the sutras and vinaya to the place where the Dharma Master resides to listen, receive the teachings, and inquire about them.

Whether it be in mountain forests, beneath trees, on monastic grounds, within rooms, or at any place where the Dharma is preached, they must go to all such locations to listen and receive the teachings.
If one fails to go there to listen, receive the teachings, and inquire, one commits a minor offense.

Regarding "newly initiated learners": this refers to Mahāsattvas who have recently received the *cittotpāda* (mind-ground) precepts. Because their studies are not yet complete, they do not understand the gravity of the Dharma;

they give rise to arrogance and indolence, thereby losing the benefits of the Great Dharma. Day by day they fail to progress, and ultimately they regress from the mind-ground. Therefore, one must especially exert oneself in this regard.
If one does not go [to the teacher], one commits minor transgressions (*laghu-āpatti*) day after day. According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra*, it does not mention [the offense] for being far away.
"Near" refers to the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, which states that if one is separated by a distance of one *yojana*, there is no offense.

This is because those who live at home have their bodies constrained by worldly affairs and cannot travel far to listen [to the Dharma]. Those who have left the household life have no such burdens and devote themselves exclusively to the practice of the Dharma;
yet, if they fear the distance and do not go, this constitutes an offense of personal negligence toward the Dharma. Regarding "listening, receiving, and inquiring": "listening" means...

The ear-consciousness hears exclusively. "Receiving" (shou) refers to the mind’s internal acceptance, which consists of the two wisdoms of hearing and reflection (*śruta-mayī-prajñā* and *cintā-mayī-prajñā*).
"Inquiring" (zi) means to pose questions; that is, having heard, one reflects deeply. When reflecting but not yet attaining full understanding, one again raises questions regarding what is doubted.

Once doubts are resolved, one relies upon this to cultivate progress and enter the Dharma-gate of the Mahāyāna Mind-Ground. The previous mention of "all places" was general; [this section] is specific.
