To be a leader who does not skillfully settle the assembly, who guards property without knowing how to manage its expenditure, and who harms both oneself and others—this is not the compassionate and harmonious mind of a Great Being.
O disciples of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, you shall act as masters of the Dharma, masters of the practice of the Dharma, and masters of the monasteries. You must teach...
The Master of Transformation, the Master of Seated Meditation, and the Master of Conduct:
when the Tathāgata was in the world, everyone personally received his transformative teachings, and tainted phenomena (*āsrava-dharma*) did not arise.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, as time distanced us from the Sage, tainted phenomena increased day by day, and errors and substitutions were not absent. Nevertheless, its...
Those who are corrupted are mostly those who hold positions of authority; therefore, I shall now briefly enumerate six types of such persons.

First is the Master of Teaching the Dharma, who proclaims the teachings on behalf of the Buddha and expounds the twelve divisions of the scriptures for the assembly. Second is the Master of Practicing the Dharma, whose practice accords with his understanding, causing the assembly to act in accordance with what has been taught.
Third is the Master of the Monastery (Sanghārāma), known in Sanskrit as *māmaka* and translated here as "Temple Master."

This refers to the bhikṣu who founded the monastery, or what is called the *karmadāna* (administrator). He was one who understood the principles and managed the affairs of the permanent monastic community;

he is the person currently known as the *jianyuan* or *jiansi*. The *Sengshi lüe* states: "To examine the origins of the monastery head (*sizhu*), it began with the Baima Monastery during the Eastern Han dynasty.

Once a monastery was established as a dwelling place, someone must necessarily preside over it. Although at that time there was no specific title for 'monastery head,' [the role existed nonetheless]."
There were those who served as administrators (*karmadāna*). Since the Eastern Jin dynasty, this office has flourished.

Thus, when Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty established Guangzhai Monastery, he summoned Fayun to serve as its head and instituted monastic regulations; these were the rules of the Eastern Land (China) and did not pertain to the original system of the Western Land (India).
Originally, in the Western Land, the *sthavira* (senior elder) was held in the highest esteem and served as the titular master of the monastery. If there was any business...
Upon arrival, he deliberated together with the assembly; only when the multitude gave their consent did he act, and if they did not approve, he immediately desisted.
There was no private initiative undertaken alone, which truly accords with the vast transformation of the Great Sage. As for the one who leads in teaching and transforming:

he teaches people to cultivate merit and transforms them toward goodness, causing them to recognize the Triple Gem as a fertile field of blessings. He inspires faith and takes refuge, encouraging the promotion and honoring of offerings. [He] sat.

The *chánzhǔ* (Meditation Master) leads the assembly in the practice of various *dhyāna* and *samādhi*. The *xínglái zhǔ* (Master of Arrivals and Departures) oversees matters concerning the coming and going of the monastic community;
he was, for example, the Venerable Trapusa in former times, who is now known as the *zhīzhòng* (Master of the Assembly) or *zhīgù* (Guest Master).
One should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, skillfully reconcile disputes, and properly guard the property of the Triple Gem; do not use it recklessly as if it were one's own.
To instead incite disorder among the assembly through strife and to use the property of the Triple Gem according to one's own whims constitutes a minor offense.

In this context, both matters are primarily governed by a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); therefore, it is mentioned first. First, by means of a mind of loving-kindness, one skillfully reconciles disputes so that the community may dwell in peace and happiness.

Now, there are four kinds of disputes: disputes concerning speech (*vāda*), disputes concerning accusations (*anuvāda*), disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti*), and disputes concerning legal procedures (*kṛtya*).
These should be extinguished through the seven methods, such as the *sammukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties), as prescribed in the Vinaya Piṭaka.

This is explained extensively. Second, because one should act with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one must properly guard the property of the Three Jewels so that the assembly may receive and use it in accordance with the Dharma.
Regarding "properly guarding," this means that the property of the Buddha and the property of the Saṃgha each have their own designated ownership; they must not be mixed or confused with one another.

One must exercise moderation and refrain from acting according to one's own whims or desires, as if using one's own property. If it is property belonging to the Buddha, it may not be used for the Dharma or the Sangha;
property belonging to the Dharma may not be used for the Buddha or the Sangha; and property belonging to the Sangha may not be used for the Buddha or the Dharma.
This [image] of the Buddha may not be used for that [image] of the Buddha; this hall may not be used for that hall; nor this stupa.
One shall not construct that stūpa with this sūtra-dharma, nor employ this sūtra-dharma for that sūtra-dharma;

one shall not employ the property of the permanently resident Saṃgha for the property of the present Saṃgha at another location. One must not, even by a fraction of a grain or a measure of liquid, misappropriate or exchange these items between them.
A single grain of salt, a single grain of rice, a single needle, a single blade of grass, a single sheet of paper, or a single medicinal herb must not be used privately.

The present moment passes easily, but the retribution of the future is difficult to exhaust. Other details are clearly explained in the sutras and vinayas. If there is a surplus after constructing a Buddha hall...
One may fashion images of the Buddha; if there are surplus Buddha images, they should be made into offering implements for before the Buddha, but must not be used for the hall.
If there is a surplus of Buddha halls, they must not be converted into Bodhisattva halls. Images of the Buddha and images of Bodhisattvas must not be substituted for one another.
If there is a surplus of Dharma objects, one should transcribe Buddhist scriptures and attend to the Dharma seat. As for the property of the Sangha...
The remainder should be stored in the treasury to provide for the Sangha of the ten directions. Funds intended for feeding the Sangha must not be used to construct a refectory;

otherwise, one will fall into the Hell of the Fire-Brand Collar. One should truly take this as a warning. Money for bricks must not be used for tiles, and money for tiles must not be used for bricks. The *Bao yin jing* states:

"Regarding the two types of property belonging to the Buddha and the Dharma, they must not be used interchangeably. This is because there is no one appointed to act as the steward for the property of the Buddha and the Dharma. Furthermore...
There is nothing to be consulted regarding this; it is not the same as communal property belonging to the Sangha or to permanent or guest-monasteries, which may be consulted with one another.
As for items belonging to a Buddha-stūpa—even those worth as little as a single coin—they were offered because of the donor’s profound sincerity.

Both devas and humans regard these items as being the Buddha himself or the stūpa itself. Therefore, even if they are blown away by the wind or rot and decay, they must never be traded for precious goods.
Offerings: Regarding items belonging to a Tathāgata’s stūpa, no one may set a price upon them. The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:

The Buddha said, "A bhikṣu who manages affairs should not conceive the thought of ownership over any property. Even if there is a minor matter to be transacted, he must act only with the permission of the community;

he must not use it on his own authority. This applies even to the property of the *saṃgha* present before him or the property of the *saṃgha* from the four directions. They must not [be used] interchangeably.
If temple property and items belonging to a *stūpa* are mixed together and accumulated interchangeably, one must properly prevent this. Regarding such an inversion, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If a monk serves as the master of a monastery (*vihārasvāmin*) but there is no property for the *stūpa*, he may think: 'The reason people make offerings to the Saṃgha is that they all receive the grace of the Buddha;
thus, making offerings to the Buddha is equivalent to making offerings to the Saṃgha. He then takes monastic property to perform repairs [on the *stūpa*]."
Regarding the repair of a stūpa: the abbot incurs the offense of *pratikṣepaṇīya* (abandonment). The same applies to using stūpa property for the sake of the Saṃgha.

If it is borrowed and used in accordance with the Dharma, it is permissible; however, one must maintain clear and distinct records, specifying the time it was borrowed and the time it shall be returned.

At the time of the transaction, the record must be read aloud before the Saṃgha, and the transfer must be clearly documented. The Vinaya provides explicit instructions on this matter; one must not act according to one's own whims.
The accumulation of offenses over a thousand lifetimes is difficult to escape. Because one does not protect others with a compassionate heart, one instead brings disorder to the assembly.
Because one does not maintain oneself well with a compassionate heart, one acts without restraint, causing disputes among the multitude and thereby committing minor defilements (*āpatti*).
If one errs in the application [of the precepts], one commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
○ The twenty-sixth precept, against receiving offerings alone:
This violates the donor’s spirit of impartiality and forfeits the Bodhisattva’s practice of benefiting others.
Because one does not follow the proper order of the Sangha and intends instead to divert benefits to oneself, it is called "receiving alone."
If a disciple of the Buddha is already residing within a monastic dwelling (*saṃghārāma*), and later sees visiting Bodhisattvas or Bhikṣus entering a monastery,
a private residence, a city, or even the palace of a king, as well as a place for summer retreat (*varṣā*) or a great assembly,

the monks who were already residing there should welcome them upon arrival and see them off at departure; they should provide offerings of food and drink, and provide rooms, bedding, and rope-cots or wooden benches.

A bed. He provides everything. If he has no goods, he should sell himself, or even his sons and daughters; or he should cut the flesh from his own body and sell it, providing whatever is required and giving it all to them.
"Sengfang" (Monastery) refers to the temple where monks reside. In Sanskrit, it is called *saṃghārāma*, which means "Garden of the Community.
This signifies a place where the sprouts of the Buddha's sons and the fruits of the Path are cultivated.

It is also called *vihāra*, meaning "place of wandering" (referring to the temple grounds where monks travel and dwell). Alternatively, it is called *saṃghārāma*, meaning "Community Enclosure," referring to the residence of the monastic community.
This is the monastery. In the past, when Kāśyapa Mātanga first arrived, Emperor Ming ordered him to be accommodated at the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglù sì).
Although a separate residence was later constructed for him, he did not forget his original name; thus, it was again called a "sì" (temple).

As for "the royal residence," this refers to halls and chambers built by a king to provide shelter for the *saṃgha*. As for "the place for the summer retreat (*varṣā*)," it may be established by kings, ministers, or donors.
The *yuè* (invitation) refers to requesting the *saṃgha* to observe the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*) at that location. Regarding "great assemblies":

these may be an unrestricted assembly (*anāvṛta-pūjā*), or an assembly for the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, or an assembly for the Buddha’s birth or enlightenment, or an assembly for the *pravāraṇā* of the *saṃgha*, and so forth.
Those who reside there first are the hosts; those who arrive later are the guests. The host shall welcome the guest and provide for them in every matter.
"To give it" refers to those who sell their bodies or cut their own flesh; this is said to emphasize the gravity of their intention to provide for guests.
If even flesh can be cut, how much more so money and other external possessions? Why then should one alone receive offerings and sustenance?
Regarding "men and women," this also serves as a regulation for lay bodhisattvas, who should not begrudge their own lives, bodies, or kinsmen when providing for visiting monks. Within the text...
Although it is said that Bodhisattvas and Bhikṣus [participate], the Śrāvaka Saṃgha is also included in the distribution.
The presiding official excludes laypeople, Śrāmaṇeras, Śrāmaṇerīs, and Śikṣamāṇās, because they are not those who manage monastic affairs; only Bhikṣus are capable of fulfilling these duties.
This edict ordains that they shall receive greetings and offerings, and below this, they shall be dispatched in order to attend the invitations.

If a donor comes to invite the assembly of monks, and there are guest monks entitled to a share of the offerings, the master of the monastery should assign the guest monks to receive the invitation in due order.
If the resident monks alone accept the invitation while failing to assign the guest monks, the master of the monastery incurs immeasurable sin.
He is no different from an animal; he is not a śramaṇa, nor is he of the Śākya lineage. This constitutes a transgression of a minor offense (laghu-āpatti).
Regarding the term *dānapati*: *dāna* is a Sanskrit word, which here means "giving" (*śī*). *Patī* means "to transcend.

This refers to a person who, by practicing giving, immediately transcends the ocean of suffering of poverty. Regarding "guest monks": this includes all monastic communities from the ten directions, encompassing both the Mahayana and Hinayana vehicles.
Regarding "those entitled to a share of offerings": these are the gifts provided by the *dānapati*, such as food.

Whether it be robes, undergarments, communal invitations (*pūqing*), or restricted invitations (*xianqing*), the principle applies universally to all beings throughout the ten directions, whether ordinary or sagely, and makes no distinction between host and guest;
thus, it is said that "there is a share. Regarding those assigned by order:

this refers to cases where a donor (*dānapati*) is unable to invite the entire assembly, but instead restricts the invitation to five, ten, or even thirty-five or fifty people, according to their seniority.

[The assembly] shall sit. They shall be dispatched in successive order. If someone has already been dispatched on a previous day due to an invitation from a separate donor, one should now dispatch in rotation those who have not yet accepted the invitation according to the sequence; one must not bypass the order in dispatching them.

If it is known that the turn has reached this person, yet they are not dispatched to attend, the former host commits only a minor offense (*āpattika*), because at the time of the dispatch, their mind...

If there is doubt as to whether monks might come from outside the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), and a person who is indeed qualified to attend arrives, the presiding elder (*sthavira*) should yield the invitation to him;

thus, for one who is truly qualified, there is no offense of exclusive appropriation. However, the original host merely commits an offense of non-appointment, which is a minor transgression (*duskrta*).
If it is known that no monks will come from outside the boundary, yet after the appointment has already been finalized, one fails to appoint someone who is truly qualified to attend.
Therefore, other persons were intentionally assigned. Regarding those assigned and those who receive [the food], both are clearly aware that they commit the offense of theft.
Prior to the act, whether it be the food itself or the undergarment, if its value is calculated at five *kārsāpaṇas*, it constitutes a grave offense; thus it is said that one incurs immeasurable sin.

However, knowing only that there is food while being ignorant of the proper sequence, one is no different from a beast. Because this violates the constant laws of the Saṃgha, one is not a *śramaṇa* and commits an offense.

The offense for theft is grave. Therefore, one who is not of the Śākya clan incurs the same fault if they do not first welcome and provide for [the guest], nor later share the property of the Saṃgha with them.
However, if a donor does not intend to feed the monks but invites a resident monk for some other reason, there is no offense for the resident monk to go.
If the donor’s intention is indeed to invite both [the guest and the resident] together, yet the resident monk... [acts intentionally].

If there are obstacles and one incurs blame; or if one knows that the donor would be displeased upon seeing them, or if it would hinder their affairs—there is no offense in not going together with them.
A hungry ghost asked Maudgalyāyana: "Since my birth, I have constantly suffered from hunger and thirst.
I wish to go to the latrine to take some excrement to eat, but there is a powerful ghost at the latrine who strikes me with a staff."
"You have drawn near. By what offense was this brought about? Maudgalyāyana replied, "When you were a human being, you served as the master of a Buddhist temple.
When visiting monks arrived, you were stingy and refused them food; only after the guests had departed did you give to the resident monks.

Because you were miserly regarding the property of the Sangha, you now receive this preliminary retribution, and the fruit [of your karma] will be to enter hell. Another ghost asked, "I have lived out my life..."
"Come," he said. On his shoulder was a copper vessel filled to the brim with molten copper, which he poured over my head; the pain was beyond description.
"By what sin was this caused? Maudgalyāyana replied, "When you were a human being, you served as the *karmadāna* (steward) for the Saṃgha and managed its affairs."
There was a jar of ghee stored elsewhere which he did not distribute to the visiting monks. Only after the visitors had departed did he distribute it to the resident monks.
This ghee was the property of the *caitya* (public) Sangha, to which all have an equal share; yet, because he was stingy with the Sangha's property, [he acted thus].

"Now they receive this provisional retribution; ultimately, they shall enter hell. The Buddha told Saṃgharakṣita, "That which you see as the fourth monastery is not a monastic temple, nor are those there bhikṣus.
They are inhabitants of hell who were renunciants during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha.
While they resided permanently in that monastery, various donors would bring them fine food. This was to be distributed among those present. At that time, there was a guest monk..."
"Come! Because of a stingy mind, the resident bhikṣus waited until the guests had departed before they wished to divide [the food].

Before they could even divide it, insects devoured it and it became putrid and rotten; they then cast it away outside. Due to these causes and conditions, they entered hell, where they eat excrement and drink urine.
Since the parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa Buddha, they have suffered without ceasing. Furthermore, you see the second..."
As for these six monasteries, they are not monasteries of the Sangha, nor do they belong to bhikṣus; rather, they belong to those who are in hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they were renunciants who did not strike the *gandi* bell, but instead drank the sweet syrup of the Sangha in silence, fearing that monks from outside might arrive.
Due to the causes and conditions of stinginess, you fell into hell, where you have been drinking and swallowing molten copper; your suffering continues to this day without ceasing.
Furthermore, as for that second large mound of flesh which you see—it is not actually a mound, but a person from hell.

During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, this person was an ordained monk who served as the administrator of a monastery. He selected the finest rooms for his own personal use and gave [the remainder] to those he knew.

Śīta. Because he did not rely on the Vinaya teachings and distributed rooms according to seniority rather than equitably, by this cause and condition he entered hell and became a great flesh altar, undergoing myriad forms of suffering that continue unabated to this day. The rest is explained in detail in such works as the *Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra*.
○ The twenty-seventh: The precept against accepting individual invitations.
This violates the principle and benefit of the six harmonies of the ten directions and contravenes the impartial mind of filial obedience characteristic of a Mahāsattva.

If you are a disciple of the Buddha, you must under no circumstances accept individual invitations so that gain and offerings enter your own person; for such gain and offerings belong to the ten directions.

To separately accept an invitation while belonging to the Sangha of the ten directions is to take the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for one’s own use. Furthermore, among the eight fields of merit,
it constitutes a minor offense (light defilement) because one uses for oneself the property belonging to the Buddhas and sages, each individual teacher, parents, and the sick.
"Everyone" refers to kings, ministers, commoners, and scholars; the five groups of the ordained; and the two groups of the laity.

If one intends to select and specifically invite only certain individuals, those invited may not accept [the invitation], because the benefits of the gift belong to the collective possession of the Sangha of the ten directions.
If one were to accept such an invitation, it would be equivalent to taking monastic property for oneself. Not only that—
To take monastic property for one’s own use is likewise to seize the goods belonging to the eight fields of merit and appropriate them for personal use.

For when the Sangha receives offerings and gains sustenance, these are used to make supreme offerings to the Field of Reverence (the Triple Gem), middle offerings to the Field of Gratitude (parents and teachers), and lower cultivation toward the Field of Compassion (all sentient beings).
Therefore, there is no offense in the following cases: if one is requested to preach the Dharma or confer the precepts; if one perceives a specific opportunity (*kāla-yukti*);

or if one knows that the donor is free from the notion of "mine" and thus does not seek to cultivate merit for oneself. Furthermore, there is no offense if among those invited—even down to a group of four—there is at least one who belongs to the regular succession of the Saṃgha.
"Saṃgha" refers to a harmonious assembly; one, two, or three individuals do not constitute [the Saṃgha].
"Saṃgha" refers to a group of four or more, up to hundreds or thousands; only then is it designated as "Saṃgha.
This concludes the fifth fascicle of the *Brief Commentary on the "Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground Chapter" of the Buddha-Bhāṣita Brahmajāla Sūtra*, including the phonetic glossary.
The Buddha told Saṃgharakṣita: "That person you see on the second high seat is not actually a Dharma master; he is a denizen of hell.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was a great Dharma master who taught the Dharma through wrong livelihoods (*mithyājīva*).

When he received offerings and sustenance, he spoke in accordance with the truth; but when he received no offerings, he preached what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and what is the Dharma as not the Dharma. Because of this..."
Due to these causes and conditions, he entered hell and sat upon a high iron throne, suffering from the burning flames without ceasing even until now.
As for "essential path" (*yādo*), it means that by unifying all paths into one, it serves as the essential principle for all doctrines; therefore, it is called the "essential path."
"Tenet" (zhongzhi) refers to the intended meaning; it denotes the core purpose that the sutra venerates and honors.

Regarding the five grades of the Iron Wheel, which are the five stages of the outer ordinary person in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): first is the mind of sympathetic joy (*suixixin*); second is reading and reciting.
Third, the teaching of the Dharma; fourth, practicing the six perfections concurrently; fifth, practicing the six perfections correctly.
The Iron Wheel refers to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Through perfect hearing and perfect faith, one cultivates perfect practice;

by progressing from the preceding stage of external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), one becomes doubly and increasingly profound and clear, thereby attaining entry into the ten faiths of the Perfect [Teaching]. The ten faiths are explained as before. Formerly, Master Huisi of Mount Nanyue...
He attained the purification of the six sense faculties. As he approached his death, the assembly suspected that the Master had realized the tenth stage (bhūmi).

The Master said: "Throughout my life, I hoped to enter the Bronze Wheel [age] to lead disciples; however, because I benefited others too early at the expense of myself, I have dwelt only in the Iron Wheel [age].
When the Dharma heir of Nanyue, the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai, was about to pass away, his disciples asked him: "We do not know for certain—into what [stage] has the Master entered?"
The Master said, "You are too lazy to plant roots of goodness, yet you ask about the merits of others; it is like a blind man asking about milk—what benefit is there in telling you the truth?
I shall now destroy your doubts for you. I do not lead disciples; I must purify my six sense-faculties.
To harm myself for the sake of others is merely the level of the five ranks."
Sumeru, here translated as "Wondrous High Mountain," is composed of four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and is thus called "wondrous.
Because it rises above all other mountains, it is called "high."
The eight winds are: first, gain; second, loss; third, defamation; fourth, praise; fifth, renown; sixth, insignificance; seventh, suffering; and eighth, pleasure.
These eight can fan and stir the human mind, giving rise to love and hatred; therefore, they are called "winds."
The four floods (*ogha*) are the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*).

Dharmakṣema—translated here as Fǎfēng (Abundant Dharma)—was a native of Central India. He could recite ten thousand words daily and was well-versed in incantations, spells, and the treatises of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
In the first year of Xuānshí during the Northern Liáng dynasty, he arrived at Gūzàng carrying the *Nirvāṇa* [Sūtra].

The *Bānqián* (Pūrva-vibhāga) consists of ten fascicles, along with the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*. When Juqu Mengxun heard of Kumārajīva’s name, he treated him with great hospitality and requested that he translate these works.
"Là" (鑞) is pronounced "lā"; it refers to tin.
The character for *tǒu* (鍮) is pronounced like *tōu*. *Tǒushí* (鍮石) is brass; it resembles gold. The four *māras* are:
the *kleśamāra* (affliction-māra), the *skandhamāra* (aggregate-māra), the *mṛtyumāra* (death-māra), and the *devaputramāra* (son-of-heaven māra).
The three realms are: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
*Sāṃkhya* (translated here as *xiūliú*, "owl") is the name of a non-Buddhist school.

A person of this school appeared eight hundred years before the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*). The treatise he composed is named *Vaiśeṣika*, which means "Unconquerable" (*wu sheng*).
It consists of one hundred thousand verses and concerns the science of calculation and logic (*śulka-śāstra*).
Siddham (悉曇). This is translated as "the accomplishment of that which is produced. It was originally created by the deity Brahmā.
The Siddham script is the root of all written characters; it is described as "half" (ardha), while the remaining scripts and characters are complete and are thus called "full" (pūrṇa).
Furthermore, twelve of the scripts are all termed "half," while the other sutras and records [are termed full].
The treatise is for the sake of fulfillment. It is similar to this region [of China], wherein all characters are produced from thirty-six phonemes (*akṣara*).
*Vyākaraṇa*, also known as *Vyañjana*, is translated here as *Śabdānuśāsana* (Treatise on the Record of Sounds and Names).

Because it extensively records all phenomena (*dharma*) that are capable of signification, it is called "Sounds and Names. It records the establishment of the world at the beginning of the Kalpa of Brahmā.
The King spoke it in one million verses; Śakra, Lord of Devas at the beginning of the kalpa, abridged it into one hundred thousand verses.

Hexi said: "This is the root of all worldly scripts and the treatise on phonology and sound. It expounds the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), censures worldly dharmas, and praises the dharma of renunciation.
Its phrasing is elegant and refined, and its principles are profound. Although it is a non-Buddhist treatise,"

Yet there is no heterodox teaching therein; could this not be the work of a Mahāsattva of skillful means (*upāya*)? Even if it were indeed the work of one with skillful means, its outward traces appear to be those of a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*).
Moreover, it records many worldly affairs rather than matters concerning transcendence from the world, though its diction is elegant and refined.

These belong to worldly conventions and are not the study of the Mahāyāna within the mental ground of the Great Beings (mahāsattva); therefore, they are not permitted for study. The five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) are:

first, the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*), which explains glosses, defines characters, and distinguishes categories; second, the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthānavidyā*), including technical skills, mechanical devices, and the calculation of yin-yang and calendrical cycles;
third, the science of medicine (*cikitsāvidyā*), involving medicinal herbs, stones, acupuncture, and moxibustion; fourth, the science of spells and incantations (*hetuvidyā*).

Prohibitive incantations ward off evil. The five sciences of logic (*pramāṇa*) examine and determine the heterodox and the orthodox, and investigate the true and the false; they concern the discourses of non-Buddhists.

Generally, in the Western Regions, when first initiating and guiding students, one first studies the Twelve Chapters; after the age of seven, one gradually receives instruction in the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*).
Regarding the categories of the Classics, History, Philosophy, and Collections: "Classics" refers to the Five Classics; "History" refers to the historical records of various states;

"Philosophy" refers to the various schools of thought and the hundred masters; and "Collections" refers to compilations of excerpts by the worthy and good of past and present, such as the *Yùlǎn* (Imperial Readings) and similar works.
Thus, these four categories encompass all books without exception.
The "Chronicles" (Zhuan) refer to the *Gongyang*, *Guliang*, and *Zuo* commentaries on the Spring and Autumn Annals; the "Records" (Ji) refer to the *Zhouli*, *Yili*, and *Liji*.
Together with the three aforementioned classics among the Five Classics, these constitute the Nine Classics (*jiujing*).
*Zhāotí* (招提) is here translated as "the Sangha of the four directions.
*Huì* (膾) is pronounced *huì*; it is a phonetic transcription.

The *Chánshī Zhǔqiúfǎ Gāosēng Zhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks Who Sought the Dharma as Abbot of Temples) states: "The Sanskrit term is *vihāra-samiti*, which is translated here as 'temple' (*sì*)."
"Master" refers to the person who founded the monastery. "Māmādī" is a term from the Hu (Central Asian) language.
If one serves as a rotating official in charge of the monastery gates and mediates matters for the monks, he is called a *vihārapāla*, translated as "Protector of the Monastery."
If one strikes the *gandī* or acts as the supervisor of meals, they are called a *karmadāna*, translated as "distributor of affairs" (*shoushi*).

The term *vinaya* (or *weina*) is an abbreviation. *Dāna* means "bestowing," and *karman* means "affairs. The intended meaning is that [the office] manages the various miscellaneous affairs of the community.

Regarding the term "Weina" (維那) used for one who instructs others: the old translation is incorrect. "Wei" (維) is a Chinese word meaning "mainstay" or "framework," while "na" (那) is a Sanskrit sound that is an abbreviation of the term *karmadāna*.

The *Sengshi lüe* (Abridged History of the Sangha) translates it as "one who manages affairs" (*zhishi*) and also calls it "one who gladdens the assembly" (*yuezhong*), meaning one who understands their duties and brings joy to the community. According to the *Nanshan shenglun*, *weina* is translated as [the aforementioned].
*The Sequential Order*. This refers to knowing the sequence of monastic affairs.

Composed by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Baoxiang Forest Monastery in Guangzhou.
Twenty-eighth: The Precept Against Inviting Monks Individually.

To violate this is to contravene the mind of signlessness (animitta-citta) and to lose the merit of equality. When the three spheres (trimaṇḍala) are not empty, it is not the practice of the Great Being’s dāna-pāramitā.
It is like honey.

If, O sons of the Buddha, there are monastic bodhisattvas, lay bodhisattvas, or any donors who, when inviting the Sangha as a field of merit to seek the fulfillment of their vows, should enter the monastery and inquire of the administrative officer: "I now wish to invite the Sangha to seek the fulfillment of my vows. The [officer] shall...
The attendant replied: "To invite according to the sequence of the assembly is to obtain the assembly of worthy and holy ones from the ten directions.
Yet, if worldly people separately invite five hundred arhats or bodhisattvas, it is not equal to inviting even a single ordinary monk according to the sequence of the assembly."

The worthy sages possess both the provisional and the real. The real refers to those who have already realized the four fruits [of the śrāvaka], the three stages of worthiness, and the ten stages of sagehood.

The provisional refers to those who, though still ordinary beings, have already received the great precepts of the original source-ground and are practicing and studying the correct path of the worthy sages.

They are also called "worthy sages" (*ārya*). Therefore, the Sangha encompasses both ordinary beings and sages; its giving extends universally throughout the ten directions, and its mental conduct is impartial. Its merit is equal to the realm of space.

If one gives with a mind that discriminates, the retribution will be limited. This is especially so when it is difficult to distinguish between the noble and the ordinary, and how could one possibly fathom their relative excellence?
For this reason, Piṇḍola was beaten and the śrāmaṇera did not receive the gift of robes; thus we know that one does not need to wait for a long time to become a worthy sage.
How much more so for the Tathāgata, who has already commanded the sixteen great arhats, each leading a retinue of hundreds of thousands.

They had all realized the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path], yet they manifested traces identical to those of ordinary people so that no one could recognize them; thus they served as fields of merit for those who offered alms.
According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* and the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*, when the mother Viśākhā invited five hundred arhats for a separate meal, the Buddha said:
"The mother Viśākhā is ignorant and unskilled; she will not obtain great merit. Had she instead invited [the monks] from the Saṃgha in their regular order..."
"One person" attains great merit; the fruit and benefit of their reward are most supreme. Question: Is it then that five hundred noble monks (*ārya-saṃgha*) do not equal one ordinary monk?
Answer: One must understand that when discussing the "field" (*kṣetra*), even a hundred thousand million times [the merit] does not equal that of a noble one.
Thus, in the past, Aniruddha offered a single meal to a Pratyekabuddha, and from that time onward, for ninety...

For one kalpa, they will receive inexhaustible blessings among devas and humans. As stated in the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*, from giving food to an evil person up to giving to the Tathāgata, the merit is clearly evident. When considering the mind, the merit is equal and great.

Therefore, the Tathāgata instructed Śāriputra to give food to a dog. However, in principle, one should accord with the circumstances and grasp what is most significant; do not be dogmatically attached to a single point.
The Dharma is such that it does not involve mutual obstruction. This treatise discusses the impartiality of the mind in giving; it does not discuss the seeking of the Dharma.

To seek the Dharma, one must possess the eye of discernment (*dharmapravicaya*). It is no small matter to lose one's way on the Great Path by failing to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, or the worthy and the foolish.

(This sutra was spoken by the Tathāgata when he first sat beneath the Bodhi tree. Since the mother Viśākhā had not yet been born, how can it say she separately invited five hundred [monks]? This may be...)
The Tathāgata has spoken of events in past lives concerning former Buddhas, sometimes providing a prediction that such-and-such an event would certainly occur for Viśākhā in the future.
To invite the Saṃgha separately is the practice of non-Buddhists; among the Seven Buddhas, there was no method of separate invitation, as it does not accord with the Way of Filial Piety.
If one intentionally invites the Saṃgha separately, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
To follow the teachings of external paths and not abide by the Buddha’s regulations is to oppose the Buddha and transgress the Dharma;
it is furthermore to contradict the principle of viewing ordinary beings and sages with equal compassion. Therefore, it is said that such conduct does not accord with the way of filial piety.

As for the Seven Buddhas, they all manifested through transformation within this Sahā world, their traces being within the span of a hundred kalpas. Those in the Heaven of Longevity have all seen them; thus, they are frequently cited in various places.
The seven Buddhas serve as witnesses to make it easy for people to understand.
Ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Vipaśyin, also known as Viśvabhū. During the intervening kalpas, no Buddhas appeared.
Then, in the thirty-first kalpa, two Buddhas appeared in the world: the first was named Śikhin, and the second was named Viśvabhū. This was the ninety-first [kalpa].
This kalpa is named the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Kalpa), during which one thousand Buddhas appear in the world. The first is Krakucchanda Buddha;
the second is Kanakamuni Buddha; the third is Kāśyapa Buddha; the fourth is Śākyamuni Buddha; and so on, until the final thousandth, named Ruci Buddha.
Previously, he alone received offerings and maintained the precepts, and thus guest monks were not dispatched to attend invitations.
This constitutes an offense. Next is the precept against accepting individual invitations; this refers to incurring an offense by personally accepting separate invitations from others.

The present precept concerns the offense incurred when one personally selects and invites the Saṃgha. There is no offense in cases where one does not seek merit by inviting the Saṃgha for a meal, but rather invites them individually because of some discussion with acquaintances or friends.
○ The twenty-ninth precept: Abstaining from wrong livelihood.
To seek profit through false teachings to sustain one’s own life, or to harm living beings to nourish oneself, is not the compassionate mind nor the pure mind of a Mahāsattva.
If, O sons of the Buddha, out of an evil mind and for the sake of profit, you engage in the trade of men and women; prepare food with your own hands; grind and husk grain yourself;
practice physiognomy on men and women; interpret the good or bad fortune of dreams; determine whether a child will be male or female; employ incantations and crafts; train hawks;
compound hundreds or thousands of varieties of poisonous drugs, including snake venom, poisons derived from living gold and silver, and *gū* (insect-poison).
Poisonous. It is entirely devoid of a heart of compassion and a heart of filial obedience. If one intentionally commits such acts, one incurs a minor offense (light impurity).
"With an evil mind" clarifies that it is not a wholesome mind; "for the sake of profit and sustenance" clarifies that it is not for the benefit of sentient beings.
"Selling the sexual favors of men and women" refers to purchasing young men and women to sell them to others for carnal desires. "Preparing food with one's own hands."

This refers to personally tending the fire and cooking. "Grinding and pounding" refers to grinding and pounding the five grains. "Divining and physiognomizing men and women": "divining" (zhan) means using divination;

"physiognomizing" (xiang) means examining physical forms and observing the vital breath (*qi*). Both involve falsely judging whether men and women will live long or die young, or whether their fortunes will be prosperous or impoverished.
"Interpreting dreams" means analyzing dreams to determine good or bad fortune, calamity or blessing. As for "the fetus being male or... [the text continues].
“Women. “Incantations” refers to the heterodox spells, talismans, and registers of non-Buddhists.
“Arts and crafts” refers to the skills and techniques of the hundred artisans. “Taming hawks” refers to training hawks and dogs for hunting.
“A hundred kinds and a thousand kinds of poisons” means employing all manner of worldly poisons—compounded into decoctions, ointments, pills, and powders—to harm living beings. “Snake venom.”
Furthermore, the venom of a snake resides in its head or its tail; one may injure a person by taking its brain or its reproductive fluid.

Raw gold and silver, when ingested, immediately end one's life. As for *gū* (poisonous miasma), it is formed when toxic drugs are compounded and consumed, causing the abdomen to swell and become infested with worms.
One who possesses no heart of compassion—such a person the Great Being (*mahāsattva*) should regard with loving-kindness and pity.

Sentient beings are like one's own infants; yet, while one should conceive the thought of sacrificing oneself to benefit others, instead one harms others for the sake of one's own livelihood, which is like eating the flesh of one's own child—this is to lack a heart of compassion. A Bodhisattva regards sentient beings as his own parents.
On the contrary, to harm one’s own parents for the sake of self-interest is the height of filial disobedience; it is a lack of a heart of filial piety.
Therefore, the author [of the precepts] makes this clear so that it is not taken as a mere error. This constitutes a minor offense (*āpatti*) because one seeks a livelihood through improper means.

If a living being dies, one commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). However, if one is a layperson who maintains oneself according to the Dharma through incantations, crafts, or medicine, there is no harm.

Regarding "objects": there is no offense. If one who has left the household life uses authentic incantations and arts to rescue those in peril and alleviate distress, provided they have no heart for seeking profit, this is also permitted.
Question: Grinding and pounding to prepare food—how can one living at home avoid this? Answer: There are two meanings to this. First, it is for the sake of sustaining one's own livelihood.
Because it is not the practice of a Great Being (mahāsattva). Second, because within the firewood, rice, and other grains used for the five cereals, there are many insects;
thus, if one does not harm living beings, it is not a wrong way of seeking a livelihood. This is also permitted for the two lower groups of the ordained. According to the sūtras and śāstras:

There are five kinds or four kinds of wrong ways of seeking a livelihood, which correspond to those found in the present precepts. First, for the sake of gain and offerings, one falsely displays extraordinary feats.
Second, for the sake of gain and offerings, one speaks of one's own virtues. Third, for the sake of gain and offerings, one practices divination of good and bad fortune.
Fourth, for the sake of gain and offerings, one raises one's voice and displays an air of authority to cause others to feel awe and reverence. Fifth, for the sake of... [the text continues].

Because they seek sustenance, they speak of the offerings they have received to move the hearts of others. Furthermore, there are four kinds of improper food by which those who have left the household life sustain their lives:
first, downward-facing food, which refers to medicine, geomancy, and the cultivation of fields and gardens;

second, upward-facing food, which refers to observing celestial phenomena such as the sun, moon, and the five planets; third, sideways-facing food, which refers to fawning upon and flattery toward those of high power and influence.

Acting as envoys to the four quarters, using clever speech to seek much, and subsisting on the mouths of others in the four directions—meaning learning various incantations and divining good or bad fortune—if one acts contrary to the above, it is called "pure livelihood" (śuddhājīva). There are, furthermore, four kinds of pure livelihood.
First, fruits and vegetables from deep in the mountains; second, constantly practicing alms-gathering; third, food sent by donors; fourth, pure food within the Sangha.
Sustaining one’s life by these means without defiling the mind-ground is called "pure livelihood" (the secular term for geomancy is *kānyú*).
○ The thirtieth precept: Not revering auspicious times.
To fail to know how to show reverence during auspicious times is not an expression of faith or filial piety; it is a discrepancy between words and deeds, and a lack of a correct or sincere mind.

This applies to the six fast days, the ten fast days, the three long periods of fasting, days when great spiritual powers are manifested, and even the Buddha’s birthday, his attainment of enlightenment, and other such occasions.
Nirvana, the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, and so forth—these are all auspicious times.
Yet, if a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, slanders the Triple Gem himself while feigning intimacy and attachment, and speaks of emptiness with his mouth;
To engage in worldly affairs, manage the business of laypeople, act as an intermediary for men and women to engage in sexual intercourse, and create various bonds and attachments;
and on the six days of fasting or during the three months of the long fast, to commit acts of killing, robbery, or theft that violate the fast and transgress the precepts—
these constitute a minor offense of defilement.
An evil mind refers to failing to give rise to a heart of reverence toward the Triple Gem and failing to serve them;

instead of skillfully guiding others, one falsely and deceitfully pretends to be close to the Triple Gem in order to cause others to believe in and revere it. When speaking, every word discusses emptiness, yet when acting, every thought remains attached to existence.
Thus, words and deeds contradict one another, deviating from what is correct and true; for this reason, it is called slandering the Triple Gem.

"Managing affairs" refers to managing and attending to the household matters of laypeople (*avadātavasana*), even to the point of acting as a go-between for their private sexual liaisons or arranging marriages and the like—filthy, loathsome, and base activities.
"Creating various bonds and attachments" means performing such impure acts as described above; these are all entanglements for oneself and others that lead to the three evil realms (*durgati*).
In this state, one wanders through birth and death and fails to attain liberation. Regarding the six days of fasting (*ṣaḍ-upoṣadha*), the *Caturmahārājakāyika-sūtra* states:

"On these days of fasting, the various devas observe the good and evil of human beings. Each of the Four Heavenly Kings governs one quarter [of the world] and regularly dispatches messengers on the eighth and twenty-third days of the month to descend and inspect the human realm, examining their virtues and vices. (10)
On the twenty-ninth day of the fourth month, the Crown Prince descends. On the fifteenth and thirtieth days of the month, the Four Heavenly Kings descend in person.

They command the sun, moon, five planets, and the twenty-eight lunar mansions to diligently observe the good and evil deeds of sentient beings, and report all matters together to Śakra, Lord of the Devas.
This concerns the performance of auspicious and inauspicious rites. As for the three months of the "Long Fast" (Trīṇi Dīrghopavāsa-māsāḥ), they are the first, fifth, and ninth months.
During these months, Śakra Devendra uses his great precious mirror to clearly illuminate Jambudvīpa and examine its transgressions and merits.

Furthermore, the Four Heavenly Kings each govern one of the four great continents during these months; specifically, during these three months, it is the turn of the Northern Vaiśravaṇa Heavenly King to govern the south.

This is the month for examining the good and evil of humans. Such days and such months are entirely times when ghosts and spirits exert their power, and when the Heavenly Kings successively conduct their tours of inspection.
It is precisely at these times that one ought to avoid evil and cultivate goodness.
To fail to recognize such auspicious occasions and instead further neglect and violate the precepts, without giving rise to shame or fear—this is exactly what [is condemned].
This refers to an evil mind. Regarding "killing and stealing," these are the first two of the ten grave precepts, cited here as representatives of all the grave offenses;

for each act committed, one incurs a *pārājika* offense. Furthermore, upon these grave offenses, one adds a minor defilement (*āpatti*), similar to how one might be subjected to flogging in addition to a death sentence. This applies if one has transgressed any of the forty-eight minor precepts.

Furthermore, one incurs the offense of disrespecting the auspicious time. Regarding the breaking of the fast: for laypeople, on the six fasting days and during the months of extended fasting, they undertake the eightfold precepts of the *upavāsa* (fasting).
To abstain from food after midday constitutes the fast; if one violates this by eating at an improper time, it is a breach of the fast.
Therefore, it is said that the fast is broken. For one who has left the household life, one must not eat at improper times for the rest of one’s life.

Thus, on such a day of fasting, if one commits the offense of eating at an improper time, the transgression is increased by one degree. The *Yingluo jing* states: "If there is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva..."
One should cultivate the pure dharmas of the six perfections and concurrently practice the eight precepts, the prohibitions of all Buddhas.
Such good sons and good daughters possess the complete and pure conduct of the dharma of the six perfections, as described in the sutras.
How could they possibly treat the fast and precepts lightly, abandon the eight precepts without upholding them, and willingly become those who break the fast and violate the precepts?

These ten precepts should be studied, revered, and upheld. They are explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Formulation of Precepts," from the precept against striking others in retaliation out of anger to this precept against disrespecting auspicious times.

These ten precepts should be diligently practiced, respectfully maintained, and never forgotten. The remainder is as clearly set forth in detail in the "Chapter on the Formulation of Precepts" in the Great Text.
○ The thirty-first precept: Not providing rescue or ransom.
To see suffering and not offer relief is to lack a heart of compassion; to know that someone is being sold yet fail to redeem them is to violate the way of filial piety and obedience.

The Buddha said, "O Son of the Buddha: after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in this degenerate age, if you see non-Buddhists, various evil persons, or bandits who sell images of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or one's parents;
or who sell the sūtras and the Vinaya; or who trade in bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs;
or who even sell those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta—those Bodhisattvas and practitioners of the Way—or who act as agents for the government for all manner of people."
Regarding "slaves":
this clearly refers to the degenerate age of the Final Dharma after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. During the time when the Buddha was in the world, all people knew what was virtuous;
therefore, such things did not exist. Regarding "images": whether they are carved, modeled, or painted, if they are forcibly seized by wicked people...
Or perhaps they were stolen and sold by bandits. Now, by mentioning the two assemblies of bhikṣus, one already encompasses all seven assemblies.
One who has resolved to attain bodhicitta is a person who has first aroused the great mind; a "path-maker" (dōjin) is one who practices the Great Path of the Bodhisattva.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One who has attained the Way is called a path-maker. Other renunciants, although they have not yet attained the Way, because they practice...
Because they follow the supramundane path, they are also called "men of the Way" (*dharma-pudgala*). "Government officials and messengers" refers to those dispatched for service by the government.
"All people" refers to the various classes, such as scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants.
When a bodhisattva sees such things, they should give rise to a mind of compassion and employ skillful means to rescue and protect them.

They should go everywhere to teach and convert others so that objects may be acquired to redeem images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and those who have resolved their minds for enlightenment (bodhisattvas), and all sūtras and vinayas.
If one does not redeem them, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

Buddha images are the Buddha Jewel. The Sūtras and Vinaya are the Dharma Jewel. Those who have resolved their minds toward the Way, as well as the physical forms of Bodhisattvas, are the Mahāyāna Saṅgha Jewel.
Bhikṣus are the Hīnayāna Saṅgha Jewel. Parents are the field of gratitude; they are the very heaven and earth for their children.
It is precisely the Great Being’s duty, amidst this final age of evil, to protect and uphold the Buddha-Dharma.
To cause the Three Jewels to flourish, to extensively perform virtuous deeds, and to transform and guide sentient beings—how could one simply sit idly by while witnessing such acts of humiliation?
Therefore, one ought to redeem them. If one lacks personal power or wealth, one should employ various skillful means to exhort and persuade others to redeem and liberate them.
If one is indolent or intentionally fails to redeem them, in either case, one commits an offense.
○ The thirty-second precept: Refraining from harming sentient beings.

One should distance oneself from the causes of harm and abandon the karmic actions of killing, stealing, and binding. Thus, from the outset, one does not contravene the compassionate mind of a Mahāsattva.
It is the mind of compassion; it is the mind of benefiting others.

O Disciples of the Buddha, you must not engage in the trade of swords, staves, bows, or arrows; nor may you keep light scales or small measures, nor exploit the power and influence of government officials.

To seize the property of others; to bind others with a harmful intent; to ruin successful undertakings; or to raise cats, wildcats, pigs, and dogs—if one intentionally raises such creatures, one commits a minor offense.
Swords, staves, bows, and arrows; fetters; cats, wildcats, pigs, and dogs—these harm the primary retribution of sentient beings, namely their physical bodies and life spans.
Other items, such as weights and measures, all harm the secondary retribution of sentient beings, namely their resources for enjoyment.

If one uses small [weights] when exiting, one must necessarily use large ones when entering. The same principle applies to the length of cubits and feet. As for "form and power" (xing-shi), it may be...
Using one's own official power, or relying on the power of another official, to bind—meaning to bind with a malicious and private heart—and to injure the limbs of sentient beings;

this is not the binding of a criminal with an impartial mind. Even if they are a criminal, one must still give rise to a heart of compassion and pity, mindful of their ignorance and lack of wisdom, and should employ skillful means to exhort and persuade them so that they may develop [wholesome resolve].

A "wholesome mind" is one that reforms previous transgressions. "Destroying successful achievements" refers to when another person’s endeavor is about to be completed or has already been accomplished, yet one uses an evil mind to cause it to be ruined or abandoned. "Nurturing" means to rear or sustain.
Cats and kittens are both creatures that catch mice; pigs and dogs, out of greed for wealth, harm living beings. To sell them constitutes a minor offense; to kill them is a grave one.

This constitutes the first grave offense. As for using false weights and measures, or taking things by force, or destroying another’s livelihood—all these constitute the second grave offense, termed "deceptive acquisition" or "coercive acquisition.
Therefore, the act of raising [animals] is mentioned last as a summary that encompasses the preceding five offenses, all of which involve harm;
thus, they are transgressions. The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* likewise does not permit the keeping of such animals.
This extends even to pigs, sheep, silkworms, and so forth. In the Vinaya, for the sake of protection, the keeping of puppies is permitted.
The *Saṃyukta-piṭaka-sūtra* states: A certain ghost said to Maudgalyāyana, "My scrotum is as large as a jar;
when walking, I carry it upon my shoulder, and when standing still, I sit upon it. My every movement is plagued by suffering. For what reason? Maudgalyāyana replied, "In a previous life..."
In this world, they constantly gave using light scales and small measures, yet took using heavy scales and large measures.

Desiring to gain great profit for themselves while encroaching upon and exploiting others, they thus receive this retribution; this is the "flower reward" (the preliminary sign), while the bitter fruit of hell awaits them hereafter.
○ Thirty-third: The Precept Against Erroneous Mental Application (*vitarka*) and Discernment (*vicāra*).

When the initial mind suddenly arises and briefly reflects, it is called *vitarka* (applied thought). When the subtle mind discriminates and contemplates deeply, it is called *vicāra* (sustained thought).
If one contemplates supramundane dharmas, it is termed "right application. If one contemplates mundane, miscellaneous affairs, it is therefore called "erroneous application. There is...
This disrupts the Right Path and violates the essence of the mind-precepts (this precept text is identical to that in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*).
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, watches all men and women fighting, or armies, generals,
and bandits fighting.

An "evil mind" refers to that which is not the virtuous intention of using skillful means to reconcile those who see the opportunity, nor the provisional display of conformity to their wrong actions in order to entice them back to the Right Path.
It consists of two types: first, the strife of body and speech between a man and a woman; second, the combat of military arrays.
Third, when three or more bandits fight each other out of mutual animosity—this refers to the "superior" category, such as elephants, horses, oxen, and dogs fighting.

The Great Sūtra states that one must not watch even chickens, pheasants, or parrots fighting. As for the "inferior" category, this refers to the fighting of violent, drunken, and unprincipled individuals;
watching such scenes will inevitably result in injury and will cause unwholesome thoughts to arise in people.
One will lose one’s own dignified deportment and incur the ridicule and criticism of the laity; this is the first precept regarding observing combat.
Furthermore, one must not listen to the sounds of conch shells, drums, horns, lutes, harps, zithers, flutes, *konghou* lutes, singing, shouting, or the music of performers.

The conch (*śaṅkha*) is a sea shell. The lute (*vīṇā*) has seven strings or five strings. The zither (*tūṇava*) has twenty-five strings. The *zheng* has thirteen strings. The *konghou* has twenty-four strings.
The flute is one chi four cun long with seven holes. These eight items above all produce sound by means of external objects.
Singing and shouting refer to the vocal chanting and recitation performed by men and women themselves. As for "prostitutes' music" (*gīta-vādya*), it includes the conch, drums, and so forth...
The *sheng* and *huang*, the *xiao* and *guan*, the *pipa*, the three-stringed lute, the two-stringed lute, singing girls, and the like—all these belong to the category of music and performance.

In ancient times, women were frequently employed to perform them; thus, the characters for these instruments include the "woman" radical (*nǚ*). These are all gateways to dissipation that obstruct the cultivation of the path and practice.
They merely increase sensual pleasure and provide no benefit to sentient beings. One should not even go to watch or listen to them, let alone participate in them oneself.

Is it permissible? According to the *Yìshù* (Commentary on Meaning), making [musical instruments] for the purpose of making offerings to the Triple Gem is permitted; however, making them for one's own amusement is not allowed.
Furthermore, this does not permit the Sangha to do so themselves, but rather requires that laypeople make them. This is the second precept concerning entertainment.

One must not engage in gambling with dice, go-boarded chess, the game of *bala-sekhiya* (the "elephant" game), *tanqi* (stone-throwing chess), *liubo* (six-sided dice), ball-pounding, stone-throwing at a pitch, or games such as *quandao*,
*badao*, *xingcheng*, and so forth.
*Chupu* (chess-like games) is the general name for board games involving dice and pieces. The *Bowuzhi* states that Laozi created these while in the Hu regions.
Since Laozi is revered as a sage in this land, how could he have invented gambling games to disturb the minds and wills of people?

This is clearly explained below in the response of Confucius to Duke Ai. As for *weiqi* (go), there were formerly three hundred and sixty lines; nowadays, there are only ten horizontal and vertical lines.
The ninth section: On the game of *pāśaka*. "Pāra" is a Sanskrit term; "sèxì" (塞戲) is a Chinese term. "Sè" is pronounced like "sài," referring to *bósè* (博塞).
This means that when dice (*cǎi*) compete for victory, it is called *sè*. The *Yuánshuō* (苑說) states: "Moving the pieces so as to block one another is called *sè*.
As for *tánqí* (彈棊), according to this region, Han palace ladies used it as a diversion with their cosmetic boxes, or they used chessmen (*qí*).
The "Son" (zi) game involves mutual striking; it is also called *tanqi* (stone-tossing). *Liubo* (six-dice) is the game of *shuanglu* (double-six).
*Paiqu* (ball-beating) is the game of kicking a ball. Regarding "throwing stones and casting into the vase": in antiquity one used stones to throw, whereas nowadays one uses arrows to cast.
As for "the eight paths of the *qian dao* and the moving city": this is the Indian game of chess (*chaturanga*), with eight rows and eight columns, using chess pieces.
One should not practice such things as these, including chess and the like. All the aforementioned games are mentioned by name in both the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The *Jia Yu* records that Duke Ai asked Confucius: "I have heard it said that a gentleman does not play at dice; is this so? Confucius replied:
"It is so, because it involves the simultaneous practice of an evil path. Alas! Even the scholars of the world still feel shame [at such conduct].

If this is so for them, how much more so for a Great Being who cultivates the Great Way of the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena—would it be appropriate for such a one to harbor a mind of victory and defeat to deceive sentient beings? This is the third precept concerning frivolous games.
They perform divination using fingernails, mirrors, *shichō* stalks, willow branches, alms bowls, and skulls. Regarding the fingernail mirror:
either medicinal substances are applied to the fingernails, or incantations are recited over the fingers, causing them to become as clear as a mirror.

This refers to manifesting matters such as auspiciousness and misfortune. As in the Esoteric Section (Guhyatantra), one may manifest such matters on the fingernails through incantations, or—as with Fotucheng—manifest them upon his fingers.
There is no offense for those who do so without a desire for profit, solely for the benefit of sentient beings. Regarding the *shichao* (millet stalks):

they grow in clusters of a hundred stalks, and when mature, they invariably reach a height of one zhang. In ancient times, they emerged from the tomb of Fuxi and Wenwang, with clouds and vapors covering them above.
Below, one guards the numinous tortoise and uses forty-nine stalks to perform divination. One divides them into two parts, sets one aside, counts by fours, and returns the remainders;
three changes form a line (爻), and eighteen changes form a hexagram (卦), whereby one determines good or ill fortune.

Although this region claims these stalks originate from the tombs of Fuxi and King Wen, the people of India also use this grass as their stalks. As for willow branches, they are used when the milfoil stalks (蓍草) are unavailable.

They take willow twigs as whips. Furthermore, it is like the shamans of this land who, through incantations and sacrifices, transform *zhāngliǔ* (catalpa) wood into spirits to report matters of fortune and calamity;
such is the case here. As for the alms bowl (*pātra*), they fill the bowl with water and incantate it, whereby good or ill fortune is manifested.
As for the skull, by means of heterodox arts, they incantate and sacrifice to the skull, and it can then [speak] from beside a person's ear.
This refers to reporting various matters. As for divination: using tortoise shells is called *bu* (divination), and using milfoil stalks is called *shi* (calculation).

However, these collectively encompass the aforementioned five matters used to determine good and ill fortune; all such practices are termed *bu-shi*. These activities all obstruct the Right Path and give rise to false views in people.
Therefore, this fourth precept prohibits divination and fortune-telling.
One must not serve as a messenger for thieves.
Even serving as a state envoy is forbidden; how much more so to act as a messenger for bandits? The harm caused by this is no small matter. If a thief kills a person...
To obtain wealth by instructing others in killing or stealing—whether according to the number of beings killed or the gravity of the stolen property—one incurs a grave offense.
This is the fifth precept: the evil occupation of a messenger.
One must not engage in any of these individually. If one deliberately does so, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
This summarizes the five aforementioned matters: namely, that quarreling gives rise to a violent and malevolent mind;

entertainment leads to the arousal of lustful thoughts; frivolous games cause the mind to become distracted; divination and fortune-telling give birth to heterodox delusions; and acting as a messenger harbors a treacherous heart.
Deceitfulness: All such things as these obstruct the precepts, disturb meditative concentration, and hinder wisdom; therefore, they are prohibited.
As for all other arts, such as poetry and painting, if they conflict with the supramundane right path, one should forever abandon them.

For example, although the former Chan Master Huiquan accumulated great merit through seated meditation, he did not cease his external studies and consequently could not avoid being reborn into a Brahmin family.
Therefore, the harm caused is not slight. The *Xianyu jing* (Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish) states: The Buddha said, "In a past age, there was a king named Dharmavardhana.
Possessing a heart of compassion, he governed the kingdom with righteous laws. Having no affairs and being at leisure, he engaged in board games with others."
At that time, there was a man who had committed a crime. The ministers informed the king, "There is a man outside who has violated the king's law;
how shall he be punished? At that moment, the king was absorbed in playing at dice and failed to give an answer. The ministers then executed him according to the legal code.
Once the king had finished his game, he asked the ministers, "Where is that criminal now? The ministers replied, "He has been dealt with according to the laws of the state."

The rule of law was thus ended. Upon hearing this, the king fainted and fell to the ground; after a long while, he regained consciousness and abandoned his kingdom to enter the mountains and dwell in seclusion.
When the king’s life there came to an end, he was reborn in the great ocean as a makara fish, seven hundred yojanas in length.
Because many insects were devouring his body, he scratched himself against a crystal mountain, which shattered [into pieces].
They kill various insects, and the flowing blood pollutes the sea until it is crimson for a hundred li. Due to these karmic conditions, at the end of their lives they fall into the great hells.
Since such transgressions exist, can one not exercise restraint?
○ Thirty-fourth: Momentarily thinking of the precepts of the Hīnayāna.
The mind desires to turn away from the Mahāyāna toward the Hīnayāna, yet the intention is not yet resolved; this constitutes an offense against the eighth [precept] mentioned previously.

If the mind becomes determined [to abandon the Mahāyāna], one loses the precepts and commits the tenth grave offense. The present precept states that the mind does not desire to turn away from the Mahāyāna, yet [one] speaks of the Hīnayāna.

The vehicle of the Easy Practice is easy to cultivate. One should first sever the afflictions of views and thought, realize *nirvāṇa*, and only then engage in the transformation of sentient beings; it would not be too late.

Yet, by momentarily giving rise to this thought, one immediately abandons the Great Vow and ultimately falls into the stage of a Śrāvaka. How could one know that a Bodhisattva carries along these afflictions?
Yet they are able to extensively benefit all sentient beings. Thus, the *Zhi guan* says: "To regress from the Great Vehicle and adopt the Lesser Vehicle is what all the sages condemn.
A Bodhisattva is not like this; seeing the suffering of sentient beings as their own, they give rise to great compassion and love them as if they were their only child."
Just as a mother who has obtained food constantly thinks of her child, if one dwells in emptiness, there would be the fault of abandoning others;
furthermore, one would be unable to purify buddha-fields, teach and transform sentient beings, or fully perfect the Buddha-dharma—none of these could be accomplished.
Although one enters the world, birth-and-death and afflictions cannot impair one’s wisdom; although the path of the Buddha is long and distant, it does not...
They consider [the path] to be remote. Although the number of sentient beings is vast, their resolve is courageous and their minds are firm without retreat.

With diligent application and energetic advancement, they never experience weariness or indolence. Therefore it is said that a bodhisattva possesses courage regarding birth and death (*saṃsāra*), yet does not relish *nirvāṇa*.
Being courageous in birth and death, they manifest birth without being born, remaining unstained by birth and death, like a lotus flower in [water].
"Mud. It is not defiled by the mud. The *Fuyuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "The sutras say that lotus flowers do not grow on high plateaus or dry land;
rather, it is in low-lying, damp mud that lotus flowers grow. Thus we know that in the 'high plateau' of nirvana, the flowers of a bodhisattva’s great compassion do not grow;
it is within the mud of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) that there exists the bodhisattva’s supreme function of benefiting sentient beings. Although [the bodhisattva] remains in birth..."
One dies, yet remains unstained by birth and death; this is because the Great Being’s vows are firm and his resolve is courageous.

How much more so for those who take refuge in the precepts of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), which do not depart from the Bodhisattva precepts. By the power of the Bodhisattva precepts, one is able to achieve perfection.
Thus, the Great can encompass the Small, whereas the Small lacks the utility of the Great. Why, then, say that it is not too late for such beings to be transformed?

If you, O sons of the Buddha, protect and uphold the prohibitive precepts, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, you should recite these precepts during the six periods of day and night as if they were a diamond,
like one carrying a life-preserving float while wishing to cross the great ocean, or like the bhikṣu bound by grass.

These fifty-eight precepts were all personally established by Śākyamuni; therefore, they are called "prohibitory precepts" (śīla). Just as with a king’s prohibitions and edicts, no one dares to intentionally transgress them.
For this reason, O Mahāsattva, you should maintain and uphold them within the four modes of deportment (*catur-iryāpatha*) and refrain from violating them.

Study them diligently day and night, reciting and chanting them until they are mastered, so that they may never be forgotten. Vajra, these precepts are like a diamond, for they can shatter all [obstacles].
The "afflictions and fetters" are like bandits; the Great Being’s mind is firm in its protection and maintenance, like a diamond (*vajra*). As for the "life-preserving bag" (*uraga-saṃghāṭī*):
in India, those who cross the sea either make it from a pouch of bird feathers, or from the hide of an ox or sheep, or they carry an ox bladder, always wearing it with them.
If the sea vessel is wrecked, they blow air into it to float their bodies and thereby cross the great ocean.
The Ocean: This now serves as a metaphor for a Mahāsattva who wishes to cross the great ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Without the precepts, one cannot reach the other shore. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Suppose there were a rākṣasa who, following those crossing the sea, asked each for a life-preserving float (*uḍupa*).
The crosser replied, 'I would rather sacrifice my own life than give up this float. The rākṣasa spoke again, 'If you are unwilling to give it entirely...'"
When he saw this, he offered half of it; yet that person would not give it. In this manner, they went on begging for as little as a speck of dust, but that person still would not give it.

This is a metaphor for when a Bodhisattva maintains the prohibitive precepts, and the Rākṣasa of the afflictions instructs the Bodhisattva to violate the ten grave offenses while protecting the remaining minor ones; the Bodhisattva does not comply. In this way, they successively urge him toward transgression.
Regarding the remaining articles: even for offenses as minor as light defilements (*āpatti*) or transgressions of bad conduct (*duṣkṛta*), a bodhisattva is likewise unwilling to comply with them.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva upholds the ten grave prohibitions as well as the other light defilements and transgressions of bad conduct with equal reverence and firm resolve;
there is no difference between them. As for the "monk bound by grass": the Tathāgata established a precept that a bhikṣu must not damage or destroy grasses and trees.
In the past, there were certain bhikṣus traveling through a wilderness who were plundered by bandits.
The bandits stripped them of their clothes and, fearing that the bhikṣus would go and inform the village headman, intended to kill all the bhikṣus. Among the bandits was one man.
Knowing that the bhikṣus would not harm the grass, he tied them up with it and departed.
The bhikṣus were scorched by the sun and bitten by mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and lice from dawn until night. Wild beasts roamed about crosswise, creating a most terrifying scene.
They exhorted one another, saying: "We must only protect our precepts; we would rather die than transgress them. Each of them set their own body upright and remained steadfast.
He did not move even when shaken. The next day, the king went out hunting and saw that the bhikṣus were guarding their precepts, preferring death to violating them.
The king’s heart was filled with joy, and he immediately untied the grass for them. This is detailed in the *Nidāna-sūtra* and the *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*.
Regarding this present *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the Tathāgata preached it all at once when he first sat beneath the Bodhi tree; at that time, there were as yet no bhikṣus.
How, then, could there have been binding with grass? This was either a prophetic prediction by the Tathāgata, or it concerns the affairs of bhikṣus from the time of past Buddhas.
This is cited as proof: For example, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, a bhikṣu practicing dhyāna plucked a leaf from an ill-smelling *elā* tree, which fell into the midst of a dragon.
A foul-smelling tree grew upon the dragon's head; when the wind blew and shook it, its pus and filth defiled the great ocean.

For hundreds of thousands of millions of years, he endured various agonies until the appearance of Maitreya Buddha in the world, at which point he was finally released from his dragon body. Thus says the Tripiṭaka.

Throughout [the scriptures], this is cited as proof in various places. Nowadays, those of "mad Chan" claim that liberation lies in the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), while regarding the adherence to precepts as a hindrance;
