they think there is no harm in cutting grass or digging the earth. Yet, they lack the hand of one who has realized the essence and severed the snake, nor do they possess the virtue of one who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and, while plowing a field, allowed insects to remain four inches away from the furrow. One should observe this dragon: is this liberation? Or is it attachment?
It is truly so. To damage but a single leaf of a tree and receive such a retribution—how could this not cause one’s heart to chill and one’s gallbladder to fail?

One should constantly give rise to the wholesome faith of the Mahāyāna, knowing for oneself that "I am a Buddha who is yet to be perfected," while "the Buddhas are Buddhas who have already been perfected.

One should resolve upon bodhicitta, never allowing it to depart from the mind for even a single thought-moment. Should a single thought of the two vehicles or of non-Buddhist paths arise, [one must immediately repent].
One commits a minor offense (light defilement).

Although one may be able to firmly guard the prohibitive precepts, if one lacks correct faith in the Mahāyāna, there remains the fear of falling into the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), ultimately losing the supreme fruit of Buddhahood and consequently forfeiting the great vow to deliver sentient beings; therefore, one must constantly cultivate [this faith].
Virtuous believer: believe in me and in all sentient beings—that these shall become Buddhas who have yet to achieve it, and that the various Buddhas are those who have already achieved it.
Although one possesses such faith, if one does not give rise to the bodhicitta, that faith will have no basis;
therefore, one should give rise to this great mind to strengthen that faith. Knowing that my own mind is the very mind of all Buddhas, one seeks the Buddha-way above. Thus one knows...
My mind is the very mind of sentient beings; therefore, I transform them below. Yet, regarding this mind and this thought, one must not be separated from them for even a moment.

Hence it is said: "Thought after thought, they do not depart from the mind. If one were to be separated from this thought for even a moment, the mind of the Two Vehicles that seeks only self-deliverance would arise.
As for what is called "transforming those below," it does not mean transforming the sentient beings of only a single world, nor even just a hundred...
Regarding the sentient beings of worlds as numerous as the sands of a thousand Ganges Rivers who are said to "seek above":
this does not mean they serve the Buddhas of only a single world, nor even those of hundreds or thousands of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; rather, they seek the Unsurpassed Way.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "A Bodhisattva does not resolve upon Bodhicitta for the sake of teaching and transforming the sentient beings of a single world."

The mind... even not for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings in as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable trillions of three-thousandfold great thousandfold world systems does one resolve upon bodhicitta;
nor for the sake of making offerings to the Tathāgatas who arise in succession within a single world system does one resolve upon bodhicitta; and so on, even not for...

They resolve upon the mind of enlightenment in order to make offerings to the Tathāgatas who appear successively in worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields, and with the desire to teach, transform, and subdue all sentient beings.
Because there is nothing left out, one generates the bodhicitta. Because one wishes to serve and make offerings to all Buddhas without exception, one generates the bodhicitta.
Question: From what does the Great Bodhicitta arise? Answer: It arises from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
As the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "It is for the sake of wishing to rescue and deliver all sentient beings that it is aroused."
Through the power of compassion and vows, one seeks supreme enlightenment; were it not for the sake of delivering sentient beings, I would never have given rise to this bodhicitta.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "From the first stage through to the tenth stage, within each and every stage..."
All [qualities] take great compassion as their primary basis. The *Bodhicittavivaraṇa* states: "From compassion arises the great bodhicitta;
all the most excellent qualities of the Buddha-dharma have compassion as their root. The *Nirvikalpapraveśadhāraṇī* states: "At the time of the cause, it is bodhicitta;
when the fruit is perfected and virtue is complete, it is called Perfect Enlightenment (samyaksaṃbuddha). Thus, bodhicitta...
The Dharma is inconceivable; all Buddhas and Tathāgatas praise it. The *Vimaladattāparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"The merit produced by generating the bodhicitta is as vast, supreme, and inexhaustible as the realm of empty space."

Even if someone were to fill Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with precious jewels and offer them to the World-Honored One, if there were another who, with palms joined in utmost sincerity, were to once give rise to the unsurpassed, right, and equal mind of enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta), this merit would surpass the former merit beyond all calculation. As the *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood* says: "All phenomena are without marks."
Having performed this contemplation on the characteristic of space, it is called the ultimate bodhicitta. One should know that all phenomena are empty;
by realizing that phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, the essence of mind remains as it is.

Not perceiving body or mind, one abides in quiescent extinction, in equality and the ultimate, with true wisdom that allows for no retrogression. If deluded thoughts arise, recognize them and do not follow after them.
When delusion ceases, the source of the mind is empty and tranquil; all virtues are fully present, and its wondrous function is inexhaustible.

Therefore, the Buddhas of the ten directions take supreme meaning and practice as their precepts. One who possesses this mind alone is able to turn the wheel of Dharma, benefiting both self and others.
The rest is clarified in the sixty-fourth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and in the "Chapter on Generating the Bodhicitta."
○ The thirty-fifth precept: Not making vows.

A "vow" (praṇidhāna) has the meaning of aspiring for and desiring [attainment]. Since all extraordinary causes and sublime fruits, as well as immeasurable wholesome dharmas, cannot be accomplished without a heart that aspires and desires them, one must constantly make great vows.
If you are a Buddha’s disciple, you should always resolve to make all vows: to be filial toward your parents and respectful toward your teachers and the Sangha;

to wish for an excellent teacher and virtuous spiritual friends as fellow students who constantly instruct you in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, and in the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, and the ten adamantine stages.
The Ten Grounds. May I attain understanding and realization, practice according to the Dharma, and firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts.
Even at the cost of my body and life, may these [precepts] never depart from my mind for even a single thought-moment. If any Bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense.
"All vows" refers to the ten subsequent vows. The first vow is to be filial toward the four [parents] and others; this is the vow of upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

Since filial piety is defined as the precepts, it constitutes the root of the ten vows. If the root is deficient, the remaining nine will consequently be lost. The second vow is to obtain a good teacher.
A "good teacher" is one who is fully endowed with both practice and understanding. If one has understanding but lacks practice, how...
They are able to lead me forward. If there were practice without understanding, how could they open my mind-ground?

Therefore, the repayment to one's parents and the flourishing of the Triple Gem both rely on the power of the teacher’s instruction for their accomplishment; thus, among the ten vows, the teacher is the most essential.
Even if one possesses faith, without the guidance of a virtuous teacher, one will not become a vessel of the Dharma. In these present times...
In the age of the Final Dharma, it is truly rare to find one who possesses both practice and understanding. For now, follow that which has understanding and cultivate according to that understanding;

by diligently applying effort and striving forward, you shall eventually realize non-arising and reach the Precious Abode. As for those who have practice but lack understanding, their practice is not correct;
you must strictly avoid relying upon them. It would be like taking a blind person as a guide—you would mistakenly fall onto a wrong path and remain lost forever.
There is no end to this cycle. Now, even seeking right view and right understanding is not easily encountered, let alone attaining both practice and understanding in their entirety.
Regarding the first mention of "teacher and monk," it means one should be filial toward one's teacher. Regarding the subsequent mention of "a good teacher," it means one must select a wise guide.
Third, the wish to obtain fellow students who are spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) is because they share the same Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*).
Regarding the study of the fundamental doctrine (*mūlaśāstra*): it is a virtuous friend who skillfully understands the Dharma-gates of the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*).

Even if one encounters an enlightened master, if one lacks a worthy friend, one will be deficient in the benefits of mutual cultivation, refinement, and mutual encouragement. Fourth is the aspiration for excellent instruction; that is, the aspiration for superior masters and friends.

He constantly instructed me in the principles of the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, inspiring in me right faith and leading me to cultivate and advance through the ten stages of "setting forth" (*daśa-prasthāna*), so that I might avoid falling into the one-sided emptiness of the two vehicles or the erroneous attachments of external paths. My fifth vow is to cultivate the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*).

Therefore, it is said that the tenth [stage] is the "Ten Approaches" (*daśa-prasthāna*). Because one cultivates the ten practices through the sixth vow, it is called the "Ten Nourishings" (*daśa-poṣadha*).

Because one cultivates the ten dedications through the seventh vow, it is called the "Ten Vajras" (*daśa-vajra*). Because one cultivates and realizes the ten noble stages through the eighth vow, it is called the "Ten Grounds" (*daśa-bhūmi*).

The ninth is the comprehensive vow to practice in accordance with the Dharma; this refers to the aforementioned Mahāyāna teachings, all of which must be received and cultivated through teachers and friends.

I vow that according to the Dharma I have received, may my mind be opened and my understanding be perfected; following this understanding, I shall practice and realize the stages of the Three Sages and Ten Sages.
May these ten vows be firm as I uphold the precepts. Initially, filial piety was taken as the precept;
now, with this tenth vow, it is concluded once again by upholding the precepts. Thus we know that from beginning to end, the pure precepts of the mind-ground are regarded as supreme.

This is the essential purpose of the vehicle. Thus, there are no immeasurable Dharma-gates, hundreds of thousands of supreme concentrations, or untainted sublime wisdoms that do not arise from the precepts.
From the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood up to the ultimate fruit of wondrous enlightenment, all are attained through the precepts.

Therefore, this Dharma of the precepts is especially worthy of being honored; one should rather sacrifice body and life than allow them to depart from the mind for even a single thought-moment. This means:
Regarding the ten previous vows, one should develop a firm resolve and maintain them in mind without forgetfulness.

Even if one encounters circumstances that threaten one's life, one vows not to cherish or begrudge the four great elements (the physical body) to the point of abandoning this resolve or violating the precepts.
It is said that those Bodhisattvas who do not make these vows—from the initial attainment of the precepts up to the tenth stage—do not produce these ten great [vows].

If one lacks aspiration, the will will not be firm; even with diligent application and cultivation, one may still fear being obstructed by Māra, leading to stagnation midway and making it impossible to reach the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment. Therefore, it is said that the task of adorning the Buddha-realm is great;
merit cultivated in isolation cannot achieve it, and thus it must be sustained by the power of aspiration. It is like the strength of an ox, which, though capable of pulling...
A carriage requires a driver to reach its destination; thus we know that one's resolve must be firm and one's vow must be made.
Therefore, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says: "One should give rise to the pure great vows of a bodhisattva and speak these words:"

May I now abide in the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment (Vajraśekhara). In seeking a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), may I not encounter non-Buddhists (tīrthika) or those of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

Relying on my vow to practice, may I gradually sever all hindrances. When the hindrances are exhausted and the vow fulfilled, I shall ascend to the palace of pure Dharma, realize Great Perfect Enlightenment, and enter the realm of wondrous adornment. This is it.
○ Thirty-sixth: The Precept of Not Renouncing One’s Vow.
A vow is the mind of resolute determination and courageous resolve among the ten great vows.

By means of the vow, one fulfills the aspiration so that not even a single thought of retreat or cowardice arises; thus one accomplishes that which the Mahāsattva cultivates and seeks, according to his wish.
Fulfilling the Vows (this precept text is identical to that in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*):
"If a son or daughter of the Buddha, having made these ten great vows, upholds the prohibitive precepts of the Buddha, they shall make this solemn oath:"

The Great Being upholds the prohibitive precepts of the Buddha. He takes the Ten Vows as his primary guide and subsequently strengthens those vows with the Five Oaths so that he may be free from fear and cowardice, ensuring their ultimate fulfillment.
These are: first, the oath to remain free from the taints of desire; second, the oath regarding the acceptance of offerings;
third, the oath regarding the acceptance of reverence; fourth, the oath to purify the six sense faculties; and fifth, the oath to deliver all sentient beings.

I would rather cast this body into a great pit of blazing, fierce fire or onto a mountain of knives than ever violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods of time by engaging in impure conduct with any woman.
"寧以者" (Ning yi zhe) is a phrase used to express a firm vow, meaning "I would rather do this" or "I vow not to do that. It is an emphatic expression used for comparison.

Since desire is the primary root of wandering through birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and impure conduct is the foremost source of defilement within the ground of the mind, one should first make a great vow, saying: "I would rather cast my body [into the fire]..."
They enter into fierce flames and undergo the suffering of being burned, scorched, and mangled; they fall into great pits and chasms and undergo the suffering of tumbling and drowning;
they ascend mountains of swords and blades and undergo the suffering of their limbs, joints, intestines, and organs being sliced and pierced.
Though beset by a thousand kinds of agonizing poisons and ten thousand sufferings, they never violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas by engaging in sexual acts with women.

This concerns the matter of impurity. Why is this? Just as the aforementioned fierce fires and mountains of blades destroy the physical body in a single moment, engaging in impure conduct ultimately causes one to lose the life of wisdom for ten thousand kalpas.

Therefore, that all sentient beings have been submerged in the ocean of suffering since beginningless time and are unable to escape is entirely due to being bound by female form; they are blind, lacking the eye of wisdom.
Failing to perceive the great pit of birth and death causes many to fall into it. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"If there is a bodhisattva who, although not engaging in union with a woman, converses with her using flirtatious speech and laughter, or hears the sound of bracelets and anklets from outside a wall, or even sees men and women pursuing one another—such a bodhisattva violates and destroys the pure precepts."
This defiles the holy life and renders the precepts impure; one cannot be said to be fully endowed with pure precepts.
If even hearing sounds or seeing forms leads to such impurity, how much more so when a bodhisattva gives rise to impure thoughts—how could they possibly be fully endowed with the precepts?

He further made this vow: "I would rather have my body encircled by a thousand layers of glowing iron mesh than ever accept any clothing from a faithful donor with this body of broken precepts. He further made this vow:
"I would rather swallow glowing iron balls and great, raging torrents of fire with this mouth for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever [use it to break the precepts]."
Guard your mouth. When eating the food of a faithful donor consisting of the hundred flavors, make this vow:
"I would rather let this body lie upon a great torrent, amidst fierce flames, or upon a ground of iron nets and glowing heat, than ever again use this body that has broken the precepts."
When receiving hundreds of kinds of seats from faithful donors, he further made this vow:

"I would rather let this body receive three hundred spears piercing it for one kalpa or two kalpas, than ever accept the medicines of a hundred flavors from faithful donors with this body of broken precepts.
He further made this vow: "I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of molten iron..."
For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they shall never, with this body of broken precepts, receive from faithful donors the thousand kinds of dwellings,
houses, gardens, groves, fields, and lands.
The preceding text speaks of "making such a vow," while the present text speaks of "further making such a wish.

Thus, we know that a vow (*śapatha*) is the resolute and courageous determination within a wish. All clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, dwellings, fields, and gardens have been offered to me by faithful donors for the sake of seeking merit. If my precepts...

In short, one must still cultivate a deep sense of shame and remorse, practicing frugality by bestowing gifts upon the two fields of compassion and reverence, so that merit and goodness may arise in succession.
If the precepts are deficient, even a single grain of rice is difficult to digest; how then could one repay what others seek?
Therefore, this solemn oath is established in advance to serve as a warning and a safeguard for oneself.

He further made this vow: "I would rather have an iron hammer crush this body from head to foot until it is reduced to fine dust than ever accept the respectful prostrations and offerings of a faithful donor with this body of broken precepts."

Regarding prostration: although it does not cost wealth, because the mind of faith is earnest and profound, there are those who, before the Triple Gem, with a heart of reverence, offer even a single gaze or a single prostration;
their transgressions are extinguished immeasurably and merit is generated boundlessly. As the *Yingluo jing* says:
When the Bodhisattva was first born, he took seven steps. Then, raising his left foot, he filled the entire realm of empty space throughout the three thousandfold world system.

He did not disturb sentient beings, and there was no one who perceived him. Yet, those sentient beings who beheld the mark of the wheel upon his feet all conceived the aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
This is due to the retribution of the Tathāgata’s past acts of prostration and reverence; thus it is known that [this merit] is attained.

Since one’s merit is already so great, how could the transgressions incurred be few? Now, with a body that has broken the precepts, even receiving the prostrations and respect of others diminishes one’s own merit no small amount;
how then could one cause them to gain any benefit or goodness? Those who possess a sense of shame and remorse should reflect deeply upon this.

He further made this vow: "I would rather have my two eyes gouged out by a hundred thousand heated iron swords and spears than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, look upon the beautiful forms of others. He further made this vow:
"I would rather have my faculty of hearing pierced by a hundred thousand iron awls for one kalpa or two kalpas than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, listen to pleasant sounds. Furthermore...
He makes this vow: "I would rather have my nose cut off by a hundred thousand sharp blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, greedily sniff the various fragrances.

Again he makes this vow: "I would rather have my tongue severed by a hundred thousand sharp blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, eat the hundred flavors of pure food belonging to others. Again he makes this vow: "I would rather, with a sharp..."
With an axe, he shall sever his body; yet he shall never, with this mind of broken precepts, crave pleasant tactile sensations.

Previously, he vowed that his body and speech were unfit to receive the four requisites and other offerings from others; now, he vows that his six sense faculties must not indulge in defilement by the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
As for the reason why the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is not explicitly mentioned: it is because all five faculties are described as being "the mind of broken precepts," and the mind is—
This is the meaning. Furthermore, since the faculty of mind (*manas*) has no physical form and mental objects (*dharmāḥ*) have no visual image, they cannot be compared to the five physical faculties.
Nevertheless, when the faculty of mind perceives the objects of the five [physical] sense-fields and discriminates between the beautiful and the foul, that very act constitutes the mental object;

therefore, one need not establish a separate category for mental objects. Thus, these six faculties become defiled by the six objects, like flies clinging to saliva or a monkey [clinging to its prey].

Five: Now, by observing the precepts for the sake of the deceased, one’s life of wisdom is forever lost. Therefore, one must make a solemn vow to guard against this, and establish grave prohibitions to restrain it.

Thus, one would rather endure the agonizing pain of hundreds of thousands of blades, spears, and awls than look upon beautiful forms—even down to being greedily attached to pleasant tactile sensations.
Pleasant tactile sensations refer to light garments, fine robes, bedding, and so forth. Now...
With this resolute mind, one cuts off the source of evil; only then can the various roots of goodness arise. Therefore, the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (Yijiao jing) says:
"The calamities of the five faculties bring disaster upon successive generations; their harm is extremely grave, and one must not fail to be cautious.

For this reason, the wise person restrains them and does not follow them, holding them as if they were bandits. Even if one were to let them loose, they would not last long before their [consequences] are seen."
[This refers to] the grinding away [of merit]. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: As the Buddha’s verse says:

"It would be better to roll a red-hot iron ball in one's eyes than to look upon the forms of women with a defiled mind. A person of wisdom should not look at them; if they wish to observe them," [they must do so with a pure mind].
One should regard them as one would a mother or a sister, observing them with clear discernment. They are filled with impurities; yet the fire of lust is not extinguished, and one is consumed by it.
Since this is the case regarding visible forms, the same may be inferred for the remaining objects: sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles.
He further made this vow: "May all sentient beings attain Buddhahood.

Although the previous four vows are said to concern one's own deliverance, they nevertheless encompass others as well. Why is this? The Bodhisattva’s practice is fundamentally for the sake of sentient beings;
if one does not deliver oneself, how can one deliver others? This is not like the solitary benefit of the Two Vehicles. Therefore, now...
This vow—“I pray to become a Buddha”—clearly manifests the original aspiration of the Mahāsattva: the great vow to achieve the Buddha-way for both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
If a Bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense (light impurity).
Those who do not make these vows do not establish the five oaths mentioned above.
If one does not make the ten vows and five oaths, then even if they practice cultivation, they will either fall into the Two Vehicles or merely elicit the meritorious rewards of humans and devas.
○ The thirty-seventh precept: Traveling while disregarding dangers.

Since karma has been bound across many lifetimes, its retribution will be experienced at an uncertain time. When conditions meet, it responds like an echo; if it has not yet matured, one must wait for another occasion.
To travel while disregarding dangers is like a moth throwing itself into a flame; how much more so when human existence is so difficult to obtain?

It is like a blind turtle encountering a floating log with a single hole; yet, should one encounter adverse conditions and momentarily forget the illumination of wisdom, one will immediately give rise to great anguish and distress.
Consequently, one falls into the three miserable realms, presently losing the excellent vessel for receiving the Path and wandering forever through the bitter shoals of kalpas.
Furthermore, who can guarantee that various calamities, both great and small, will not befall you? To bring about one's own premature death is truly pitiable.
If a Buddha’s disciple, one should constantly practice *dhūta* during two seasons and engage in seated meditation during winter and summer.
These two seasons are spring and autumn, when the climate is harmonious and pleasant, and neither cold nor heat intrudes; it is during these times that the Great Being travels to transform others.
It means to be without injury or loss. In Sanskrit, it is called *dhūta*; it is also transliterated as *duo-duo*. In the language of China, it means "to shake off.
This refers to shaking off the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion within the three realms, thereby attaining liberation from the bonds of love that bind one to birth and death.
There are twelve such practices, as set forth in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: first, dwelling in an *araṇya* (here translated as a "place of tranquility," being secluded from... [text continues]).

1. Dwelling five or six *li* outside the village; 2. Constantly begging for food; 3. Wearing rag-robes (i.e., refuse-rags); 4. Eating in a single sitting (eating only one meal per day); 5. Moderating the amount of food consumed; 6.
Not drinking liquids after midday (liquids include fruit juices); 7. Sitting among burial mounds; 8. Dwelling at the foot of trees.
Ninth, dwelling in the open air; tenth, sitting constantly without lying down; eleventh, begging for food in regular order (without discriminating between the poor and the wealthy);
twelfth, possessing only the three robes (not accumulating any extra clothing). These involve having no attachment to food, clothing, or dwelling places;

this is the removal of hindrances and obstacles, through which one swiftly attains liberation. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The precepts established by the Buddha are to be received and upheld by his disciples."

The twelve dhūtas are not themselves called "precepts. If one is able to practice them, they constitute the adornment of precepts; if one is unable to practice them, it does not constitute a violation of the precepts.

This is like the case of giving: if one is able to practice it, one obtains merit; if one is unable to practice it, there is likewise no fault. As for those who practice seated meditation during both winter and summer:
in winter there is cold and snow, and in summer there is scorching heat; furthermore, there are many insects, ants, and termites. If one were to wander about [during these seasons],...
Exposure to cold and heat harms the body and further injures living beings; therefore, it is appropriate to practice seated meditation during the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

During the summer retreat, one should regularly use the following items: a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), cleansing powder (*snānacūrṇa*), the three robes (*tricīvara*), a water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*) and alms bowl (*pātra*), a sitting mat (*niṣīdana*), a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), an incense burner and casket, a water-strainer (*parisrāvaṇa*), a hand towel, a small knife, a fire-starter, tweezers, a rope bed, and the Sūtras, Vinaya, images of the Buddha, and images of Bodhisattvas.

Regarding these physical requisites: when a bodhisattva practices *dhūta* austerities or travels abroad, even if he journeys for hundreds or thousands of *li*, these eighteen kinds of items always accompany his person. As for the practice of *dhūta*, it consists of two periods:

from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month, and from the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month; during these two times, these ten...
There are eight items that constantly accompany the body, like the two wings of a bird.

There are eighteen items that follow the person, like a bird possessing two wings, allowing one to go and come as desired, traveling a hundred or a thousand *li*, with no lack in what is required for use.
While the facts are thus, in principle, each item has its symbolic significance. As for the use of the *yāñcī* (willow branch):
One purifies the karma of speech; with cleansing powder (*śāṭī*), one purifies the karma of body; and with water from the flask, one cleanses the karma of mind.
With a single alms bowl, one is content and thereby abandons wrong livelihood. With the three robes, one eliminates the three poisons. One dons the armor of great vows.
With the sitting mat, one brings peace to the fivefold Dharma-body. With the mendicant’s staff, one raises the banner of the noble ones. And with incense, one manifests the virtue of the precepts.
The fragrant aroma represents the firmness of upholding the precepts. The casket is a perfume box; its base being level and even represents the impartiality of the Bodhisattva’s mind-ground.
The water-strainer is the compassionate practice of saving living beings. The hand-towel is for removing the grime and grease of shamelessness and lack of remorse.
The knife is used for subduing the four māras. The fire-stirring rod represents the light of wisdom, used to shatter ignorance.
Ignorance is darkness; the tweezers symbolize the uprooting of the roots of affliction; the meditation bench represents the seat of the emptiness of dharmas;
the sutras and vinayas elucidate the source of the Mahayana mind-essence; and the Buddha image represents the ultimate fruition of the Tathagata.
The image of the Bodhisattva represents the wondrous causes of a Mahāsattva. To attain the ultimate fruit, one must rely on wondrous causes;
to ascend toward these wondrous causes, one must first clarify the mind-ground (*citta-bhūmi*). Thus, these eighteen kinds of articles are complete in function and sufficient in principle;

they must not be separated from one’s person for even a moment. To be separated from them is to fail in practicing the Great Path of the Bodhisattva. As for those who enter the summer retreat (*varṣā-vāsa*), from—

It is bound on the sixteenth day of the fourth month and released on the fifteenth day of the seventh month; this constitutes the ninety-day period of *kaṭhina* (restricting the feet), the essential time for three months of diligent cultivation.
On the day of the *poṣadha*, a newly initiated bodhisattva shall regularly perform the *poṣadha* every half-month, reciting the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts.
When reciting the precepts, one should do so before images of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
Whether it is a single person performing the *poṣadha*, or two, three, up to a hundred thousand people, only one person shall recite them. As for the one who recites:
The one on the high seat shall remain seated while those listening descend from their seats; each shall don the nine-strip, seven-strip, or five-strip *kāṣāya*.
When observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one should likewise act in accordance with the Dharma in every respect.

Regarding "constant observance of the *poṣadha*": this refers to reciting the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* every half-month, during both the waxing and waning phases, throughout the year, without allowing even a single omission.
Here, we mention only the beginner for the sake of illustration; those who have studied for a long time already know the constant rule of the Buddhas to recite the precepts every half-month.
We fear only that the beginner may not yet be familiar with the *poṣadha* held every half-month.

This is the established formula. It does not mean that those who have studied for a long time are excluded from recitation; therefore, the preceding text states: "This is what Rocana recites; I also recite thus;
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time also recite thus. From this, it is known that it is not only the newly initiated students who recite.
As for the instruction to recite before images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is intended to clarify that the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) are no different from them.
This is the recitation performed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Regarding the *poṣadha* for a single person: this refers to one who dwells alone;

even when there are as many as a hundred or a thousand people, it is likewise a single person who recites so as not to disturb the assembly’s listening, allowing each individual to maintain a single-minded focus.
The reciter sits upon a high seat with a clear and resonant voice, thereby manifesting that the Dharma of the Precepts is worthy of veneration. The listeners sit on lower seats.
This is universally heard; it also clarifies that one should be humble and reverent toward the precepts. *Kāṣāya*—in Sanskrit, this is fully called *kāṣāya*;

in the language of China, it means "dyed color" (*huài sè*), and is also called "red color. It is dyed with blue, black, or madder to produce a dark robe, like the color of ripe mulberry fruit, in order to distinguish it from the five primary colors.
As for its symbolic functions, its names and meanings are not uniform; a detailed [explanation] follows.
As in other places: the five-fold robe is called the *antarvāsa*, here translated as the "lower garment";
the seven-fold robe is called the *uttarāsaṅga*, here translated as the "upper garment"; the nine-fold robe is called the *saṃghāṭī*, here translated as the "double-layered robe.
This consists of nine grades, ranging from nine strips to twenty-five strips; here we briefly cite the first grade, which also represents the half-month [observance].
The recitation of the precepts is the primary gateway for transcending the nine realms of existence and benefiting the ninefold world.

"Each instance must be performed according to the Dharma" means that one should not only recite them every half-month at other times, but even during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), one must likewise recite them every half-month according to the Dharma, without any omission. If one is due to enter the retreat but fails to do so, it constitutes a transgression.
They traveled through cold and heat; this is also called "traveling while braving hardships. Now, the time since the Sage departed is remote;

the periods of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma have already passed, and we have arrived at the age of the Final Dharma. The *poṣadha* has long been abandoned, and the authentic teaching is rarely heard. In the monastic centers throughout various regions...
Though there are nineteen [precepts], they are not practiced. Sometimes, on the days of the new or full moon, one ascends the seat to address the assembly, calling this "poṣadha.
Even going so far as to serve tea and hold nocturnal conversations, they call it "karmavācanā. Alas! The Dharma is about to perish; who will act rightly?

It was solely by relying on powerful great beings who sustained the noble lineage and followed the path of the *vinaya* that the collapsing纲 (network of discipline) was rescued at this time and the net of the Teaching was spread in the final age.
Although far removed from the Sage, they were no different from those who awaken the world;
yet, some abandoned the *poṣadha* to establish their own doctrines, whereupon they were rebuked and expelled by the divine. The Arhat, reflecting upon his own purity, [remained steadfast].

The World-Honored One himself would go to summon them to the assembly. Who are we that we dare to treat this with negligence? Now, I shall briefly cite one or two instances to shame myself and serve as a warning.
Formerly, at Dajue Monastery east of Ye in the Qi dynasty, there was the monk Fǎn, whose preceptual virtue was pure and lofty, and who maintained the prohibitions without flaw.
Once, while staying at another temple, he desired to hear the recitation of the precepts. On the night of the fifteenth day, the assembly—

They deliberated on suspending the recitation and instead establishing a formal exposition (*yùnyì*). They ordered a monk to ascend the seat and declare: "To establish the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) is to deeply accord with the intent of the Sage;
why labor over the *poṣadha*? This is something monks hear constantly. Suddenly, they saw a deity whose form was over ten feet tall.
His courageous bearing was startling and awe-inspiring. He questioned a junior monk who was expounding the doctrine, asking, "What day is it today? The monk replied, "It is the day of the *poṣadha*.

The deity immediately struck him and dragged him down from his seat; he was left prostrate and on the verge of death. He then questioned two or three senior monks, and their answers were all the same as the first.
A deity repeatedly harassed him; even when struck, he was on the verge of death. The deity then shook its arms and departed.
This was witnessed by both monastics and laypeople more than once. From that time forth, Master Fan exhorted himself throughout his life to reverently recite the *Prātimokṣa*.
Furthermore, at Baoming Monastery in Ye, the monk Sengyun led the great assembly. On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, as the multitude gathered intending to recite the precepts, Yun—

Occupying the position of preeminent leader, he addressed the assembly, saying, "The core of the precepts is to prevent wrongdoing; everyone can recite them. Why trouble ourselves by reciting them repeatedly?

We should instead have one monk expound upon their meaning to bring enlightenment to those who come after. Yun’s presence and character were so commanding at that time that no one dared to oppose him.
Consequently, the recitation of the precepts was frequently suspended until the end of the summer retreat. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he gathered the assembly.

He wished to perform the *prātimokṣa* ceremony, but suddenly lost track of Yun’s whereabouts. He searched in all directions for three *li* from the side of the monastery before finding him inside an ancient tomb.
Yun’s entire body was covered in blood as if he had been cut with a blade. When questioned, Yun said:
"A man wielding a three-foot-long great sword shouted at me in a fierce voice, 'How can you alter the *poṣadha* and falsely take on the role of a lecturer? Then he struck me with his sword."
He sliced my body; the agony was unbearable. The assembly received him back to the monastery, where he exhausted his efforts in repentance for ten years.
He made the recitation of the precepts and the *poṣadha* ceremony his constant practice. On the day of his death, a rare fragrance welcomed him.

When practicing the dhūta austerities, one must not enter dangerous places. Whether it be a wicked country, a wicked king, terrain that is uneven, dense vegetation, lions, tigers, wolves, or dangers from water, fire, and wind, as well as bandits, venomous snakes on the road, or any such perilous locations—one must never enter them.
This applies whether one is practicing the dhūta path or even during the summer retreat of the rains.
One must not enter any of these perilous places. Should one intentionally enter them, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).
A wicked realm is one where both the people and the environment are unwholesome; a wicked king does not believe in the Triple Gem and will surely disparage and revile śramaṇas.
As for the terrain, it is uneven with mountains and hills that are stony and barren, and the land is largely low-lying and damp, making it difficult to dwell there.
It is unsettling. In deep, dense forests, venomous beasts and malevolent spirits gather in great numbers; lions, tigers, and wolves are predatory creatures that harm human beings.
There are floods that sweep away all, fires that consume everything, and winds that topple and shatter. Furthermore, there are bandits who plunder and rob.
Regarding "venomous snakes harming people" and "all difficulties," the first eight have been briefly cited; since the remaining obstacles are not limited to these alone, they are termed "all.
Whenever there is an obstacle that threatens one's life or hinders the holy life (*brahmacarya*), one must not enter [the forest].
If one enters intentionally despite knowing this, one commits an offense. Some may say: "If even a Great Being fed his own body to a tiger, how can you abandon it to flee to a distance? This...

Such statements may be said to fail to reach the correct principle. To sacrifice one’s body to feed a tiger in order to save it from starvation, or to offer one’s own person as a substitute for a dove to rescue its life—by thus recklessly exposing oneself to the fire and water of a hostile land, or casting oneself before bandits and venomous snakes—if these acts provide no benefit to those beings, what advantage do they bring to the Dharma-gate?
Moreover, for a bodhisattva at the initial stage of practice, the power of patience is not yet fully prepared.

In vain they lose their physical forms, yet my vision of them has not yet faded; right mindfulness is lost, and they must wait for the emptiness of the aggregates. Their supernormal powers manifest swiftly:
some enter the boiling cauldrons and fiery furnaces to take upon themselves the suffering, while others transform into great bodies of flesh-mountains to relieve the hunger of others.
This is precisely the sublime function of a Great Being extensively practicing the six perfections; how could it be compared to traveling while recklessly courting danger?
Question: If one does not enter [the wilderness] by avoiding the aforementioned dangers, but should happen to encounter them nonetheless, what measures should be taken? Answer:
The *Bodhisattva-śikṣā-śāstra* states: "If, by some cause or condition, one encounters various difficulties, one should apply correct mindfulness as an antidote so that no alarm or fear arises.

Therefore, in the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha told Śāriputra: "If a bodhisattva, even when in the midst of the danger of ferocious beasts, does not give rise to alarm or distress, nor has any fear, why is this? It is because they form this thought: 'I shall benefit [beings]...'"

I shall benefit all sentient beings and relinquish everything. If various predatory beasts wish to devour me, I shall give myself to them, so that I may swiftly bring the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) to fulfillment.

May it be that when I attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, my buddha-field is pure and the names of such malevolent insects and beasts are not even heard. Even amidst the perils of enemies and bandits, may no [fear] arise.
He is neither distressed nor afraid. Why is this? Because this bodhisattva is able to relinquish everything he possesses, he forms this thought:
"If enemies or thieves come seeking what they require, I shall give it to them;
even if they should rob me or sever my life-force, my actions of body, speech, and mind shall remain free from anger and resentment. Thus, he swiftly attains the perfection of ethical discipline.
The *pāramitās*, as well as the attainment of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
I vow that when I shall attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, my buddha-field will be pure, such that even the names of such enemies and thieves shall not be heard.
As stated in the sutras, one will then be free from alarm, affliction, and fear, never lose right mindfulness, and will still be able to accomplish all meritorious virtues.
A Brief Commentary on the Sixth Scroll of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, "The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind," Part Two:
Glossary of Pronunciations. **Pindola Being Struck.** *Pindola* (賓頭盧) means "Immovable" (不動). Formerly, in the Western Regions, there was an elder.
Having heard that the Arhat Piṇḍola had received the Buddha’s command to serve as a field of merit for people of the末 (mò) age, he immediately prepared a great assembly and invited the Saṃgha;
however, they did not appear at three successive meetings. The elder then repented before an elderly senior monk.
The Elder said, "I accepted your invitation for all three assemblies. Yet you yourself sent a slave to block me at the gate.
Seeing that I was old and my robes were tattered, he took me for a *liṭi* ascetic and struck my right temple with a staff until it was broken.
When I came for the second assembly, he struck my middle temple until it was broken, so that I could not enter. When I came for the third assembly, he struck—"
"My left forehead has been split. Having said this, he vanished. [The master] then knew it was Piṇḍola.
Regarding the monk Huìquán of the Song dynasty: he had a disciple who had attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
While waiting for Huìquán’s illness to pass, the disciple remarked, "When you pass away, Ācārya, you shall be reborn into a Brahmin family. Huìquán replied:

"I have accumulated karma through long-term practice of seated meditation; how could I possibly be reborn there? The disciple said, "The Upādhyāya’s faith in the Way is not yet firm, and furthermore, your engagement in external studies has not ceased.
Although you possess meritorious karma, it is insufficient for transcendence. If you were to hold a single superior assembly and provide food for one Sage, you could achieve the fruit of the Path.
You should offer your saṃghāṭī robe as a gift; if anyone requires it, do not withhold it."

Fujian distinguished between the senior and junior monks. When he established a communal assembly and it reached the time for the distribution of robes, a śrāmaṇera approached Fujian to request a robe.
Fujian, thinking the boy was his own disciple, said: "I intend to offer this to the Holy Monk; how could I give it to you?"
Recalling his previous words, he thought that one must not discriminate between people when giving with joy.
On another day, seeing this śrāmaṇera, he asked, "Did you not find the robe I gave you before too large? The śrāmaṇera replied, "I did not receive the robe at all;

there was also a matter of circumstance, and I felt ashamed not to have been present for the assembly. Only then did [the master] fully realize that the previous śrāmaṇera had been a manifestation created by a sage.
Viśākhā is translated here as the lunar mansion *Dī* (the Base). This refers to the period when the moon is in conjunction with the *Dī* mansion during this month;
specifically, it spans from the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the second month.
*Nirvāṇa* is the same as *nibbāna*.
*Kanyu* refers to the earth (*dharā*), which is able to carry all things like a carriage (*yū*); therefore, those who select the ground are called *kanyu*.
The five planets are Mars (Flu-huo-xing), Saturn (Zhen-xing), Jupiter (Sui-xing), Venus (Tai-bai-xing), and Mercury (Chen-xing).
There are many varieties of *li-li*; those not permitted to be kept under the current regulations are the *shu-li-li*. The small ones resemble mice, while the large ones resemble cats;
they are skilled at catching rats.
It is like the monkey glue of the past. Long ago, there was a hunter who smeared birdlime upon the grass at a place frequented by monkeys.
A wise monkey avoided it from afar and departed; however, a foolish monkey lightly touched it with his hand, and immediately his hand became stuck.
Seeking to free himself, he tried to pull it off with both hands, and immediately both hands became stuck. Seeking further release, he used his feet, and they too became stuck.

The two-footed [deer] bites the grass with its mouth, but it immediately becomes stuck; all five parts become stuck together, and as it lies on the ground, the hunter pierces it with a staff and carries it away.
Thus, foolish worldlings do not skillfully guard their bodies; their five faculties are stained by and attached to the five desires.
Once bound by the five fetters, one is carried away according to the will of Māra.
*Zhēng* (筝) is a musical instrument.
*Kōnghóu* (箜篌)—the upper character is pronounced *kōng* and the lower *hóu*—is also a musical instrument.
"Pao" (pronounced pāo) refers to the bladder. Regarding the "nine realms":
the six paths of the desire realm constitute one ground; the four dhyāna heavens of the form realm constitute four grounds;
and the four empty-heaven levels of the formless realm constitute four grounds. Together, these comprise nine grounds, all of which involve birth and death; hence it is so called.
The nine existences:
nine realms consist of one hell, two hungry ghosts, three animals, four asuras, five humans, six devas,
seven śrāvakas, eight pratyekabuddhas, and nine bodhisattvas.
At a time when the Arhat Mahākapphiṇa was dwelling on Mount Ṛṣigiri, he thought to himself:
"Today is the day of the Poṣadha; whether I go or do not go, I am always pure.
The Buddha, knowing his thoughts, immediately flew to where he was and said to him: "If you do not respect the Poṣadha, who indeed shall respect it? You ought to..."

One should go first; one must not travel by means of supernatural powers, but should proceed on foot. Kārttika—this is translated as "the lunar mansion of the Room" (Kṛttikā)—is so named because his parents prayed to this constellation when he was born.
*Huài* (pronounced *sēng*) means finely sliced meat.
Regarding the pigeon: In the past, Śākyamuni Tathāgata was a great king named Śibi. He practiced giving without contradicting the intentions of sentient beings.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, wishing to test him, commanded other devas to transform themselves into pigeons. Śakra...
He transformed himself into a hawk and pursued a pigeon. Terrified, the pigeon threw itself at the king’s feet. The king said, "Do not fear; I shall now save you.
The hawk addressed the king, saying, "The pigeon is my food; I pray that Your Majesty will return him to me. The king replied, "The pigeon has sought refuge with me."

The hawk said, "I desire only this pigeon; I do not seek any other flesh. If Your Majesty is compassionate and benevolent, you may cut flesh from your own body to equal the weight of the pigeon, and I shall joyfully accept it.
The king then immediately cut the flesh from his own thigh and weighed it against the bird, yet the pigeon’s body remained heavier.
He cut away his own flesh until it was exhausted, yet it still did not equal the weight of the pigeon. The King then proceeded to pull up his sinews and bones onto the scale to weigh them.
The Heavenly Emperor immediately restored his original form, praised him with prostrations, and departed. The King’s body returned to its former state, as it had been before.
The Great-Fleshed Śākyamuni Tathāgata was once a Cakravartin King named Ajita.
Having resolved his mind upon Bodhicitta, he left the household life to practice the Way. At that time, encountering a great famine, he wished to offer his own flesh as food for sentient beings.
He immediately established a great vow and climbed to the summit of Mount Shuishan, where he cast himself down by virtue of his original aspiration.
Consequently, it became a mountain of flesh, one *yojana* in height and breadth. People, birds, and beasts came to eat the flesh and blood;
the flesh and blood grew day and night, gradually increasing in height and breadth until they reached one thousand *yojanas*.
It was complete with heads, eyes, limbs, and all bodily parts, such that for ten thousand years, the flesh and blood of his body filled the entirety of Jambudvīpa.
When people are taken away at night, or even when eaten by birds and beasts, they do not give rise to a single thought of regret.
The ten days of observance are the first, the eighth, the fourteenth, the fifteenth, the eighteenth,
the twenty-third, the twenty-fourth, the twenty-eighth, the twenty-ninth, and the thirtieth.
The Tathāgata manifested great supernormal powers from the first day of the twelfth month until the fifteenth day.
"Inexpressible-inexpressible revolutions" refers to the tenth number among the ten great numbers:
one "inexpressible-inexpressible" constitutes one "inexpressible revolution," and an "inexpressible-inexpressible revolution" constitutes... [an inexpressible-inexpressible revolution].
First, it is unspeakably unspeakable. The ten great numbers are as they appear at the beginning of the first fascicle.

Regarding the non-emptiness of the three wheels: if one realizes that the self who gives, the recipient who receives, and the object given—all three are fundamentally empty—then one can immediately destroy the signs of attachment.
The pronunciation of *chī* (黐) is like that of *chí* (癡). Sticky resin (*chījiāo*) is used to trap birds and beasts.
For bathing powder (*zǎodòu*), one may use small beans, large beans, *pídòu*, foreign beans (*húdòu*), peas, and so forth; these may all be ground into powder and used for washing and bathing.
However, one must not mix them with fragrant substances. If one uses *mùhuàn* seeds or *zuòjié* pods for washing, it should be done in a secluded place.
In an insect-infested area, if water is poured onto the ground, the insects will immediately die of suffocation.
The "Four Teachings" refer to the Dharma gates expounded by Śākyamuni Buddha throughout his lifetime.

The Great Master Tiantai Zhizhe, based on the underlying principles, investigated and thoroughly elucidated these four teachings, known as the *Zang*, *Tong*, *Bie*, and *Yuan*. If one diligently cultivates the six perfections and the myriad practices...
Those who practice for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, accumulating merit bit by bit to achieve Buddhahood, are Bodhisattvas according to the *Zangjiao* (Tripitaka Teaching).
Within this *Zangjiao*, there are both the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva gates; however, the present sutra belongs to the Bodhisattva precepts.
Therefore, we single out the Bodhisattva. However, the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka Teaching are partial rather than complete; they are also called "partial Bodhisattvas.

As for those who follow the preceding Shared Teaching (the *Sādhāraṇa-āgama*) and the subsequent Separate and Perfect Teachings (*Pratyekabuddha-yāna* and *Vibhūti-yāna*): some, being dull-witted, perceive only the principle of partial emptiness;

others, being sharp-witted, give rise to a resolve that accords with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Those who penetrate both the upper and lower realms are the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching. If [the text] below...

Distinguishing the Separate (Bie) from the Shared (Tong): The former is distinguished from the Perfect (Yuan). To establish a distinct teaching apart from these two [Shared and Perfect] is not yet complete;

such is the Bodhisattva of the Separate Teaching. If, at the very moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), one is able to attain Buddhahood and save sentient beings, this is the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching.
The stages of the Bodhisattva in the Separate Teaching consist of fifty-two levels, clarifying gradual cultivation. First, the External...
Generally, there are ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), twenty stages of abiding (*vihāra*), thirty stages of practice (*caryā*), and forty stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

These thirty constitute the stage of the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), the rank of the worthy (*bhadra*). The ten grounds (*bhūmi*), equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and wondrous enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*) constitute the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).

As for the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it is perfect hearing and perfect cultivation; a single mind is endowed with all practices, which differs from sequential practice. However, the names of the stages and positions in the Perfect Teaching are...

The distinction lies in this: the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) involves gradual cultivation through successive stages, whereas the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao) possesses all aspects simultaneously within a single mind.

In the Separate Teaching, each stage does not encompass the others, while in the Perfect Teaching, each stage mutually fuses and subsumes the others; this is the point of difference. First, regarding the five grades of external ordinary beings (*waihuan wupin*):
first, sympathetic joy (*suixi*); second, reading and reciting; third, preaching the Dharma; fourth, concurrently practicing the six perfections (*liudu*); and fifth, correct practice.

The six perfections. Within the stage of ordinary beings, there are the ten levels of faith (*śraddhā*). Hearing the Perfect [Teaching] and attaining Perfect Faith, one cultivates Perfect Practice; this is the stage of the five ranks (*pañca-varga*).

Through these skillful means, one advances fivefold toward greater clarity and depth, thereby entering the Perfect Stage of the ten levels of faith, where a semblance of understanding arises and the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) is attained.
Next, the stages of the sages are clarified: the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmana*), and the ten...

The stages of the Earth (bhūmi), Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), and Wondrous Enlightenment (pratyeka-buddha) are all ranks of the sages; this is detailed in the *Yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning).

Regarding the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Precepts": it means that even before one has received the precepts, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is nowhere that is not a field for my own killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is nowhere that is not a place where my killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are practiced.

Regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*): once one has received the precepts, there is no place throughout the worlds of the ten directions that is not a land of my kindness, goodness, purity, and rectitude.
There is no sentient being throughout the ten directions who is not a recipient of my kindness, goodness, purity, and rectitude. Therefore, within a single thought-moment—
One accomplishes untainted, subtle, and excellent forms, each pervading the entire dharma-realm; all thoughts are likewise so.
This is called the "Inexhaustible Treasury Chapter on Precepts. Regarding "all thoughts," this refers to non-killing.
Thus one is moved by compassion and goodness; one does not steal, even regarding the Three Jewels of the Dharma-realm.

One attains the form of not slandering the untainted (anāsrava) sublime marks. Furthermore, among the minor precepts, regarding the teachers and friends of the Dharma-realm, one attains the form of non-arrogance;
and even regarding the Dharma-gates of the Dharma-realm, one attains the form of non-destruction. Although these precepts of non-killing and so forth are without [intrinsic substance],...

Its form and characteristics are visible, yet it is manifested through the medium of matter; therefore, it is called "outflow-free material phenomena" (*anāsrava-rūpa-dharma*). Non-action (*avijñapti*) is the essence of the precepts.
In the Hīnayāna, this is obtained at the time of the fourth *jñapti-caturtha-karman*; in the Mahāyāna, it is obtained through three rounds of *karman*.
However, as for this essence of the precepts, if it does not arise, that is one thing; once it arises, it is identical with the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). This nature...
It is established through cultivation; therefore, there is "unmanifest" (avijñapti), also called "non-instruction" (avijñapti) or "unmanifest form" (avijñaptirūpa).
This refers to dharmas such as non-killing and non-stealing. Although they lack any visible form or appearance, their nature necessarily relies upon material form (rūpadharma) for its manifestation.

What is called "form not belonging to the sense-base of the eye" is "form belonging to the sense-base of mental objects" (dharmāyatana-rūpa). It is also called "untainted form" (anāsrava-rūpa). That is to say:

Killing, stealing, and so forth are *sāsrava* (outflowing) dharmas; non-killing, non-stealing, and so forth are *anāsrava* (non-outflowing) dharmas. Therefore, they are called "non-outflowing form-dharmas" (*anāsravarūpadharma*).
It is said that this essence of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*) arises by relying on a single reception from a teacher and continues until the attainment of Bodhi.
During that interval, one spontaneously ceases evil and spontaneously practices good without waiting for repeated effort; therefore, it is called "unconditioned" (*avijñapti*). Thus it is received.
If one receives it, one attains [the precepts]; if one does not receive them, they do not exist. If one upholds them, they are firm; merit increases spontaneously.
If one violates them, they are lost; one naturally falls into the evil realms. Regarding the attainment through the threefold *karmavācanā*:

when the preceptor stands before the Buddha image, at the time of the first proclamation, the wondrous and virtuous dharma of the precepts throughout the worlds of the ten directions tremble all together by the power of the mental karma.
At the second recitation of the *śuklavidhi*, the wondrous and virtuous precepts of the ten directions cover the crown of the practitioner’s head like clouds and canopies.

At the third recitation of the *śuklavidhi*, the wondrous and virtuous precepts of the ten directions flow from the crown of the practitioner’s head into their body and mind, filling the primary retribution so that they shall forever serve as the seed of Buddhahood until the end of the future. This is for those who receive them through self-vow.
It is also obtained at the time of the three-fold formal announcement (*jñapti*).
From the *Brief Commentary on the Lower Volume of the "Bodhisattva Ground Chapter" of the Brahmajāla Sūtra*,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty, Fascicle Seven.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Baoliang Forest Monastery in Guangzhou.
The Thirty-eighth Precept: Violating the Order of Honor and Humility.

If one has not yet eliminated the pride of self (māna), how can one revere those who are venerable as if they were the Buddha? Failing to rely on the True Teaching, one thus violates propriety and loses the proper order.
This is not the filial piety of a Great Being, nor is it the path of humility for a disciple of the Śākya.

O sons of the Buddha, you should sit according to the proper sequence of the Dharma: those who received the precepts first shall sit in front, and those who received the precepts later shall sit behind.
One does not inquire whether one is old or young, nor whether one is a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a person of high status, a king, a prince, or even...
Eunuchs and slaves should all sit first according to the order in which they received the precepts; those who received them later should sit in successive order.
Do not be like the foolish outsiders, whether old or young, who sit without priority or sequence, following the manner of soldiers and slaves.
Because they revere the Dharma, they discuss the sequence of preceptual virtue without distinguishing between noble and base, nor do they inquire as to whether one is old or young;

they consider only the seniority of their ordination (*śīla-varṣa*) to determine rank. To sit without regard for precedence, like ignorant outsiders who do not revere those of prior virtue, is like the behavior of ignorant soldiers or slaves who know nothing of ritual propriety (*li-fa*).
Thus, they lose the proper order of seating; yet even in the imperial court, ranks are still discussed according to noble title.

Regarding the distinctions of high and low, how could Buddhism lack a sequence of seniority based on merit? Moreover, the moment one receives the *vinaya* (prātimokṣa) is precisely the day the life-force of the body of precepts (*śīla-kāya*) and wisdom begins to grow.
How, then, can one fail to rely upon the number of years since ordination (*śīla-lakṣa*) when discussing seniority, rather than chronological age?

Question: While it is appropriate to prioritize the number of years since ordination, as for the relations between ruler and subject, father and son, or monk and nun, male and female—how can such distinctions be ignored?
"Will there not be confusion? He replied: "Now, monks and nuns shall distinguish their own precedence; men and women shall each maintain their respective order.

If Your Majesty values the Dharma, your ministers shall take precedence out of respect for the precepts. If Your Majesty adheres to worldly etiquette, your ministers shall yield their seats and remain behind.
Thus, we may avoid creating obstacles for the Buddha-dharma. If this is truly done out of reverence for the Way while setting aside personal status," [the confusion will be avoided].
When one forgets the self, the Brahma King prostrates before a celestial maiden; if we discuss the Dharma, there is neither noble nor base, such that Śakra receives the feet of a jackal.
How, then, could distinctions of old and young, or noble and base, be maintained?
Within my Buddha-dharma, those who come first sit first, and those who come later sit later.
If a bodhisattva does not sit according to this sequential order of the Dharma, they commit a minor offense.
One should not disregard the order of seniority by yielding one's seat to another; both the one who yields and the one who sits down thus commit an offense.
Formerly, King Ajātaśatru invited Mañjuśrī, but Mañjuśrī yielded precedence to Mahākāśyapa, saying that he had long been a śramaṇa and was the foremost among the assembly of arhats.
Kāśyapa, in turn, yielded to Mañjuśrī, extolling his divine wisdom, holy realization, and eloquence. Thus...
"He may be considered venerable. Mañjuśrī then proceeded forward. Because King Aśoka had attained rootless faith through Mañjuśrī, he specifically invited him;
his intention was directed toward Mañjuśrī and not toward Kāśyapa. Yet, Mañjuśrī first yielded the honor to Kāśyapa.
I dare not violate the constant regulations of the ancient Buddhas; Kāśyapa ultimately yielded to Mañjuśrī, thereby following the original intention of the host.
This is analogous to the deity of the Southern Mountains, who invited the Dharma Master of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and placed his seat above those of the five hundred arhats.
According to this principle, one may take a seat by perceiving the specific occasion (*jī*). To act contrary to the norm in such a way is to accord with the Way and respond to changing circumstances.

"Acting according to what is appropriate" is precisely the sublime and skillful application of the Great Being (Mahāsattva). Thus, we know that whether one prioritizes precepts or seated meditation is a matter of honoring the seniority of one's ordination (*śīla-varṣa*).

Possessing divine wisdom and sagely attainment, he accords with the intentions of those who make requests; he honors the Dharma and esteems people, observing the specific circumstances to act as is fitting.

He does so only for fear that in the末代 (final age), the ignorant might—clinging to their own high talent—look down upon those of venerable virtue, or rely on their own seniority in years to treat others with contempt.
Suddenly, Zhida became arrogant in his heart; he falsely claimed to have perceived the [Buddha’s] intent. Who else should bear the transgression of diminishing merit and losing virtue?
Please reflect upon this yourself.
○ Thirty-ninth: Not Cultivating Merit and Wisdom.

To cultivate both merit and wisdom is the fundamental practice for a Great Being to benefit sentient beings. When the two adornments are fully perfected, this is the ultimate fruit of a Bodhisattva’s attainment of Buddhahood.
To lack one and fail to cultivate it is like a bird with but a single wing; how could such a being soar through the sky?
How vast and sublime!
O sons of the Buddha, you should constantly teach and transform all sentient beings, establishing monastic dwellings, mountain forests, gardens, and fields, and constructing Buddhist stupas.
You should establish places for winter and summer retreats, sites for seated meditation, and all locations for the practice of the Way. You ought to establish them all.

This clarifies the cultivation of merit through the teaching and transformation of sentient beings, briefly enumerating seven matters: first, monasteries (*saṃghārāma*) for the assembly to gather and practice in peace;

second, mountain forests to provide shade for the assembly’s walking and sitting meditation; third, gardens to supply the assembly with fruits and vegetables; fourth, fields to provide sustenance for the monks;
fifth, the erection of stupas (*stūpa*) so that the assembly may rely upon them for veneration, serving as a source of supreme merit for humans and devas; sixth...
A place for sitting in meditation, established to prepare for cultivation during the two periods [of day and night]. Seventh, places for all paths of practice (*sarva-caryā-patha*):
because the locations for practicing the path-deeds are not limited to one, they are called "all.

Regarding these seven matters above, one should establish them all—whether by teaching others to do so oneself, or by exhorting others to have them built—so that all may generate the merit of humans and devas, as well as the supramundane [attainments].
Excellent. In establishing such dwellings, one must remain far removed from shrines, village altars, brothels, taverns, and the homes of butchers and executioners;
only then will there be no faults of disturbance or reproach, and the assembly will be able to cultivate their spiritual practices in tranquility.
If even for a bhikṣu building a house, it is prescribed that he avoid places of difficulty and obstruction, how much more so for a bodhisattva who seeks both self-benefit and the benefit of others?
As for "difficult locations," these are places where one is troubled by various wild beasts, down to even ants.

As for "obstructed locations," these are areas within a fathom of the four sides of a building that contain public wells or roads, or are near precipices or deep pits, or are adjacent to stūpas, government land, the grounds of non-Buddhists, or the grounds of bhikṣuṇīs. Since there are none of these difficulties or obstructions, [it is a suitable place].
Even when staying in such places, one must first preach the Dharma for them, encouraging them to spontaneously give with joy.
One must not forcibly demand or seek much, thereby causing them to lose faith and their sense of devotion, so that they hear of giving as if avoiding a debt and see monks as if encountering an enemy.
This was like the case in the past in the city of Kāśīvana in India, where the bhikṣus built dwellings for them, yet their begging was excessive.
[It was] chaotic. At that time, when the lay devotees saw the bhikṣus from afar, they each closed their doors and fled.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha. After the Buddha had rebuked the bhikṣus, he then related for them an account from the past:

on the banks of the Ganges, there was a brahmin practicing the path who was constantly encircled by a nāga as it emerged from the water; he became sorrowful and fell ill. The Buddha instructed him to beg [for protection] from the nāga.
The precious jewel beneath his neck; from that time on, the dragon no longer came to coil around him.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus in the forest who were troubled by the nocturnal cries of birds, which disturbed their meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The Buddha instructed the bhikṣus to beg for both wings from the birds.
The birds immediately left the forest and never returned. The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "You should know that even down to birds and beasts, they still [possess such qualities]."
They take no pleasure in begging; how much less could they bear being solicited by others? Yet now there are those who use public office to further private ends, feigning causes to solicit alms.
They deceive themselves regarding cause and effect, making it difficult to repay their debts for a thousand kalpas.

They squander offerings of faith, ensuring that for ten thousand generations they shall not regain a human body. Thus they harm themselves and harm others, falsely assuming names to carry out "teachings."
To perform meritorious acts [for one's own sake] is truly a great thief within the Dharma-gate.
A Bodhisattva, however, should expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya for the sake of all sentient beings, whether in times of illness or national calamity.

In times of peril from bandits; on the days of the passing away of one’s parents, brothers, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), or teachers (*ācārya*)—whether on the third week, the fourth or fifth week, or even up to the seventh week—one should likewise lecture upon the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya.

During all assemblies for fasting and the making of vows, whether traveling, engaging in livelihood, being consumed by great fires, being swept away by great floods, or when a ship is driven by black winds.
Regarding the perils of rākṣasas in rivers, streams, and the great ocean, one should likewise read, recite, and expound this sutra and its vinaya.

This extends even to all karmic retributions for offenses, the three evil realms, the eight difficult conditions, the seven heinous crimes, being bound by cangues, shackles, and pillories upon the body, as well as excessive lust and excessive anger.

There are many who are ignorant and many who are afflicted by illness; all such persons should be taught this sutra and its vinaya. If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not do so, they commit a minor offense of defilement.
"One who should expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya for the sake of all sentient beings" is a general summary of the great outline of the cultivation of wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*).
The subsequent text specifically clarifies the objective conditions for the cultivation of wisdom. Regarding "those afflicted by illness":

it is because these sūtras and vinaya can cure the afflictions, evil karma, and karmic retributions of sentient beings. Regarding "national calamities": it is because these sūtras and vinaya can provide protection.
It is the King who Protects the Heart, for it extinguishes all enemies and various calamities. Regarding "the perils of thieves":
by means of this sutra and its vinaya, one can destroy the six thieves as well as all plunderers. Regarding "the death and extinction of parents and others":

because this sutra and its vinaya benefit both the living and the deceased, they can sustain the consciousness in the intermediate state (antarābhava), enabling rebirth in a Pure Land or among humans and devas.

Because they enjoy the retribution of bliss and ultimately proceed toward Bodhi; because those who seek through fast-day assemblies (poṣadha) possess the fundamental practices and vows contained within this sutra and vinaya, and are thus able to fulfill all that sentient beings seek;

and because those who travel for livelihood possess the various treasures of the Dharma contained within this sutra and vinaya, and are thus able to accomplish the precious benefits and interests of sentient beings.
Regarding "the great fire": because this sutra and vinaya can extinguish the fires of affliction and anger in sentient beings, how much more so the flames of grass and trees?

Regarding "the great water": because this sutra and vinaya can dry up the great river of craving, desire, birth, and death for sentient beings, how much more so the calamity of being swept away and drowned? Regarding "blown by black winds": because this sutra and vinaya can...
It acts as a great vessel of compassion upon the ocean of suffering, ferrying all sentient beings directly to the other shore;
how much more so would it enable one to transcend the perils of the world’s rākṣasa-demon lands? Regarding "all retributions for sin": such retributions are not of a single kind;
therefore, several types are briefly enumerated below. As for the "three evil realms, eight difficulties, and seven heinous offenses," this refers to this sutra.
The Vinaya is the source for severing evil and giving rise to goodness; thus, it enables sentient beings to emerge from the three evil realms and be reborn in the three good realms.
Furthermore, these sutras and the Vinaya are preeminent in transforming calamity into fortune; thus, one can transcend the eight difficulties and obtain all manner of superior retributions.
Moreover, these sutras and the Vinaya are the foundation of filial piety; thus, they can eliminate the seven heinous offenses.

This is the retribution for transgressions. As for the shackles, fetters, and stocks: because this sutra and its vinaya possess the wondrous function of liberation, they are able to eliminate the suffering of internal and external entanglements for sentient beings. As for those with much lust, anger, and delusion:
because this sutra and its vinaya give rise to the pure mind, the mind of compassion, and the mind of wisdom, they are able to extinguish the three [poisons] of all sentient beings.
As for the harm of poison: "many illnesses" refers to the suffering of a single ailment mentioned previously;
here, "many" means that, in brief, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) deviate from their natural state, resulting in various pains and afflictions;
