in detail, it refers to the four hundred and four diseases, where eighty-four thousand defilements (*kleśa*) press in upon one another. Yet this sutra and its vinaya are fundamentally endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
The four virtues give rise to eighty-four thousand gates of wholesome dharmas; therefore, they are able to heal the myriad sufferings and ten thousand ailments of all sentient beings.
If it is not otherwise—that is, if one does not extensively cultivate merit and wisdom as described above for each individual case—it constitutes an offense.
However, there is no offense if one lacks the capacity to do so.
These nine precepts should be studied and respectfully upheld. They shall be explained in detail in the Chapter on the Brahma-Altar (Brahmāyusūtra).
From the precept against redeeming [a slave] up to these nine precepts concerning the non-cultivation of merit and wisdom, one should diligently train in them.
One should reverently uphold this. If one wishes to know it in detail, it should be as clarified in the "Chapter on the Brahma Altar" (*Brahmamaṇḍala*) of the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra].
○ Forty: The Precept for Discerning the Reception of Precepts.
The Great Being takes universal salvation as his mission and cherishes compassion in his heart. He does not refuse those who seek help, and there is nowhere he does not provide relief;
thus, he makes no distinctions whatsoever.
If, O Sons of the Buddha, when conferring the precepts upon others, you must not discriminate among any kings, princes, ministers, officials, bhikṣus,
bhikṣuṇīs, laymen, laywomen, lustful men, lustful women, the eighteen Brahmā heavens, the sons of the six heavens of desire,
those without sexual organs, those with dual sexual organs, eunuchs, slaves, or any ghosts and spirits— all of them are fully entitled to receive the precepts.
Because the source is fundamentally equal, one does not fall into the numerical categories of humans and devas, noble and base, or hidden and manifest.
Since the ground of the mind is replete with all dharmas, it universally encompasses the virtuous minds of those high and low, monastic and lay, pure and impure.
Furthermore, since the Great Beings regard all sentient beings as their only child, how could there be any selection or discrimination?
One should instruct that all the saffron-colored robes worn on the body be dyed with colors that have been altered to accord with the Way;
they should all be dyed blue, yellow, red, black, or purple. All dyed garments, even down to bedding and mats, must be entirely of altered colors; such are the robes to be worn on the body.
All dyed colors: whatever garments are worn by the people of any kingdom within all lands, a bhikṣu must ensure that his secular clothing differs from theirs.
That which is esteemed by the worldly consists of the five primary colors. Those who have left the household life do not conform to secular customs;
therefore, it is said that they must all wear "dyed" colors (*kāsāya*) to remain in accord with the Way. As for blue, it is not a deep blue nor a pure blue, but rather a clay-blue.
As for yellow, it is not a deep saffron nor a pale yellow, but rather a dye of yellow mixed with red, which is the color of maulana. As for black, it is not...
It is entirely blackish-brown (*kṛṣṇa-śyāma*), like the robes of non-Buddhists, yet it is further dyed with purple, like a ripe mulberry; thus it is called a "black robe" (*kāṣāya*).
Therefore, among these five types of colors, they all employ "discolored" (*kaṣāya*) hues to distinguish them from the five kinds of brilliant worldly colors—blue, yellow, red, black, and purple.
According to the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, these five colors represent the five schools (*pañca-nikāya*).
It is possible. It is not that [the dye] truly causes attachment; if it did cause attachment, it would be identical to the five colors of the world—how then could it be called "dyed color" (壞色)?
To differ from the clothing of the laity is precisely what avoids the reproach that, in the Dharma-ending age, the *kāṣāya* will turn into the five colors.
Regarding the clothing worn by people in all lands, this refers to the various garments produced in different countries, each of which is distinct.
Nevertheless, there are two types: first, differences in shape; second, differences in color.

That which is manufactured here [in this land] is the sleeved robe (*kāsāya*), for which the five primary colors are esteemed. That which is manufactured in India is similar to the robes of the Brahmā realm;
while the colors are likewise the five primary ones, white is most highly esteemed. The robes worn by those who have left the household life are all cut into pieces and dyed.

Because [the robes] are dyed with a discolored hue, it is said that bhikṣus must differ from those who wear secular clothing. It has never been stated that this applies to those receiving the precepts while remaining laypeople.
Nowadays, there are teachers who are unacquainted with the purport of the sūtras and vinaya, and who fail to distinguish between the regulations for monastics and the laity;
they bestow the five precepts upon lay men and women and command them to wear the five-strip *kaṣāya* robe of a bhikṣu. They bestow [the precepts] upon the laity...

Regarding the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva precepts, if one causes [the practitioner] to wear a twenty-five-fold *saṃghāṭī*, it will lead to confusion between the monastic and the laity, which greatly violates the sacred regulations and incurs even more severe transgressions.
This has already been fully analyzed in the "Section on Resolving Doubts Concerning the Three Robes" by the Song dynasty master Ciyun.

You may investigate this for yourself. The *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* permits the keeping of the three robes (*tricīvara*), intending that they be used for making offerings, recognizing them as the "field of merit" garment (*puṇyakṣetra-cīvara*), wearing them free from defilement, and maintaining mindfulness of liberation in order to seek transcendence.

It does not mean that one must wear them [at all times]. When the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing traveled personally to the Western Regions, he observed śrāmaṇeras there, yet he had never before seen anyone [wearing them in that manner].
The bhikṣus wear the five-strip robe and the seven-strip robe; as for what they wear, it is only the *pātra* (alms bowl).
Because they have not yet entered the ranks of the Saṅgha Jewel, they are not yet fit to wear the robes of the Field of Merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); to wear them would incur transgression.
Yet, how could these laypersons be fit to serve as a Field of Merit for humans and devas? Nevertheless, a lay bodhisattva should follow the regulations established by their own country.
It may only be dyed to change its color, or worn according to what is appropriate; however, it must not be for the sake of mere ornamentation.

If it is not dyed, there is no offense. Just as the robes of kings and ministers each have their own regulations, and those of men and women likewise differ, how can one fail to distinguish between black and white and instead offer a haphazard generalization?
As for the statement that "even bedding should all be dyed with a changed color," this refers to—
Aside from his three robes, all other garments possessed by Kāśyapa, down to his bedding, were entirely dyed in a discolored hue.
"Bedding" refers here to such items as curtains, woolen blankets, and mattresses.
When one wishes to receive the precepts, the master should ask: "In this present life, have you not committed any of the seven heinous crimes?
A Bodhisattva Dharma Master must not confer the precepts upon one who has committed the seven heinous crimes in this life. The seven heinous crimes are:

shedding the blood of a Buddha, killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing one's *upādhyāya* (preceptor), killing one's *ācārya* (teacher), disrupting the *saṃgha* that performs the *karmavācanā* or turns the wheel of the Dharma, and killing a noble being (*ārya*).
If one has committed the seven heinous offenses, one will not obtain the precepts in this present life; all other persons, however, may fully receive the precepts.
The Tathāgata’s practice is perfected and his fruit is complete; his past obstructions have long since been stilled, such that neither humans, devas, nor Māras can find any opportunity to harm him.
Regarding what is now called "shedding the blood of the Buddha's body," it was as when Devadatta pushed a rock to crush the Buddha;

because a fragment of the stone flew off and wounded the Buddha’s toe, this is what constitutes shedding the blood of the Buddha's body. Although there is currently no Buddha, one must still inquire according to the Dharma.
One's parents possess the great kindness of giving birth and raising one; preceptors and teachers possess the kindness of generating the body of precepts.
The profound virtue of the precious life of wisdom. Regarding "one who breaks the *karmavācanā* of the Saṃgha":
*Karmavācanā* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "performing rituals to accomplish affairs. The *Saṃgha* is one of the Three Jewels.

"Breaking" refers to when, within a single great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), even with as few as eight bhikṣus at the minimum, they divide into two factions, each faction of four persons performing the *poṣadha-karmavācanā* separately.
Regarding monastic affairs, this is called "schism. It is the same for the community of bhikṣuṇīs when they perform formal legal acts (karmavācanā) separately.
As for "schism in the Saṃgha that turns the Wheel of Dharma," the "Wheel" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path. It requires at least nine bhikṣus, with one person claiming for himself to be a Buddha.
The other four parties join them, perverting the explanation of the Sūtras and Vinaya to cause people to abandon right view and enter into false views.

They destroy everything, whether within or outside the boundaries [of the Sangha], yet they alone cannot destroy the Bhikṣuṇīs; this is because they possess bodies subject to the five outflows (*āsrava*), and no one would believe that such persons could become Buddhas.
Both of these are termed "schismatics of the harmonious Saṃgha. As for the noble ones (*ārya*), they possess great...
The Hīnayāna refers to the Arhat. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies three types of killing: killing those who have attained the three fruits [of the śrāvaka path].

This applies only to killing within the middle [stages] and not to killing those in the higher stages; therefore, it does not constitute a heinous offense (*ānantarya*). The Mahāyāna refers to the Bodhisattva. There are three [interpretations]:

some take those from the stage of "practice through understanding" (*adhimukticaryā*) upward; some take those from the seventh thought-moment (*cittotpāda*) upward; and others simply take those who do not become followers of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). That is to say—

These are the irreversible bodhisattvas. To kill any of these constitutes a transgression against the fundamental principles (*ānantarya*). Regarding "transgressions against the fundamental principles": this refers to the *pārājika* offenses;

furthermore, when one increases the severity of such acts by harming those above, it is termed a "great transgression" (*mahānantarya*). This is a crime of unrighteousness. If one commits any one of these seven transgressions, one shall not obtain the precepts.
Nevertheless, although the original source—the mind-ground—is equal and devoid of distinctions between ordinary beings and sages, [the violation of these precepts remains].

Regarding the distinction between good and evil, such individuals turn their backs on their own fundamental source; they sink into the ocean of birth and death, ruin their mental ground, and wither the sprouts of bodhi.
Failing to give rise to the essence of the precepts, the goodness of the precepts does not arise; therefore, it is said that they do not obtain the precepts.
According to the dharma of those who have left the household life, one does not prostrate before kings, nor does one prostrate before parents;
one does not show reverence to the six types of relatives, nor offer salutations to ghosts and spirits. One only understands the words of the Dharma Master.

If there are those who come from as far as a hundred or a thousand *li* to seek the Dharma, yet the Bodhisattva Dharma Master, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, does not immediately bestow the precepts upon all these sentient beings, he commits an offense.
This is a light offense of defilement (*āpatti*).

For instance, if subjects, sons, servants, or slaves should leave the household life, yet remain ignorant of the Dharma of renunciation and continue to perform the worldly etiquette of subjects, sons, servants, or slaves, they will bring disorder to the Great Way that transcends the world. This is so even if they already know the true Dharma that transcends the world.

Then one should not observe worldly etiquette. If one respects and reveres the great precepts of the mind-ground, then regardless of distinctions of noble or humble, or close or distant, as soon as one understands the Dharma Master’s words, one should immediately bestow the Bodhisattva’s true precepts upon them.
If someone has traveled from as far as a thousand li to seek the Dharma, their sincere heart and earnest intent can be known; thus, [one should grant them the precepts].
One should cause them to perform repentance in accordance with the Dharma before bestowing [the precepts] upon them.

If one does not immediately grant them the precepts, or if one refuses them out of malice or anger, or if one sells the precepts for the sake of gain and offerings, this constitutes a deliberate transgression.

Furthermore, if their faculties are not yet capable, or if they lack the aspiration to seek enlightenment above and transform beings below, seeking only fame and profit while exalting themselves, [one should likewise withhold the precepts].
Perhaps their minds were not yet sincere or their resolve not yet firm, such that they did not conceive the thought that [the Dharma] is difficult to encounter.
Thus, as when Dharmakṣema exhorted Daojin, he did not immediately confer the transmission; this was truly the Great Being’s skillful means, observing their capacities to guide and transform them.
Both parties generate much merit; how could this be compared to those who look upon others with malice or anger? As for not prostrating before rulers or parents:

it means that having left the household life, one no longer maintains the etiquette of a family member; having departed from the secular world, one does not participate in the formalities of worldly society.
Having left the household to become a child of the Buddha and a guest beyond the mundane dust, although one has not yet attained the Way, one is already a member of the Triple Gem.
The celestial Māras were struck with awe, and Śakra took refuge [in the Sangha]. Had he instead shown reverence [to worldly powers], the Jewel of the Sangha would have lost its dignity.

Once the Three Jewels are deficient, humans and devas will have no refuge. Those who have left the household life should simply apply themselves diligently to the Path to repay their sovereign and parents;

by representing their sovereign and parents in paying homage to the Three Jewels, they may pray for their well-being and peace. This is what it means for one who has left the household life to fulfill loyalty and filial piety to the utmost.
Filial piety and reverence for the ruler and love for one’s parents are the great rites of humanity;
how could they be equated with worldly conventions that define loyalty and filiality by such minor gestures as joining the palms or kneeling? The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"Kings and sovereigns certainly do not seek to receive prostrations or services from bhikṣus, for they fear it would impair their virtue and shorten their lifespan. This was as in the case of King Udayana in the past.
King Yan [Yuan] accepted the slander of a sycophantic minister, who said, "Whenever King Bin-tou-lu (Piṇḍola) comes to pay his respects, he does not rise to welcome him.
He has thus conceived an evil thought: 'If he does not rise when I go to him now, I shall take his life.
At that time, Piṇḍola knew of the king’s evil intent as he approached, and he reflected to himself: "If I rise to welcome him, he will lose his throne; if I do not rise to welcome him..."
"He would have taken my life and I would have immediately fallen into hell. It would have been better for me to lose my throne than to fall into hell.
He then rose and went out to welcome him from afar. Seven days later, he lost his royal position and was captured by King Weishichan, who shackled his feet for seven years.
Nanshan says: "Since the teaching first spread to the East, it has frequently encountered ups and downs; it has been suppressed three times and [re-established] five times."
I encountered [him] and prostrated myself. This was not an era of peace and brilliance, but rather the reign of a tyrannical ruler;

thus, he issued edicts that were not statecraft worthy of governing the nation, deviating from the norm and inviting the censure of virtuous historians. Since the principles of the matter could not be reversed, I returned to the familiar path of antiquity.
Therefore, in the sixth year of Emperor Cheng of the early Eastern Jin, when Yu Bing assisted in governance, the Emperor was still a minor. For...

The Emperor issued an edict ordering the monks to perform prostrations. At that time, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat He Chong, Xie Guang, and others proposed that such prostrations were inappropriate;
after three rounds of debate, the matter was ultimately shelved. Furthermore, during the early years of Emperor An’s reign, Grand Marshal Huan Xuan submitted a memorial ordering them to prostrate.
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat Huan Qian, Wang Mi of the Central Secretariat, and others offered a firm remonstrance, stating: "As for the śramaṇas today..."

Although his inner intention was profound in its reverence, he did not consider physical prostration to be the essence of ritual propriety. While his physical traces filled the entire land, his spiritual orientation transcended the mundane world.
Consequently, there was no sovereign of foreign lands who did not humble himself before him in deference. This was truly because the Way is revered when it resides within a person;
it is not weighed by human status. Daoyuan also sent a letter to Master Huiyuan, in which Huiyuan composed the treatise "The Śramaṇa Does Not Pay Homage to Kings."
The debate over the five treatises ceased for a time. When Emperor An resumed his governance, he returned to venerating and upholding the faith.

In the seventh year of Emperor Taowu of the Wei dynasty, the Daoist Kou Qian and the Minister of Education Cui Hao slandered the Buddha-dharma. The Emperor agreed with them and consequently suppressed the Buddhist teachings; monks were executed by beheading.
Later, the monk Yan Tanshi arrived, and the Emperor prostrated himself before him to repent for his transgressions. The Emperor was then stricken with a pestilential disease as a result.

He subsequently executed the Cui clan and restored the Buddhist Dharma. Since Fu Jian lost control of the Central Plains, although the realm was divided into sixteen states, each remained undiminished in its faith in the Dharma.
Only Helian Bobo, who occupied Xiazhou, was unrestrained in his cruelty and took pleasure in killing;
he even had an image of the Buddha fastened to his back and forced monks to prostrate before it. Later, he died after being struck by a thunderbolt from heaven.

At the time of the burial, [the tomb] was again shaken and the [relics] were brought forth. His son, Chang, succeeded to the throne; he destroyed Chang’an and extinguished the Buddha-dharma, slaughtering every monk he encountered.
The śramaṇa Tanshi was struck with a blade but remained unhurt; because of this, [Chang] changed his mind. Subsequently, the Northern Wei dynasty was overthrown by the Zhou.
Emperor Wu of the Zhou initially believed in the Buddha-dharma, but later he took up the Daoist Zhang Bin as well as Wei Yuan.
Sengzhi slandered [the Buddha] and sought to eliminate Buddhism. Dharma Master Dao’an composed the *Treatise on the Two Teachings* (*Erjiao lun*) to resist him;

consequently, both the Daoist and Buddhist teachings were abolished together. Not even five years later, he passed away and fell into the Great Hell. Emperor Taowu of the Tang dynasty [persecuted Buddhism] in the same manner.

The Buddhist Way was purged, and the mandate to prostrate before sovereigns and parents was established. An edict was issued by Wei Xiu, Daoxuan, and others, submitting a memorial as well as letters to the ministers;
however, the national deliberation was not carried out. In the fifth year of the Huichang era of Emperor Wuzong, the Daoists Liu Xuanjing and Zhao Guizhen [were appointed].
They slandered the Śākyas and purged the Buddhist temples. In the sixth year, the Emperor passed away, and Emperor Xuan ascended the throne.

He restored the Buddhist temples and executed Liu Xuansheng for the crime of destroying the monasteries. These matters are recorded in full in the *Guang hongming ji* and in the *Fengfa yao* (Essentials of Propagating the Dharma).
I have now briefly excerpted them here to inform both the clergy and the laity. I fear that those who leave the household life during the Final Dharma Age...
Out of greed for fame and profit, they disparage themselves; they willingly descend to the lowly while disregarding shame.
They kneel in the courts of princes and lords and offer obeisance at the residences of high officials. This deeply disgraces the Dharma-gate and greatly harms the True Teaching.
Regarding those whom ghosts and spirits do not honor, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "The various hosts of celestial deities [do not pay homage] toward upāsakas..."

I venture to request your reverence. Formerly, Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North, invited the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Śāriputra, and five hundred noble monks to his own palace. After providing them with offerings, he addressed the Venerables, saying:
"From this day forward, all those who have left the household life or remain at home and have received the Buddha’s precepts, when they come to my temple, shall all grant me alms."

Verse: We, along with our retinues, shall with single-minded devotion protect and uphold the True Dharma, ensuring that the Buddhist disciples—both ordained and lay—are forever free from harm at all times.
If one delights in prostrating to celestial deities, then there is no distinction between them and the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Even the Heavenly Kings do not pay such homage; how much less so other ghosts and spirits? Therefore, one should instead pay obeisance to the Honored One, the Buddha. And...
Regarding the perversion of images, the Vaipulya Sūtra states: "One must not perform sacrifices to ghosts and spirits, nor should one treat ghosts and spirits with contempt.
The Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra states: "If an upāsaka performs sacrifices to ghosts and spirits for the sake of his household, home, body, or life, he does not lose his precepts.
However, if he prostrates with a sincere heart to non-Buddhist ghosts and spirits, he loses his precepts. If...
At the time of performing sacrifices, one must not kill living beings.
○ The forty-first precept: Teaching for the sake of profit.

To lack genuine understanding oneself yet seek fame and reputation leads to both self-delusion and the delusion of others in no small measure. Even if one possesses genuine understanding, [if one teaches for profit...]
To offer such things as these for worship is neither a light matter when it involves one’s own ruin or that of others;

it truly is not the proper ritual for converting and guiding others, and it profoundly contradicts the giving of wealth and Dharma. Thus, the *Ākāśagarbha Sūtra* says: "Fame and material gain are the root of all transgressions. This is precisely what is meant.

If, O Sons of the Buddha, when teaching others to give rise to faith, a Bodhisattva acts as an instructing Dharma Master for another person, and sees one who wishes to receive the precepts, they should instruct that person to request two masters: an Upādhyāya and an Ācārya. These two masters should ask:
"Do you have the seven obstructive offenses (*saptāvaraṇa*)? If, in their present body, there are the seven obstructive offenses, the masters shall not confer the precepts upon them.

Regarding the precepts: if one is free from the seven obstructions, one may receive the precepts. If there are those who have committed the ten grave offenses, they should be instructed to repent before images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Six times throughout the day and night, they should recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts and prostrate with utmost sincerity to the thousand Buddhas of the three periods.
When they behold a favorable sign—whether after one week, two or three weeks, or even longer—[they shall be restored].
One year. One must see auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*). As for auspicious signs: the Buddha comes and strokes one’s head; one sees light; one sees flowers; or various other extraordinary signs.

Then one attains the extinction of transgressions. If there are no auspicious signs, although one performs repentance, it is of no benefit. Such a person will not attain the precepts in their present body, though they may obtain increased merit through receiving them.
If one has violated the forty-eight minor precepts, one should perform face-to-face repentance (*pratideśanā*) for the transgression.
It is then extinguished. This is not the same as the seven obstructions (*saptāvaraṇa*). Within this Dharma, the teaching master must understand each point thoroughly.

When a Great Being (*mahāsattva*) teaches others to arouse their own minds and lead them to believe that they themselves shall become Buddhas, and when those individuals wish to receive the Great Precepts of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi-mahāśīla*), the teacher should instruct them to request two masters. The two masters should then ask: "Do you have any of the seven obstructing offenses?"

No. The seven obstructions are precisely the seven heinous offenses (*ānantarya*). This means that these transgressions can obstruct the Noble Path and act in opposition to the fundamental source, the mind-ground;
therefore, one cannot receive the precepts. For those who have never previously received the precepts, there is no offense of killing the two teachers.
If one has already received the Bodhisattva precepts of the Mind-Ground and commits the seven heinous offenses, there is no way for them to be purified through repentance.

Alternatively, if a Śrāvaka now resolves to attain the Great Mind and seeks to receive the correct precepts, since a Śrāvaka possesses only five heinous offenses and lacks the offense of killing one's teacher, this matter of "killing one's teacher" must likewise be raised as a question.
According to the preceding text of this very scripture, there is only one master requested; yet here it speaks of two masters.
This constitutes the seven heinous offenses (*ānantarya*), and both interpretations are valid; however, no textual passage regarding the invitation of a teacher has been seen.

According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā*, one should invite only a single teacher. One should receive the precepts before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva, with the teacher remaining by one's side;

one must not sit with one's back turned toward the image. As a master and model, one must clearly understand every detail of the methods for receiving the precepts as found within the sūtras and śāstras. However, the original...
The method for receiving the Dharma has long been lost. One may rely on the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and the *Ratnakaranda-śrāvakācāra* to investigate and clarify it in detail for oneself.

One must not take one's own mind as the teacher, for this cannot avoid the fault of violating the teachings through ignorance; furthermore, it prevents others from attaining the precepts for the rest of their lives.

Recently, Master Sùhuā Xù compiled the *Lǜyí Jìyào Hòují* (Supplementary Collection of Essentials of Vinaya Discipline), in which the method for receiving the precepts is concise and clear. As for the other... [open]... methods, they are as follows: [End of excerpt]
The guiding strategy is set forth. One should consider the specific capacities and circumstances of others.

If there is one who has committed one of the ten grave offenses, this refers to someone who has previously received the Mind-Ground Precepts (*cittabhūmi-śīla*) and has subsequently transgressed any one of the ten *pārājika* rules.

Regarding the "thousand Buddhas of the three periods," there are one thousand Buddhas each in the past, future, and present, as set forth in the *Sūtra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas*. If [one suffers] suffering...
Upon arriving to prostrate before the Buddha and repent, the black karma of transgressing the precepts is already eliminated.

The essence of the precepts is freed from all obscurations, and non-action (avijñapti) shines forth with renewed clarity, like the moon brightening when clouds disperse; thus one beholds the light. The Bodhisattva’s ground of the mind (cittabhūmi) further attains full blooming.
Therefore, one sees flowers; all sins are extinguished, yet their substance is immediately empty, transforming into the nature-virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Thus, one sees various distinct appearances. Emptiness is the true emptiness of the real mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). The real mark has no separate marks; it is precisely these marks of sin.
To realize that these marks are fundamentally empty, then there is no sin that is not extinguished and no virtue that is not manifested. It returns to being identical with...

One of great awakening is a true son of the Buddha; therefore, the Buddha comes to touch his head with his hand. If one’s mind is not earnest and does not reach the point of extreme sincerity, then such superior signs will not appear.
Although one performs repentance, the offenses are not extinguished, the essence of the precepts is not restored, and the goodness of the precepts does not arise;

thus it is said that it is of no benefit. That those who receive the precepts obtain increase is not to say that there is never any benefit; it is simply that at present, although [the signs do not appear]...

One attains the precepts through the power of repentance; furthermore, this increases the benefit of attaining the precepts in the future, because one’s mind of repentance does not cease thereafter, but continues with such earnestness and profound sincerity that it is like the collapse of Mount Tai.

After two or three years, if one beholds a favorable sign, one immediately attains the precepts. Once a favorable sign has been seen, know that it is the causal condition for the extinction of transgressions, and do not give rise to attachment toward it.
To grasp and cling [to experiences] is to provide an opportunity for Māra. Thus, a sutra says: "If one forms a holy understanding, one falls among the various heterodoxies.

This is precisely what that means. Regarding confession before another (duìshǒu): this refers to when one commits a minor offense (qīnggòu); one should then confess and repent before a single Bodhisattva bhikṣu, and the transgression will be extinguished.
There is no need for auspicious signs (hàoxiàng). This is not the same as the case of the seven prohibitions (qīzhē), although the former [text] taught those seven...

To obstruct others from repenting for their offenses while manifesting that one has not attained the precepts oneself—yet now, when the ten grave offenses (*daśa-guru-dharma*) are committed, the signs of transgression are seen to be extinguished, and minor impurities (*laghu-āpatti*) are removed through confession before another; therefore, it is said that these cases are not the same.
One who can understand each of these points—whether repentance is permitted or not, and whether the precepts are obtained or not—is alone qualified to be a teacher of others.

Model. Now, there are three types of repentance methods: namely, the method of ritual performance (*zuo-fa*), the method of attaining signs (*qu-xiang*), and the method of non-arising (*wu-sheng*). As for the method of ritual performance:

throughout the six periods of day and night, one purifies the three karmas and, before the images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, discloses and reveals one's transgressions, repenting with utmost sincerity.
As for the method of attaining signs: one concentrates the mind and directs the imagination, taking the manifestation of specific signs as the deadline for the practice on the Path.
Within the assembly, one may see the Buddha stroke one’s head; or see light, or see flowers; or, within a dream, see various auspicious signs.
By seeing even one of these signs, one’s transgressions shall be extinguished. This is so. Regarding "non-arising":
all karmic offenses arise from a mind of false delusion and inversion. If one realizes that one's own mind does not arise, then both offense and merit...
There is no master. Contemplate the true mark (*dharmatā*) of karma; see the source of transgressions. The Dharma-realm is perfectly interfused, and True Suchness (*tathatā*) is pure.
Thus, a sutra says: "If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the true mark. All sins are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can eliminate them.
This is precisely that meaning. Question: The true mark is markless. How should one contemplate it? Answer: By means of non-...
Contemplate this contemplation. Contemplate the markless mark. By means of the markless mark, contemplate the markless contemplation.
If there were a real mark existing separately from contemplation, or if there were contemplation existing separately outside of the real mark, then it would not be the real mark of contemplation.

As for the ritual repentance (*zuo-fa chan*), it can extinguish the offenses of violating the precepts; as for the repentance that grasps marks (*qu-xiang chan*), it can extinguish innate offenses (*xing-zui*). There is no...

The *shengchan* (repentance of birth) can extinguish the offenses of ignorance and afflictions. Although there are three methods of repentance, they do not transcend the two paths of phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*).
The first two belong to phenomena; the last one belongs to principle. The *Zhiguan* states: "Phenomenal repentance repents the path of suffering and the path of karma;
principled repentance repents the path of ignorance and afflictions. The *Jinguangming ji* states: "The three types of repentance methods are simultaneous..."

Cultivation: Non-arising (*anutpāda*) is the primary practice, while the other two serve as auxiliary conditions (*sahakāri-pratyaya*). This constitutes the combined practice of the primary and the auxiliary, which—like oil augmenting a lamp’s brightness—causes the realization of principle to be even more rapid.
Although the original sūtra does not explicitly mention non-arising, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is precisely non-arising.
There are those who cultivate only the first two auxiliary paths, such as Nanyue, who established the "peaceful and blissful practice with signs" (*nimitta-śānta-sukha-caryā*). It is not...
Upon entering samādhi, merely by reciting and upholding [the text], one may likewise behold sublime and wondrous forms and signs;

this refers to the practice in the original sūtra of performing prostrations and recitations during the six periods of the day, repenting with utmost sincerity, and the Buddha coming to stroke one’s head, and so forth.
Such methods of repentance are extremely subtle; one must consult an enlightened master regarding the place for learning repentance and the methods of repentance before one can enter the Way.
The ritual procedures for these three types of repentance are extensively detailed in the sutras, śāstras, commentaries, and sub-commentaries; they shall not be described here at length.

That the essence of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*) is restored is the path of repenting karmic transgressions (*karmapatha*). That the various faculties, such as the eyes and ears, become pure is the path of repenting suffering (*duḥkha*).
If one does not understand the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas, nor the characteristics of what is light or heavy, or what is right and wrong;

and if one does not understand the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the nature of the habituated seeds (śikṣā-bīja-gotra), the nature of growth (vṛddhi-gotra), the nature of the innate seeds (prakṛti-gotra), the indestructible nature (abhedyatva-gotra), the nature of the path-seeds (mārga-bīja-gotra), and the nature of the true dharma (saddharma-gotra).

Regarding the various degrees of meditative practice and its entry and exit, the ten factors of dhyāna, and all dharmas of conditioned activity— if one fails to grasp the essential meaning within each of these dharmas,

such that one cannot discern the characteristics of their relative weight or their right and wrong, this refers to the correct precepts of this mind-ground: even a minor transgression immediately defiles the source of the mind.

Confession before another person is called "light" purification; committing a major offense results in the loss of the precepts. One must perceive auspicious signs for the offense to be removed, which is called "heavy.
To clearly analyze these two paths—light and heavy—to discern what constitutes an offense and what does not, is to be well-versed in the names and characteristics of the precepts.
As for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is this very precept of the mind-ground.

Its essence is profoundly still and tranquil; it is neither heavy nor light, yet heaviness and lightness are manifest therein. Its nature is empty and luminous; it is neither right nor wrong, yet right and wrong are vividly apparent.
It transcends the two extremes while simultaneously negating and illuminating them both, revealing the principle of the Middle Way that is beyond discourse and beyond thought;
therefore, it is called the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is what is meant by "skillfully understanding the meaning of the precepts."

Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls it the "complete precepts" (*paripūrṇa-śīla*). This means that when a bodhisattva maintains the precepts of the Middle Way, the Supreme Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they employ the wisdom of the Middle Way to universally enter into all phenomena; there is no precept that is not fully prepared. This is what is meant by the complete precepts.

If one does not understand the characteristics [of phenomena], then the distinction between maintaining and violating the precepts will remain obscure. If one does not understand the principle, then one will not recognize the source-ground of the mind.
Among these six types of nature, the nature of the stage of cultivation (*śikṣā-bīja*) corresponds to the ten stages (*daśa-vihāra*). These are called the Bodhisattvas of the Copper-Treasure Wheel;

they are the aforementioned ten minds of initial aspiration (*prathama-cittotpāda*). This means that these Bodhisattvas first enter from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), investigate and practice the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), cultivate the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), open the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*), and achieve all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Because they have attained this stage and do not regress, it is so named.

Regarding the "abiding," the "nature of nurturing" (*poṣaṇagotra*), and the "nature of the seed-lineage" (*gotragotra*): these two correspond to the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*) and are called the Bodhisattvas of the Silver Jewel-Wheel.
These refer to the aforementioned ten nurtured minds; that is to say, this Bodhisattva proceeds from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) into the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) to benefit sentient beings.

One advances in the cultivation of the provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), distinguishing the various natures (*gotra*) of the ten realms, nurturing the holy embryo, perceiving the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), opening the Dharma-eye, and accomplishing the knowledge of the paths (*mārgākārajñatā*).
Because one proceeds from these preceding ten stages (*bhūmi*) after having awakened to the true principle, this stage is called "Practice" (*caryā*).
One must not harbor the nature of ordinary beings or the nature of the path-seeds; these two categories correspond generally to the ten stages of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
This stage is named the Bodhisattva Golden Jewel Wheel. It refers to the aforementioned ten adamantine minds;

that is to say, this bodhisattva cultivates the contemplation of the Middle Way, spontaneously establishing it through the path of effortless non-action, such that practice, vows, phenomena, and principle are all completely harmonized and integrated.
It flows into the *dharmadhātu*. It turns phenomena toward principle, and even turns that which is capable of cultivation and that which is cultivated toward the *dharmadhātu*.
Because its nature is like a diamond (*vajra*), it is indestructible. Because it begins the correct cultivation in the middle [of the path], it is called the "path" (*mārga*).

In view of its subsequent ability to produce the fruit of Buddhahood, it is called the "seed" (*bīja*). That which is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is also called the "noble lineage" (*āryagotra*); this applies generally to...

The stages of the ten bhūmis, equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and wondrous enlightenment (*pratyakṣa-bodhi*). From the first bhūmi through the tenth bhūmi, one employs the contemplation of the Middle Way to sever delusions with wisdom;
this becomes increasingly profound stage by stage, as one destroys a portion of ignorance (*avidyā*) in each bhūmi and manifests a portion of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).
Upon entering the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), opening the Buddha-eye, and attaining all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), they are all called Bodhisattvas of the Lapis Lazuli Jewel Wheel.

According to the *Yingluo jing* (Sutra of the Necklaces), the nature of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and the nature of Sublime Enlightenment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) are separately distinguished.

Furthermore, by deeply penetrating the contemplation of the Middle Way, one reaches the beginningless ignorance, exhausts its very source and bottom, and brings wisdom to its ultimate limit, thereby severing the final single grade [of affliction].
Having ascended the peak of the mountain of the Middle Way, one parts from the parents of ignorance—the subtle delusions of nescience.
To possess such delusions that can still be severed is called being an "upper-grade practitioner. This is the Maṇiratnacakra Bodhisattva, the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Therein lies ultimate liberation; one is brilliantly awakened, wondrous wisdom exhausts the source, the habitual tendencies of nescience are exhausted, and one is carefree and free from all burdens.
Therefore, there are no delusions to be severed; it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating. The Sage among Sages is named the Unsurpassed One (*anuttara-puruṣa*).

This is the Bodhisattva Crystal Jewel Wheel (*sphaṭika-ratna-cakra*), which is precisely the stage of Buddhahood, the ultimate fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*vimalābhisambodhi*). Regarding those who enter and emerge from the various contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*) within this state:
it refers to those who, according to their individual faculties and natures, traverse the stages of the Three Worthies (*tri-śaikṣa*) and Ten Sages (*daśa-ārya*) from above.

Regarding the differences in the efficacy of meditative contemplation and spiritual practice between those of dull faculties and those of sharp faculties: there is a distinction between skillful and unskillful methods for severing delusions and realizing true reality.

Those of sharp faculties employ skillful means with little effort, whereas those of dull faculties employ unskillful means with much effort. This pertains to their entry into and emergence from the various dhyānas and samādhis.

Therefore, it is called "contemplative practice" (*vipaśyanā*). Regarding the ten factors of dhyāna (*daśa-dhyānāṅgāni*): among the four dhyānas, excluding those factors that appear redundantly, there are exactly ten factors:

first, applied thought (*vitarka*); second, sustained thought (*vicāra*); third, joy (*prīti*); fourth, bliss (*sukha*); fifth, one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*); sixth, internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*); seventh, equanimity (*upekṣā*).

The eight recollections, the nine wisdoms, and the tenth, which is neither suffering nor pleasure—these ten, although they belong to worldly dhyāna, enable one to enter the stages of the noble ones (ārya).

Regarding "all practices" (*sarvacaryā*), this summarizes the aforementioned meritorious practices of cultivation. As for "all dharma-gates," these refer to such contemplative practices as these dharmas;
they are explained in detail in the *Necklace of Primary Karma Sūtra* (*Āṭānāṭiya-sūtra*). Not a single one of them can be obtained without this.
Regarding the "intention within the Dharma": the methods for progressive cultivation mentioned above are profoundly deep and subtle.
If one does not understand their underlying intent point by point, then one is either greedy for profit or simply ignorant. Yet such a person acts as a preceptor for bestowing the precepts;

they are like an incompetent physician treating an illness, which will inevitably cause people to die prematurely, or like employing a blind person as a guide, which ultimately leads [the traveler] astray.
Falling into pits and ditches for the sake of momentary fame and profit causes others to spend their entire lives such that the precepts do not touch their bodies;
to act with such reckless frivolity and thereby mislead the Dharma-body and wisdom-life of others is no small matter. Therefore, this is regulated by both [the prohibitions].

Not understanding this constitutes an offense. (The four teachings are discussed throughout this sutra, yet it belongs to the Distinct and Perfect [teachings]; thus, the wheel is assigned to the [Buddha] Nature.)
Yet, for the sake of gain and fame, such bodhisattvas seek and crave excessively;
they greedily desire disciples and falsely pretend to understand all the sūtras and vinayas. For the sake of offerings, they deceive themselves and likewise deceive others.
Therefore, one who bestows the precepts upon others commits a minor offense (light impurity).
To seek [gain] for the sake of profit and fame is called "evil seeking. To covet profit without satiety is called "excessive seeking. One who studies after the teacher is called a "disciple" (dì);
one who understands through the teacher is called a "son" (zǐ). If one internally does not master the purport of the sūtras and vinaya, they lack shame.
Lack of shame constitutes self-deception. To outwardly feign the appearance of understanding is to deceive others.

The eighteenth precept, mentioned previously, was established specifically because of acting as a teacher while lacking actual understanding; this present precept is further violated for the sake of gain and profit.
According to this principle, one who is proficient in both meditative contemplation and the doctrinal teachings, and who is free from a mind that covets profit or seeks fame, [is exempt].

Only then may one be permitted to act as a preceptor; thus, there is no offense. One must not, by merely understanding a single phrase, a single verse, or a single section of the Vinaya-piṭaka, proceed to bestow the precepts upon others and thereby incur no fault.
Therefore, the *Yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning) states: "To speak of a 'preceptor,' one must discuss the accomplishment of their virtue and practice.

Such a person is an ordained Bodhisattva who is fully endowed with five virtues: first, observance of the precepts; second, [at least] twenty years of seniority (*la*); third, mastery of the Vinaya-piṭaka; fourth..."

He mastered meditative contemplation; his five treasuries of wisdom exhausted the profound mysteries. To speak of his upholding the precepts, they were as firm and steadfast as the ten vows and five oaths.

To speak of his ten years of ordination, he had already completed ten summer retreats since receiving full ordination. To speak of his mastery of the Vinaya-piṭaka, the Vinaya comprises both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles;

offenses include both those of inherent nature (*svabhāva*) and those prohibited by convention (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*); there are prohibitions and permissions, observances and transgressions; and within the precepts, there are paths, concentrations, and mundane attainments.
There is that which transcends the world; there is liberation; there is individual liberation. There are three, five, eight, and ten [precepts].

Among these ten, there are those for householders and those for renunciants; there are men and women; there are two hundred and fifty, three hundred and forty-eight, up to five hundred, and thirty-eight thousand. Truly vast is this treasury! Although it is said to be non-existent...

[All] is exhausted. As for the teacher, there is nothing they do not penetrate. To speak of "penetrating meditative contemplation" (*dhyāna-cintā*): this is a general term for all *dhyānas*, *samādhis*, and *samāpattis*.
All arise from upholding the precepts and gathering the mind, whereby deluded thoughts become stilled and tranquil, and through empty luminosity, one reflects back upon oneself.

One becomes well-versed in entering and emerging [from concentration], skillfully attaining mastery over sinking and floating, and remaining free from all dullness and distraction; this is what is meant by penetrating meditative contemplation. To speak of...
The Treasury of Wisdom (*prajñā-kośa*) encompasses all phenomena, penetrating their source and synthesizing their meaning.
Whether regarding mind or objects, facts or principles, it exhausts the subtle and attains the wondrous; it expounds according to the capacities of beings without obstruction or stagnation.
This is called the "Treasury of Wisdom that exhausts the profound mysteries. *Fayin* states: These five virtues are prized for being possessed together, though they may also exist individually.
In this world, it is difficult for the five virtues to be complete in one person. One who has few years of seniority in the precepts (*śīla*) yet possesses virtue may still be taken as a teacher;

they are superior to those who merely grow old in vain, lacking wisdom and unable to instruct others. One who possesses wisdom (*prajñā*) but lacks meditative concentration (*samādhi*) may still be taken as a teacher; they are superior to those who practice withered dhyāna like mute sheep.
One cannot preach the Dharma. Were it otherwise, the task of propagating the precepts would not be a light one;
if there is ignorance and no practice, both the bestower and the receiver shall equally incur guilt. Be cautious and regard this with gravity.
Forty-second: The precept against preaching the precepts to evil persons.
Not discerning their capacity and suitability is to lack the eye of wisdom. Since their faculties and powers are not yet capable, one instead causes them to fall.

To explain [the teachings] in advance leads to a light attitude toward receiving them later; before they have developed the Great Mind, hearing [the teachings] gives rise to slander and defamation. This applies to all who do not accept the Mahāyāna.
O Mokṣa, those who cling to worldly views—that is, the adherents of the Hinayana—are all called evil persons.

O Sons of the Buddha, for the sake of profit or sustenance, you must not preach these Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas before those who have not received the Bodhisattva precepts, nor before non-Buddhists or evil persons, nor even before those with false views; however, this does not apply to kings.
All other [circumstances] must not be mentioned.

One must not recite the precepts before non-Buddhists, evil persons, or those with wrong views; this harms not only oneself through greed for profit, but truly scorches the sprouts of their Bodhi as well.
"Reciting" means either chanting the text, explaining its meaning, conferring the precepts, or listening to them.

He heard this being recited during the *poṣadha* ceremony. However, these Great Precepts transmitted by the thousand Buddhas are not fit to be heard by those who have not yet resolved to attain Bodhicitta, nor by non-Buddhists or evil persons, because they are not suitable vessels.
It is like lion’s milk, which cannot be contained in a glass cup; yet, should one later abandon error for the right and resolve upon the vast mind, [it may be received].
Only then may one preach it. O King, you are honored by this entire nation; the Tathāgata has entrusted you to provide external protection for the Triple Gem.
Therefore, the precepts of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna may be explained to you as the Buddha permitted.

To all other people who lack faith, as well as those who have not received the Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas, it must not be preached. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the past, on the fifteenth day, the Saṃgha..."
During the time of the *poṣadha*, there was a youth who, remaining in a hidden place, eavesdropped on the recitation of the precepts.
A Vajrapāṇi, with his mallet, crushed him until his body was like fine dust. Thus one knows that a teacher must not fail to be cautious.
These wicked people do not receive the Buddha's precepts and are thus called "beasts. In every place where they are born, they do not see the Triple Gem;
like wood or stone, they lack a mind and are thus called "heretics. These people of false views are no different from wooden stumps.
If a Bodhisattva preaches the seven teachings and precepts of the Buddhas before such wicked people, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).

They cannot distinguish between good and evil, or the wise and the foolish; thus they are like beasts. Having failed to receive the Great Precepts from the thousand Buddhas, they have lost the seed of Bodhi.
Consequently, in every place of rebirth, they do not behold the Triple Gem. Though they dwell among the ranks of humanity, they do not know how to turn toward the Great Way that transcends the world;
thus they are like wood or stone, devoid of mind, passing from delusion to delusion as their six sense organs remain dark and obstructed.

Therefore, it is no different from a piece of wood. Although this precept of the mind-ground has been taught by all Buddhas of the three periods of time, it has been transmitted in recent times through the succession of the Seven Buddhas; this is precisely why its intimacy is evident.

One must not fail to exercise discernment and self-respect, nor should one lightly explain it to outsiders or those who have not received the precepts, thereby causing oneself to suffer harm and leading others into ruin—this would be a grave transgression.
This is not a minor matter. The preceding precept regulated the selection [of recipients], whereas this precept regulates the bestowing [of the precepts] upon evil persons.
While within the context of non-selection, there is nevertheless an evident selection. The prior non-selection was based on a universal mind and a mind of compassion;

now, one must exercise selection, possessing the eye of wisdom and the eye of insight. One must carefully refrain from being mired in non-selection and recklessly conferring the great precepts upon evil persons and fools.
Yet, on the contrary, they claim to be compassionate and cause others to plant roots of goodness. Even if those individuals do not give rise to slander, they have no intention to study or practice;

they do not recognize what is permitted or prohibited, nor what constitutes upholding or violating the precepts. Since their understanding of upholding and violating is obscured, they will inevitably fall into the three miserable realms.
Thus, while intending to plant roots of goodness, they instead bring about evil fruits. Bestowing the precepts in such a manner is either out of ignorance or for the sake of fame and profit.
For this reason, if you truly wish to cause them to plant roots of goodness, you may instruct them to take refuge in and place faith in the Triple Gem.
Within the five precepts, observe how many portions they are able to receive and then bestow them upon them;
or else bestow the eight precepts, instructing them to make vows and dedicate their merit toward seeking unexcelled Bodhi. Would this not be of profound benefit to those before you?
○ Forty-third: The Precept Against Receiving Alms Without Shame.
To bear sin within oneself while claiming merit for others, and to refuse to seek repentance—this is shamelessness and lack of remorse.
To indiscriminately accept the alms of the faithful, thereby harming both oneself and others—how great is such transgression!
If a disciple of the Buddha has left the household life with faith and received the Buddha’s true precepts, yet then gives rise to the intention to violate those holy precepts,
they shall not receive the offerings of any donors; nor shall they walk upon the ground of a king, nor drink the water of a king.
Having already cultivated faith and left the secular world, how could one willfully violate the pure precepts transmitted by the thousand sages?
Since the king originally bestowed the earth and water upon virtuous persons as gifts, if one were to transgress them, the virtue of the precepts would no longer exist;
thus, though the earth is vast, there would be no place to set foot, and though the rivers are full, not even a single drop could be consumed—how much more so in this case!
Dānapatis, regarding the fourfold offerings and the property of the permanently resident Sangha throughout the ten directions: are you able to utilize them properly?

Should you happen to commit even a minor transgression, you must immediately perform repentance according to the Dharma; only then will the offerings of the faithful be extinguished [of their karmic weight].

Five thousand great ghosts constantly obstructed his path ahead. The ghosts cried out, "Great thief! Whenever he entered a room, a city, or a house, the ghosts would further sweep away his footprints.
All people of the world reviled him, saying, "A thief within the Buddha-dharma. No sentient being wished to see him with their eyes;
they said that one who violates the precepts is no different from a beast, no different from a block of wood. If [he were to do so] intentionally...
To violate the right precepts constitutes a minor offense (light dust offense).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "A Bodhisattva is fully endowed with five hundred rules of training. From this we know that these fifty-eight precepts are the very foundation of the precepts.
To uphold them, one is protected by five thousand benevolent deities; to violate them, there are five... [the text here is incomplete].
A thousand great spirits follow him at all times, just as the carriages, horses, and attendants of a person of high worldly rank always accompany and protect them.

When one commits an offense against the king’s law, the cangues, shackles, and dark-clad guards constantly follow to restrain and guard them. This is the divergence between the paths of good and evil;

such is the fundamental nature of reality. To "block his way" means that it is strictly forbidden for him to travel upon the King’s domain; to call him a "great thief" refers to his infliction of harm.
Regarding the Great Precepts of the Thousand Buddhas: those who sweep away their traces and violate the precepts cannot ascend, like a turtle dragging its tail.
They detest the filthiness of the dwellings and the roads. Within the Buddha-Dharma, there are thieves who steal by donning the robes of the Buddha and pilfer by consuming the food of the Buddha;
they instead harm the Buddha-Dharma from within it, and are therefore called "thieves. As for those who maintain the precepts and dignified deportment...
All gaze upon these signs of decline resulting from violating the precepts—the evil views of sentient beings who fail to recognize what constitutes upholding or transgressing them.

How are they different from animals? Lacking the essence of the precepts in their bodies, how do they differ from wooden stumps? Thus, in this life there is no auspiciousness; merit and virtue diminish daily.

At death, one falls into the Avīci Hell, from which it will be difficult to emerge even after the exhaustion of kalpas. These "precepts" refer to those that have been violated; having already committed the offense, the guilt has been established in accordance with the transgression. It does not...
Because one is unwilling to repent according to the Dharma, lacks shame and remorse, and yet presumptuously accepts offerings and benefits, one consequently commits further minor transgressions.

Regarding the statement that five thousand benevolent deities provide protection: for each precept, the Heavenly Emperor dispatches ten deities to guard and uphold the practitioner who observes the precepts;
since there are five hundred precepts, there are thus five thousand benevolent deities. Furthermore, the human body naturally possesses deities on both shoulders.
The Guardian (Shouhu) shares the same name as the body and is born together with it; though he constantly protects the person, he must rely on the mind to be firm.
If the spirit-guardian is strong, then the precepts will be steadfast; if the precepts are not firm, the guardian will become terrified and anxious.
How could the dispatched spirits not return to the heavens? And how could five thousand great ghosts not block his path?
○ The forty-fourth precept: Not making offerings to the scriptures.

Viewing the Three Jewels as equal and cultivating the two types of adornment (merit and wisdom) side by side is the fundamental practice of a Mahāsattva. To fail to make offerings is to lose the aspiration for supreme enlightenment;
to fail to transcribe [the scriptures] is to deviate from the way of transforming others below.
O sons of the Buddha, you should always, with a single mind, receive, uphold, read, and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya.
You should even flay your own skin to make paper, draw blood for ink, use marrow as water, and split your bones to make pens to transcribe the Buddha’s precepts.

Whether using the bark of trees, rice-husk paper, silk, or bamboo slips, you should likewise transcribe and maintain them. You should always offer the seven treasures, priceless incense and flowers, and all manner of miscellaneous jewels.
A chest or bag for containing the scrolls of the Sūtras and Vinaya: if one fails to provide them with proper offerings, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

To have mindfulness without interruption is called "constant" (*nitya*); to have the mind free from distraction is called "single-minded" (*eka*). This reveals the ultimate limit of diligent and earnest resolve.
To transcribe [the scriptures] using skin, blood, and bone marrow reveals a lack of concern for one's own body in order to uphold the Dharma; it is beyond price.

To use a chest or bag made of various jewels is to value the profound Dharma more than material wealth. Within this, five types [of practice] are enumerated in total: first, receiving and upholding each with a focused mind without forgetting;

second, reading them in the dark until they are mastered; third, reciting them aloud so that others may hear; fourth, transcribing them for circulation; and fifth, reverently making offerings to them.
These five appear interchangeably in the sūtras and śāstras, sometimes as five and sometimes as six; all are termed [the five methods of propagating the Dharma].
The Dharma Master [states]: "However, there are slight differences in how these items are opened and closed, as in the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra).

There are five [practices]: first, receiving and upholding; second, reading the text; third, reciting fluently; fourth, explaining the meaning; and fifth, copying. Yet, the act of making offerings is omitted [here], while the original sutra omits 'explaining the meaning.

Nevertheless, regarding the thirty-nine precepts, the act of lecturing and expounding has already been presented; furthermore, regarding the forty-one precepts, it is said that one must understand each one thoroughly."

According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: first, the power of faith is called "receiving"; second, the power of mindfulness is called "retaining"; third, examining the text is "reading"; fourth, not forgetting it is "reciting";
fifth, proclaiming it to others is "explaining"; sixth, that which is difficult to understand must be "interpreted. This [latter] also lacks the element of making offerings.
All Buddhas attained equal and perfect enlightenment by studying the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas; thus we know this.
The Sūtras and Vinaya are the mothers of all Buddhas. If one does not offer them sincere worship in accordance with the Dharma, this is to slight the mother of the Buddhas of the three periods;
it is called filial impiety, and for this reason one incurs transgression. "Bark" refers to birch bark and the like.

"Grain" refers to the bark of the *zhǔ* tree (*Broussonetia papyrifera*), which can be used to make paper. "Silk cloth" refers to that woven from plain white thread; "plain" (*sù*) also denotes white gauze. In this region...
In ancient times, before paper was known, bamboo slips and wooden tablets were used extensively. However, the materials employed by various nations differed between antiquity and the present;
thus, one should employ them according to the time and place. For example, the people of Pamir (Wǔfū Zhú) use birch bark and *pāṭala* leaves.
As well as white cotton cloth. In this region, the manufacture of *he-ti* paper began during the Former Han dynasty;
it was during the time of Emperor Huan of the Later Han that Cai Jingzhong used tree bark, discarded cloth, and fish nets to produce paper. Nowadays, bamboo and mulberry bark are most commonly used.
By means of these materials, one writes and circulates [the teachings]; this constitutes the twofold gift of wealth and Dharma, which is widely disseminated without end.

The *Cittaviśuddhiprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "There are four kinds of Dharma-treasures: first, the Dharma of teaching; second, the Dharma of principle; third, the Dharma of practice; and fourth, the Dharma of fruition.
All are untainted (*anāsrava*) and capable of destroying ignorance, afflictions, and karmic obstructions. Sounds, names, phrases, and syllables are called the Dharma of teaching.
The existence and non-existence of all phenomena are called the Dharma of principle. The practices of precept, concentration, and wisdom are called..."

The practice of the Dharma and the unconditioned, wondrous fruit are called the "Dharma of the Fruit. These four kinds [of dharmas] guide sentient beings out of the ocean of birth and death and lead them to the other shore.
That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is precisely the Jewel of the Dharma. Why is this so?
The Buddhas of the three periods of time practice according to the Dharma, sever all hindrances, and attain Bodhi;

until the end of the future, they benefit sentient beings. For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the three periods constantly make offerings to the various pāramitās and the subtle, wondrous treasure of the Dharma;
how much more so for all sentient beings within the triple world who have not yet attained liberation?

You are unable to revere the subtle and wondrous Jewel of the Dharma. In the past, when I was a Dharma-seeking King, I entered a great pit of fire to seek the True Dharma, thereby forever severing birth and death and attaining Great Bodhi.
Therefore, the Jewel of the Dharma can shatter the prison of all birth and death like a vajra; it can illuminate the ignorant and darkened sentient beings like the sun appearing in the world.
Furthermore, it is like a guide on a perilous path who skillfully leads sentient beings to reach the place of jewels;
the sublime Dharma taught by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time contains such inconceivable matters as these.
○ The forty-fifth precept: Not Transforming Sentient Beings.

Seeking the higher while transforming those below is what first defines a Bodhisattva. To act contrary to this is for both name and reality to be at odds; how, then, can such a person be called one who practices the vows of a Great Being?
If you, O sons of the Buddha, constantly give rise to the mind of great compassion, whenever you enter any city, town, or house and see any sentient beings, you should proclaim:
"All you sentient beings, you should all receive the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts."

The Great Being takes the transformation and deliverance of others as his primary concern; his compassion for those suffering is urgent. Therefore, he constantly gives rise to the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
This mind must not be forgotten for even a moment; hence it is called "constant. As for "all sentient beings," this fundamentally encompasses the six realms of existence.
However, because a Bodhisattva has not yet attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), it is not easy to perceive them within the clamor and bustle of cities, towns, houses, and dwellings.
As for those seen among the devas, asuras, hell-beings, and hungry ghosts, there are only humans and animals.
In this present text, the purpose is to cause humans to resolve their minds toward awakening; since humans have distinctions of high and low, noble and base, the term "all" is used.
Next, it causes animals to resolve their minds. Afterwards, when entering secluded places such as mountains, forests, rivers, and fields, one then includes spirits and ghosts as well.
In such cases, one should first employ various skillful means to instruct them so that they give rise to great faith; only thereafter should one confer the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts.
If one bestows the precepts without first instructing them to resolve their minds [toward awakening], it is equivalent to conferring the precepts upon an evil person.

Therefore, cause them to turn away from evil and return to the right path by first receiving the Three Refuges. By the power of protection afforded by the Triple Gem, the offenses leading to the three evil realms and the eight difficult conditions shall be extinguished.
Next, bestow upon them the ten types of *pratimokṣa* precepts, which constitute the foundation of the Bodhisattva path.
According to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, one should cause the bodhisattvas to receive the ten wholesome dharmas, just as a śrāmaṇera does.
The text of the ten precepts is the same. According to the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, one is to receive the precepts of the ten paths of wholesome action:

first, not killing, up to tenth, not holding wrong views. By dedicating these roots of goodness toward unsurpassed bodhi, this person will swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās and attain perfect enlightenment in a pure land.
Based on this, one should administer [the precepts] according to what the recipient is capable of enduring.

It is also permissible to bestow [the precepts]. The *Sūtra of the Necklace* (*Yingluo jing*) states: "The Dharma Master first provides an exposition for them, causing them to take joy and attachment [in the teaching], and only then does he bestow [the precepts]. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra* (*Dichi jing*) states:

"If a Bodhisattva sees sentient beings practicing heterodox rites and fasts while seeking liberation, he immediately explains the Eightfold Noble Fast (*āryāṣṭāṅgopavāsa*) to them, thereby severing their false views. If they seek deliverance through physical [practice]..."
The ultimate Dharma: by bestowing a small expedient means, one obtains the great fruit of the *poṣadha*. This is what constitutes a bodhisattva;
through a small expedient means, they give rise to immeasurable roots of goodness (the eight *poṣadhas*, that is, the eight *gānzhāi* precepts).
If you see oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, or any other animals, you should mentally reflect and verbally say: "You are an animal;
arouse the bodhicitta.
When a Great Being sees any animal, they should give rise to great compassion and reflect upon its delusion throughout beginningless kalpas.
Having reflected thus—that their nature is distorted, that they falsely create afflictions and karma, and that they endure the bitter retribution of saṃsāra in vain—he spoke these words aloud:
"You are animals; you ought to seek liberation. Do not endure this suffering in vain, which knows no rest."

In this way, one causes them to know that name-and-form are suffering, so that their minds seek liberation and they turn toward the Great Being. Thereafter, one instructs them to give rise to the bodhicitta;
this mind is the perfectly luminous essence of awakening of all Buddhas and the fundamental nature of sentient beings.

If they are deluded regarding this mind and do not give rise to it, they will transmigrate through the six realms, where the three evil paths blaze intensely, continuing without end throughout kalpas. If...
When one is able to give rise to this mind, the fundamental ground of the mind—the essence of the precepts—is revealed and brought forth;

thus, the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts immediately manifest before one. At that time, the Great Being (the Bodhisattva) then acts as a witness and further bestows the characteristics of the Three Refuges and the Ten Precepts.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva enters all places—whether mountain forests, rivers, or wildernesses—they must cause all sentient beings therein to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
If this Bodhisattva does not give rise to the mind to teach and transform sentient beings, they commit a minor offense.
Previously, he caused humans and animals to resolve their minds [for enlightenment]. Now, according to their respective directions and perspectives, he causes them to resolve their minds.
This sufficiently demonstrates the Great Being’s heart of universal transformation; there is nowhere it does not benefit. His thought of rescue and deliverance is never not urgent.

As for all sentient beings—humans, devas, ghosts, and spirits; those in the borderlands, the solitary, and those in hell; even down to birds, beasts, fish, turtles, snakes, and insects—[he brings them all to liberation].
Do not assume that those who move about are devoid of cognition and thus abandon them without transforming them. Yet, among sentient beings, there are many whose awakened nature remains undeluded.
For example, a parrot heard the Four Noble Truths, was reborn in heaven, and eventually attained the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha.

A monkey offered honey, subsequently left the household life, and realized the Way. A bird listened to the sutras and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; geese heard the Dharma and were reborn [in the heavens].
The fish in the pond of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven heard a verse and were reborn as devaputras; the sea whale heard the name [of the Buddha] and the ship was spared from disaster.
Instances such as these are beyond counting. Even for those who are deluded and unaware, through the empowerment of the Dharma, they are likewise enabled to obtain benefit.
For example, when Śāriputra spoke the Three Seals of the Dharma to a sick dog and a venomous snake, both were reborn [in higher realms].
A wealthy family later attained the fruit of sainthood; those in hell were entirely delivered from the fiery pit upon hearing the title of the sutra.

Furthermore, as for mantra incantations, how could humans understand them? Yet by receiving and upholding them, one’s heart’s wishes are fulfilled—even to the point of reviving a withered tree through incantation.
It even causes flowers to bloom; if even insentient things respond thus, how much more so for sentient beings who would not fail to receive benefit?
What the Tathāgata has proclaimed from his golden mouth—not a single word or syllable—can be fathomed by ordinary minds.
Therefore, the Vinaya prescribes that whenever a bhikṣu arrives at a shrine, or at places such as beneath trees or beside water, he must recite gāthās. Now, this Great Being knows all...
Sentient beings are endowed with the nature of awakening; therefore, one must teach and transform them universally and continuously without interruption.
If one does not give rise to this mind, it violates the great vows of a bodhisattva, and thus incurs a light defilement.
○ The forty-sixth precept: Preaching the Dharma contrary to the Dharma.
The Dharma is the Mother of the Buddhas. If a Great Being does not hold himself in high esteem, how can he cause others to pay him respect?
Even a jackal knows to honor itself, and one who steals fruit knows it is contrary to the law; yet a Bodhisattva Dharma Master may deviate from these standard forms.
Indeed. O sons of the Buddha, you should constantly teach and transform others, giving rise to a heart of great compassion.

When entering the homes of wealthy patrons or among all the assembled multitudes, you must not stand while preaching the Dharma to laypeople. You should sit upon a high seat in front of the assembly of laypeople.
Because he possesses a heart of great compassion, he constantly preaches the Dharma for both the laity and those who have left the home life.
However, when preaching, it must be done in accordance with the Dharma; if it is not so, both the speaker and the listener will incur the fault of treating the Dharma with contempt.
"Noble persons" refers to officials and scholars; "all" refers to the common people. As for "laypeople" (*baiyi*), they traditionally prefer plain clothing, hence this designation.
"One should stand before the assembly" means that one must not stand behind them. "High seat" refers to ascending a high seat to sit.
"Senior seat" refers to being at the head of that assembly. These are all protocols for honoring the Dharma, not signs of personal arrogance.
Alternatively, if it is merely for a temporary instruction, there is no fault in both standing. The Vinaya-mūla states:

If another person is seated on a high seat while one is on a low seat; if another is seated while one is standing; or if another is lying down while one is seated—in all such cases, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
To do so otherwise constitutes an offense; in the case of illness, there is no offense.
The Dharma-preacher bhikṣu must not stand upon the ground while preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly.
