When he preaches the Dharma, the Dharma-preacher shall occupy a high seat and be honored with incense and flowers, while the fourfold assembly of listeners sits on lower seats, as if they were filially obedient toward their parents or reverently following the instructions of a teacher.
Just as with a Brahmin who tends the sacrificial fire, if the one who preaches the Dharma does not preach in accordance with the Dharma, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
The above was spoken generally for laypeople who have not yet received the precepts; now it is spoken specifically for the fourfold assembly, both lay and ordained.
The high seat, incense, and flowers are the weighty dharmas of these four assemblies, for they are honored persons. That the listeners sit on lower seats is their own [duty].
To be humble is the rite of revering one's superiors. It is like being filial and obedient toward one’s parents;
it is to uphold the etiquette of a disciple and show reverence for one’s teacher. It is also like serving the fire-worshipping Brahmins, who were heterodox outsiders with false views from India.
Long ago, at the beginning of this world’s kalpa, a son of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven wished to observe Jambudvīpa.
Gardens, flowing springs, and other such features descend from the heavens; having observed them, they return again to the celestial realm. Their bodily radiance is like fire.
Seeing this from afar, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) outside the grove falsely claim that because worldly people make offerings to fire, they attain rebirth in the heavenly realms.
Consequently, whenever the sun is about to set, they maintain a great bonfire throughout the entire night and prostrate themselves toward it.

Exerting one’s utmost sincerity and paying the highest respect, one performs ritual service toward it. Now, let this serve as a metaphor: reverently following the True Dharma is like that ultimate sincerity with which one respectfully serves fire.
If one does not explain according to the Dharma, it means one has deviated from the proper ritual of preaching;
it does not mean that the explanation of the Dharma is itself unskillful. If one explains what is Dharma as non-Dharma, or explains what is non-Dharma as Dharma, this belongs to the tenth [category].
Six. And the aforementioned inverted and erroneous explanations of the precepts.

When the Brahma King prostrated to the goddess, the Great Brahma Heaven King,

having heard the goddess Radiance of the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel speak of the practice of bodhi, immediately rose from his seat with the assembly of devas and reverently prostrated at the feet of the Wish-Fulfilling Goddess.
Śakra received him at his feet. The jackal—resembling a fox but smaller, with a color like that of a dog, blue-yellow in hue—had made its nest upon a high tree on a precipitous cliff.
Long ago, a certain jackal, pursued by a lion, had fallen into a deep well.
The monk Anxin died and recited a verse on impermanence. Śakra, Lord of the Devas, heard it and, together with the hosts of devas, went to the side of the well and said:
"You did not hear the holy teachings and have long dwelt in darkness; what you have just spoken was extraordinary. We pray that you will proclaim it further."
The jackal said, "O Lord of Devas, you lack instruction and do not recognize the propriety of the occasion. While the Dharma Master remains below, you have placed yourself above him;
you did not first cultivate reverence, yet you asked for the essentials of the Dharma. Thereupon, the Lord of Devas stepped down, prostrated himself, and repented.

He piled celestial jewel robes to form a high seat and requested that the Dharma Master preach the essentials of the Dharma. Furthermore, he received from him the precepts of the ten wholesome actions.
The Mountain Deity Invites Master Huayan to Suí Chándìng Sī Temple. The monk Huìwù was a native of Jīngzhào. He once lived in seclusion with another monk on Mount Zhōngnán.
Huìwù received and upheld the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, while his companion recited the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Both subsisted on wild fruits and dwelt among the crags, each devoted to his own practice.
Suddenly, a man arrived to invite them to his residence for a vegetarian feast. The two monks deferred to one another, and [the host] invited...
Someone said, "Please invite the Master of the Avatamsaka Sūtra. Dao-wu went along with him; it turned out he was a mountain deity.
They further invited five hundred arhats, all of whom deferred to Dao-wu as their presiding elder.
*Pattra* (鉢吒) is here translated as "plain strip" (*man-tiao*). It is a large cotton cloth, equal in measurement to the *kāṣāya*, consisting of a single piece.

Novice monastics (*śrāmaṇera*) are required to dye it to a discolored hue (*kṣānti-varṇa*) before wearing it. The *Ekottara-karman* states: "For those who follow the path of the *śramaṇera*, the plain strip is their garment.
To wear the five-strip robe [instead] is a grave offense of confusion. This is the case in the land of China (*Śin-chou*).
For a long time this custom has been propagated; it constitutes an unrighteous practice. Do not allow [such garments] to be worn.
*Wen* (紊) means to confuse or disorder.
*Wa* (窊) is pronounced like *wa*; it means low or sunken.
Emperor Wu of the Zhou entered hell. Emperor Wu of the Zhou suppressed Buddhism; before even a year had passed, pestilential vapors steamed from within him and sores broke out externally on his body.
When these evil signs appeared, he was filled with remorse but had no recourse. He secluded himself in the Yunyang Palace, where he passed away seven days later.
According to the *Mingbao ji* (Records of Miraculous Retribution) by Tang Lin, Minister of Personnel of the Great Tang, it states: "My maternal grandfather was the Left... [text fragment].
The Vice President, Duke Qi, personally heard Emperor Wen inquire about a deceased person who had returned to life. He said: "When I first died, I saw Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou, who said to me:
'Go and inform the Son of Heaven of the Great Sui on my behalf. Formerly, we shared food, granaries, treasuries, jade, and silk.
Now that I have caused the destruction of the Buddha-dharma, I am undergoing extreme suffering. You should perform meritorious deeds for my sake.'"
Emperor Wen subsequently issued an edict to all people under heaven, each to contribute one coin to perform meritorious rites on behalf of the deceased.
Furthermore, in the eighth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Du Qi of Jingzhao died and revived after three days, saying that he had seen King Yama.
The King asked him, "Do you know Zhou Wu? He replied, "I once served as a judicial official in the Left Imperial Guard; I know him very well. The King then ordered an official to lead [Du Qi] away.
He arrived at an iron house. Through an iron window, he saw Emperor Wu’s body, which was extremely emaciated and had turned the color of iron; he was wearing an iron collar and shackles.
Weeping, the Emperor said, "Great Master, what karmic offenses have I committed to undergo such suffering and distress?

The Master replied, "Because I believed the words of Wei Yuansong, I defamed and abolished the Buddha-dharma; therefore, I undergo this suffering. He then entreated him, saying, "Why not cite and quote [the scriptures] against Yuansong?"
Sung arrived. The Emperor said, "I once annotated it. However, officials have searched everywhere throughout the three realms and have not found it.
If he comes this morning, I shall be liberated by evening. You must go back and tell the people of the world to perform meritorious deeds for Yuan Sung so that he may come early to save me.
If he does not arrive, there will be no hope for my liberation. Pray for my recovery and use this matter of the underworld to exhort them."
Regarding the account of Zhu Zuofu: Yuansong was a native of Yizhou. He left home to become a monk in his youth; he was exceptionally intelligent yet lacked a peer.
He feigned madness and wandered aimlessly, composing verses upon whatever he encountered. He traveled extensively for over ten years, such that no one could fathom him.
A prostration to the Celestial Honored One. During the Tang dynasty, there was a monk named Baoqiong of Fushou Monastery in Yizhou. His secular surname was Ma.
He entered the monastic order in his youth and made it his constant practice to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* once every two days.
Those who heard of this from afar all came to revere him. Once, he encountered a Daoist master holding a religious assembly for the common people and was invited to attend; Baoqiong went there.
He did not prostrate himself and sat down. The assembly of Daoist followers all said, "He does not pay homage to the Celestial Honored One; does he slight our ancestral dharma?
Sengqiong said, "The heterodox and the orthodox differ in their paths, and what each serves is distinct. Since one does not even pay homage to Heaven, how much less to the Lord Lao?

The assembly’s discussion became tumultuous, and they began to treat him with contempt and derision. Sengqiong said, "My failure to prostrate was because it was not where I ought to prostrate; I feared only bringing disgrace upon my ancestors. He then performed his prostrations.
He prostrated once; the statue of the Way and its pedestal shook all at once. He prostrated another time; together with the pedestal, it toppled over and fell to the ground, shattered and destroyed.
The Daoists were ashamed and cried out that it was the work of a wind-spirit. They vied with one another to come and right it, and he prostrated yet again.

The situation was reversed. Huiqiong said, "The sky is clear and the weather is harmoniously pleasant, yet you speak of resenting the wind. Your foolishness and obstinacy mean you do not fathom my wind.

The entire assembly was struck with awe and fear; they single-mindedly prostrated before Huiqiong, all abandoned their Daoist path to take refuge in the Buddha, and requested that Huiqiong confer upon them the Bodhisattva precepts.
*Ci* (pronounced *shì*) in the first tone means a shrine (*miào*). It also means to sacrifice. This refers to performing sacrifices to Heaven, the ancestral temple, and the spirits and deities.

The *Ghost Questions Maudgalyāyana Sūtra* states: A ghost asked, "Since my birth until now, I have at times ascended the mountain of knives and the tree of swords in hell, and at other times fallen into the fire pit or the boiling cauldron in hell; I have suffered all manner of pains without any respite."
[He] sighed. "By what offense was this brought about? Maudgalyāyana replied, "When you were a human being, you served as the master of a celestial shrine.
You slaughtered the three sacrificial animals to offer them to the heavenly deities, sprinkling their blood and flesh in the four directions.

You spoke to the multitude, saying, 'Through your sacrifices, you shall obtain great prosperity and good fortune. By uttering such demonic and heterodox words, you acted as a teacher of calamity. You slighted..."
They deceive the common people and mislead their parents; for this reason, they ultimately enter hell.
The Tathāgata of the Three Virtues enters nirvana, yet he is fundamentally endowed with the three virtues—namely, the secret treasury of the three: Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti.
Regarding the factors of the four dhyānas: the first dhyāna has five factors: first, the factor of applied thought (*vitarka*); second, the factor of sustained thought (*vicāra*);

third, the factor of joy (*prīti*); fourth, the factor of bliss (*sukha*); and fifth, the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). The second dhyāna has four factors: first, the factor of internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*); second, the factor of joy; and third, the factor of bliss.

The fourth dhyāna has one factor: the factor of single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*). The third dhyāna has five factors: first, the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā*); second, the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*);

third, the factor of wisdom (*prajñā*); fourth, the factor of bliss (*sukha*); and fifth, the factor of single-mindedness. The fourth dhyāna has four factors: first, the factor of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*);

second, the factor of equanimity; third, the factor of mindfulness; and fourth, the factor of single-mindedness. These four dhyānas together comprise eighteen factors, though those factors that do not recur are not counted twice. As for...
The Sūtra clarifies:
those with the five outflows (āsrava) cannot become Brahmā Devarāja; they cannot become Śakra;
they cannot become Māra; they cannot become a Cakravartin King; and they cannot become a Buddha.
*Gǔ* (pronounced like *gǔ*) refers to the paper mulberry (*broussonetia*), the bark of which can be made into paper.
*Huà* (pronounced like *huà*) refers to the *bhūrja* leaf—here translated as "shore-like shape"—which resembles the *tāla* palm; it is straight and tall, with long and broad leaves.
The color was glossy; it was used for writing.
*He-ti* (literally "ancient hoof")—this is the name of the paper.
When the parrot heard the Four Noble Truths, there were two parrots in the house of the elder Sudatta: one was named Lü... [text fragment].

The second was named Śalati. When the Venerable Ānanda went to the house of the elder, he preached the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—to the bird.
Having heard the Dharma, the bird rejoiced and recited it. While staying overnight in a tree, it was eaten by a wild cat.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, it was reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, and subsequently, through successive births, it reached the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations.

"O Deva, in this manner he was reborn seven times among the gods of the six heavens of desire, and subsequently was born among human beings, where he left the household life and became a Pratyekabuddha.
Regarding the monkey offering honey: once, when the Buddha was sitting in a forest with his bhikṣus, there was a monkey."

He immediately took the Buddha’s bowl, climbed a tree, filled it to the brim with honey, and offered it to the Buddha. The Buddha accepted it and distributed it among the assembly of monks until everyone had received their share.
The monkey was filled with joy; he leaped and danced about, but fell into a pit and died.
He was then reborn in the household of the elder Śreṣṭhin, endowed with a handsome and upright appearance. He left the household life and became an arhat, named Madhupradāna (Honey-Offerrer).
Elder, there was once a bhikṣu reciting a sūtra in a forest; his voice was harmonious and elegant.
At that time, a bird heard the Dharma and conceived a sense of reverence and affection. It perched upon a tree to listen to him, but was struck by a hunter with an arrow.

When his life ended, by virtue of these roots of goodness, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Immediately taking celestial incense and flowers, he went to where the bhikṣu was and made offerings with reverence.
The bhikṣu then preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The Geese Hear the Dharma: Long ago, when the Buddha was in a forest grove in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, he was preaching the Dharma for the sake of humans and devas.
At that time, there was a flock of five hundred geese in the sky who, upon hearing the Buddha’s voice, felt deep affection and joy.
They circled and descended, but a hunter spread his nets and killed them; they were all reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and have now come from that celestial realm.
They descended and offered flowers to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained the first fruit of enlightenment (*srotāpanna*).

As for the fish in the pond who heard the verses: countless eons ago, when Śākyamuni Tathāgata was the son of a wealthy merchant named Flowing Water (*Jalavāhana*), he was in a pond in a desolate marsh and, for the sake of ten thousand fish, recited the name of Ratnaśikhin Tathāgata and preached the Dharma.
According to the verses on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, after ten thousand fish had simultaneously passed away during the latter part of the night,

they were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. When the Tathāgata attained enlightenment and first turned the Wheel of Dharma, they descended from heaven to hear the teaching and all together attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
The sea whale is known by the Sanskrit name *makara*, which here is translated as "whale-fish.
It is a great fish of the ocean, with a body length ranging from three hundred to seven hundred *yojanas*. When it encounters a ship, it is capable of swallowing it whole.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants who had set out upon the sea in a vessel to retrieve treasures; they encountered the whale opening its mouth above the water.
The current rushed forward as if entering a great pit. The boatman said, "We are all going to die. The merchants each prayed to their respective deities, but to no avail.
Among them was a lay devotee (upāsaka) who addressed the crowd, saying, "The Buddha is the compassionate father of all sentient beings."

"Let us join our efforts and together cry out, 'Namo Buddha'! The multitude then chanted it with one voice. Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, the fish immediately closed its mouth, and the multitude was thus delivered from the peril.
Regarding the dog afflicted by poison: Once there was a dog that stole food from a merchant and ate it. The merchant immediately cut off its four paws and cast it into a pit.
It could neither find life nor find death. Śāriputra, observing this with his divine eye, filled his alms bowl with rice and flew to where the dog was.
He used the rice to extinguish the fire of the dog’s hunger and then preached the Three Seals of the Dharma for it.
He said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all dharmas are without self; nirvana is quiescent extinction.
You should now, in my presence, give rise to a pure mind. Having cast off this body of an animal, you shall be reborn in a fortunate realm.
Long ago, there was a great venomous snake in the mountains that was scorched by fire, its skin charred and its flesh rotting. Śāriputra also went there to preach the Dharma for it.
Regarding the three Dharma seals: the latter two were both born into the families of wealthy elders and left the household life as disciples of Śāriputra;
both attained the fruit of arhatship.
Hearing the Title of the Sutra in Hell: Once, a man died a violent death and entered hell.
The hell-warden impaled him with an iron fork and thrust him into a cauldron of boiling oil. He immediately cried out, "Namo to the Great Vaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra.
At that moment, the cauldron of boiling oil transformed into a lotus pond, and all who heard [the title] were delivered from hell.
*Gāthā* is translated here as "verse. These are verses spoken by the Buddha that possess great supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), capable of benefiting both oneself and others.
The verse says: "The worldly pleasures of the five desires, or even the joys of the various heavens—compared to the bliss of the exhaustion of craving, they do not equal even a thousandth part.
From accumulation (*saṃskāra*) suffering arises; from suffering, accumulation arises again. The Eightfold Noble Path can transcend them."
One reaches the most sublime state of Nirvana. It is said that those who practice generosity will certainly obtain its benefit;
if one gives for the sake of happiness, one will certainly attain peace and joy in the future.
In the distant past, countless eons ago, there was a Tathāgata named Most Victorious (Jinvarāja).
He dwelt within mountain forests, practicing the path of the rishis and attaining the five supernormal powers.
Constantly exercising a mind of loving-kindness, he would travel to cities and villages to seek out teachers of the Dharma everywhere for the sake of hearing the teachings. At that time, there was...

A celestial Mara came and said to the seer, "I have a verse. If you can flay your skin to serve as paper, draw blood for ink, and split your bones to serve as pens, and then write down this verse, I shall recite it to you. Having heard this, the seer thought to himself:
"I have suffered through immeasurable kalpas without any benefit whatsoever. Now I shall cast off this insubstantial body to easily obtain the sublime Dharma.
With great joy and exultation, he immediately used a sharp blade to flay his skin, pierce his flesh for blood, and break his bones.
With palms joined toward the heavens, he requested that the Buddha’s verses be spoken. When Māra saw this, he became sorrowful and anxious, and immediately vanished.
The rishi then said, "For the sake of seeking the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, I do not spare my own body or life; my sincerity is not in vain.
If there is one in another world who possesses great compassion and is able to preach the Dharma, may they appear before me. At that time, two [beings] departed from here to the east.

In the twelfth land, there was a buddha-field named Universal Stainless. There dwelt a buddha named King of Pure Fame who suddenly appeared before him and emitted a great radiance that illuminated the body of the rishi. His suffering was immediately dispelled, and he was restored to his former state.
The buddha then extensively expounded for him the *Sarvapuṇyasamuccaya-samādhi-sūtra*. Upon hearing this Dharma, the rishi attained unimpeded eloquence.
He then extensively expounded the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, causing immeasurable beings to abide in the path of the Three Vehicles.
After a thousand years had passed, his life came to an end, and he was reborn in the land of Universal Purity of King Pure Name Buddha, due to his reverence for the Dharma.
"Now he has attained Buddhahood.
Regarding the fruit of theft: once, there was a man who climbed a tree to steal its fruit. Just then, a king and a brahmin arrived at the foot of the tree.
The man was terrified and cowed; he could not remain at ease. At that time, the king sat in meditative composure, while the brahmin...
Candapradyota established his resolve and preached the Dharma for the king. The man immediately descended from the tree and said, "I have committed a transgression by stealing these fruits;
yet Your Majesty neither shows me respect nor does this brahmin acknowledge his own insignificance—both of us act contrary to the Dharma.
Now that I too am found innocent," he prostrated himself and departed.
The Celestial Honored One (Tianzun) Buddha is the God among Gods and the Sage among Sages; therefore, in ancient translations, the Buddha was rendered as "Celestial Honored One.

Later, Daoists usurped the name "Celestial Honored One" and adopted it as a title for Laozi. Consequently, later scriptures revised the translation to "World-Honored One" (Shizun), signifying that he is the honored one within both the heavens and the world.

Regarding the "Dharma of the Place of Repentance": in the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the place is the sequential third contemplation; in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), the place is the wondrous [contemplation].

As for "Dharma," it refers to the ritual procedure (*dharmakarma*), meaning that body and speech rely upon the Dharma to grasp the signs (*nimitta*). This takes the manifestation of the signs as the deadline;
once the non-arising [of phenomena] is realized, both sin and merit have no master.

Regarding the forty-first section on the six natures within the precepts: the six kinds of natures pertain to the fifty-two stages of the Bodhisattva in the Separate Teaching (*pratyekadeśanā*), which involve sequential cultivation.
The seven kinds of jewel wheels pertain to the stages of the Bodhisattva in the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇadeśanā*).
The rest is as clarified in the aforementioned four teachings.
